speechtext:

subsubtopic: CALL FOR CHANGES WITHIN PENITENTIARY SYSTEM-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on an urgent and serious matter, under Standing Order 43, dealing with the lack of safety within our penitentiary system. My motion, therefore, does not require a lengthy preamble as members are well aware of the necessity to improve the system in this regard, as underlined once again in the recent tragic events at Millhaven and Collins Bay penitentiaries. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Huron-Middlesex (Mr. McKinley):
That this House instruct the Solicitor General to implement forthwith measures dealing with changes related to the safety within the Canadian penitentiary system as outlined in the parliamentary subcommittee report on the penitentiary system in Canada, currently collecting dust and, further, introduce legislation outlining a return to capital punishment for first degree, premeditated murders.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that Treasury Board is currently deliberating next year's budget for the Canadian search and rescue service, and recognizing that 60 per cent of search and rescue incidents during 1977 occurred on Canada's Pacific coast, whereas only 30 per cent of the search and rescue vessels operate on the west coast, and because the 1978-79 search and rescue plan does not significantly alter this disproportionate situation, thereby putting the lives of west coast seafarers at risk, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro):
That the government move immediately to distribute the resources of the search and rescue program in a more equitable fashion, bearing in mind the disproportionately larger number of rescue calls on the west coast.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF SUBSIDY ON DOMESTICALLY CONSUMED WHEAT-ALLEGED BREACH OF FAITH WITH CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since this is the Prime Minister's day for being helpful in the House, I would like to direct a question to him. Some five years ago the Prime Minister's government made a commitment to the Canadian people, as enshrined in the Two-Price Wheat Act, that wheat used for human consumption in Canada would be subsidized by the government paying the difference between the floor price and the world price. That legislation was to operate for seven years.
Today, on the order paper, there is a bill from the minister in charge of the Wheat Board which will remove that subsidy, thereby adding some $30 a year to the grocery bill of every family in Canada. Does the Prime Minister not consider that this is a breach of faith and that his government is breaking its word to the Canadian people by terminating this commitment two years before it was due to expire?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF SUBSIDY ON DOMESTICALLY CONSUMED WHEAT-ALLEGED BREACH OF FAITH WITH CONSUMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously this is an argument that the hon. member will want to put forward when the bill is debated in the House. We have presented this bill in the expectation that the results would be better, generally, for Canadian farmers and consumers in the long run.
I would remind the hon. member that during this period of seven years there have been many measures, including some adopted just last week, and currently before the House, which have transferred to Canadian consumers-particularly the less favoured ones in our nation-various forms of assistance including indexation of pensions, increased pensions, family allowances, and so on. One cannot discuss this subject in the abstract without looking at the total picture and the general assistance given to those consumers in Canada who need
December 1, 1978

assistance. The government will be very happy to discuss this matter with the hon. member when the bill is called for second reading.

Mr. Speaker, I understand the Scriptures to say that the Lord giveth and the Lord taketh away, but 1 did not know that it applied to the Prime Minister. He is telling us that the government has given us certain legislation to help the less fortunate people in Canada, and this piece of legislation takes it away. It seems to me that that is no argument at all.
Would the Prime Minister tell the House why it is that a subsidy which at the present time amounts to about 3.3 cents per loaf is to be removed, when it is estimated by the Bakery Council of Canada that as a result the increase in the price of bread will be seven cents, plus another five cents for increased energy, labour and transportation costs? It seems to me that for the government to save 3.3 cents per loaf, and for consumers to have to pay seven cents extra per loaf, is not very good economics: it is not carrying out the program to which the government claims it is committed, namely, to hold down inflation at this critical time.

Once again, after the third question from the hon. member, it becomes obvious there is a difference of approach between the two parties on this particular matter. It is a basic difference. The hon. member would like the Canadian government to subsidize everybody who consumes bread: him, me, the poor, the rich, and everybody else. speechtext:

non-utilized and non-traditional species. It really does not make sense.

subsubtopic: MILITARY AIRCRAFT CAUSING DAMAGE TO RESIDENTIAL PROPERTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is to the Minister of National Defence. I have here a copy of a transcript of the November 17 hearing of the People's Food Commission in Alberta which points out that farmers in the Cold Lake, Alberta, area have been troubled with bombs falling from Canadian military aircraft at the nearby base, damaging fields and some farm buildings. speakeroldname: Hon. Barney Danson (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: MILITARY AIRCRAFT CAUSING DAMAGE TO RESIDENTIAL PROPERTIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, certainly all safety precautions are taken. The only accident I am aware of was one practice bomb going through a grain silo, I believe it was, where compensation was offered. It was not a bomb that exploded. In 1974, I believe, there was a crash in a farmer's field. There is aviation training there that is obviously a hazard. But every possible precaution is taken to minimize those dangers.

subsubtopic: MILITARY AIRCRAFT CAUSING DAMAGE TO RESIDENTIAL PROPERTIES
speechtext:
At the same commission hearing, a military officer from the base said:
Mufflers fall off cars-you can't expect perfection when you're attaching bombs to a plane.
Surely the minister and his department can do better than that. Since these planes fly at about 650 miles an hour, at some 250 feet, over farm buildings and farmsteads, can the minister assure the farmers there will be safety precautions taken and that adequate compensation will be paid, as there are some cases where farmers have not been compensated at all for damage caused by bombs or aircraft that crash within 500 feet of a farmer's house?

subsubtopic: MILITARY AIRCRAFT CAUSING DAMAGE TO RESIDENTIAL PROPERTIES
speechtext: Certainly I can give the assurance that every possible safety precaution has been taken. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I can confirm that an agreement was reached with the government of Alberta with respect to discount pricing or incentive pricing of natural gas. That was made clear by my statement and the response of the Premier of Alberta at the first ministers' conference earlier this week. Mr. Speaker, I would refer to my point of order in terms of the right to reserve a question and also as the dilemma of a member who, almost without exception, has to wait three days before gaining recognition. Since this is the second day of rising, I did not really expect to be recognized by you, Mr. Speaker, today. I know, for example, that the hon. member for Burnaby-Seymour (Mr. Raines) has risen on many more days than I have and has not been recognized either. speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is still in the House and I am pleased about that because the question of privilege I want to raise involves him and the answers he gave today to the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). The question of privilege relates to those questions and to an intervention by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) the other day with respect to Cossette-Trudel and Lanctot, and whether or not there had been any contact with the Canadian embassy. At that time there were stories in the newspapers, as the Prime Minister will recall.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Is that a point of order?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
No, a question of privilege.
As the Prime Minister will recall, there were stories in the newspapers. The Secretary of State for External Affairs was asked specifically by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) whether there had been any contact by those two with the Canadian embassy with a view to their return to Canada.
I want to allay any suspicion the Prime Minister may have with respect to this party's position on it. We would be delighted if they would never come back to Canada and would stay away. In any event, the answer given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs was to the effect that there had been no such contact, and I recollect that the minister was quite emphatic with respect to that.
We are now faced with stories in the press, which might or might not be true-I do not know. The purport of the question put by the hon. member for Calgary North today was with respect to the substance to the stories. Also there was a question to the Prime Minister of whether or not there had
December 1, 1978

been any contact with the embassy, as reported in the newspapers only incidentally.
The Prime Minister, by skating around the question, trying to turn it, making it into some form of comic relief with respect to a matter that is quite serious to the Canadian public, has left the impression with the House that he really does not know. His ambassador in France is in town today, I do not know for what purpose, but I think it would be important, if there is a change from the answer given previously by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, that the House be advised of it.
The question really is-and I think the House and the country are entitled to know-whether Cossette-Trudel and Lanctot made contact with the Canadian embassy with respect to their return to Canada and, if so, when, and any other particulars asked by the hon. member, because the position may very well have changed. That was the purport of the question.
Second, and this is a thing that does concern me, I am worried that the Prime Minister-who had such great interest, understandably, at the time of the FLQ incidents in Quebec and the release of Mr. Cross, with respect to negotiating, discussing and perhaps initiating discussions with the provincial government at that time-should be so disinterested now in initiating those discussions.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Order, please. Whether or not the hon. member has an interest in that, it has no basis in procedure. I do not know if the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) wants to take this opportunity to respond, but this is not a procedural point in any way.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD

I agree with Your Honour. It is a complete abuse of procedure. There is no question of privilege involved, and you recognize it, except that the hon. member has now put on the record things which presumably should have come during the question period, since it is a repetition of a question. I can only but answer that question again, lest the impression be gained that the answer has not been given.
A question was asked of me by the hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) yesterday. I believe it was asked of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) a few days before that. We gave a very clear, unequivocal and unambiguous answer: no, there had been no contact between the Canadian government and the Cossette-Trudels, or the embassy and the Cossette-Trudels. There had been no contact with the Quebec government, which was the question asked this morning by the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams). The answer was very clear; there have been none.
I do not know why the hon. member is getting up and saying that somehow we were ambiguous, and that he is puzzled because we had been interested in Mr. Cross' fate in 1970 and we were not following up the goings-on of the Cossette-Trudels, or any of the others who are abroad and who might have
Privilege-Mr. W. Baker
been involved in the FLQ. I do not know why the suggestion was made.
In so far as turning the question, I made very clear to the hon. member for Calgary North, saying that it was the government's responsibility to contact the Quebec government in the whole matter of getting the Cossette-Trudels back to Canada before Christmas-

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: He did not say that.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: I do not say that it is our responsibility. We went over that. The question was very clear.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Don't mislead the House.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: It was very clear. Perhaps he did not ask it the way he intended to ask, but there is no duty on the part of the government to contact either the Quebec authorities or the Cossette-Trudels. We have not done that, and we say that there is no responsibility on our part to do that. The hon. member for Calgary North suggested that there was a responsibility on our part.

Mr. Speaker, 1 see the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is leaving. At no time- I am glad to see the Prime Minister returning. At no time did I make any suggestion, either in the preamble or the question, that my party or myself wanted any of these FLQ people back to Canada.
I suggest to the Prime Minister that he is hiding the facts. He made a deal, sir.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD

The hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) was entitled to the opportunity he just had to straighten the record, because some reference was made to his own intent in the language which he used in his questions. 1 should like him to take a brief opportunity to straighten the record, and that will be the end of this procedural matter.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: Thank you very much for your graciousness. At no time did I suggest, either in my question or my preamble-and the record will show that-that I wanted, or my party wanted them home at any time, whether it was Christmas, New Year's or Thanksgiving. I suggested that it was in the newspaper they were going to be home for Christmas, that there had been discussions with the Canadian embassy in Paris, and that members of the Quebec government made that suggestion, from the newspaper article. 1 wanted to find out from the Prime Minister if that was correct.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD

And he said, no.

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext: He made the deal, his government, to send these people out of the country. Was it in writing or was it verbally? What were the ramifications of that agreement? speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the hon. member has just stated very clearly that I was hiding the facts. I should like him to withdraw that accusation.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. BAKER (GRENVILLE-CARLETON)-ANSWERS GIVEN BY PRIME MINISTER DURING QUESTION PERIOD
speechtext:
The exact language used in terms of hiding facts is one which comes very close to an unparliamentary expression. It is not an expression of deceiving or misleading the House, lying, or anything of that nature, but it comes very close. Again it points out the difficulty that once beginning on a point which is not in fact based on procedure, the subsequent contributions to it become more and more dangerous in terms of the procedures of the House. This is the risk which has arisen.
I wonder if the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) at this time would reconsider the force of the expression he used, or whether he would prefer to reflect on it and examine the record to see himself how it conforms with precedents. It is acceptable to me either way. I simply point out to the House the danger we get into the minute we embark upon a point which, in the first place, did not have a proper basis in procedure.
A question has been raised respecting the propriety of that language. As usual, I think the hon. member ought to have an opportunity, as the Chair will, to examine the record to see whether, on precedent, it is the kind of remark that I must insist upon him withdrawing. The hon. member may want to have the same reflection over the weekend.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext: That this House deplores the double standard applied by the government in deliberately reducing the buying power of Canadian workers and families while allowing an increase in the interest rates which will result in higher revenues for financial institutions, an increase in the inflation rate, as well as a heavier public debt.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext: The House should note that proceedings on this motion expire pursuant to Standing Order 58(11).

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to move a motion which will be of great interest, I am sure, to the House and to all hon. members, and which reads as follows:
That this House deplores the double standard applied by the government in deliberately reducing the buying power of Canadian workers and families while allowing an increase in the interest rates which will result in higher revenues for financial institutions, an increase in the inflation rate, as well as a heavier public debt.
Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity not to criticize the government in particular but to denounce once again our vicious and antisocial fiscal system which gives priority to money capital over human capital. That system runs counter to the philosophy of the Social Credit Party of Canada according to which the wealth of Canada should be put at the service of all the people in Canada and not in the hands of a few profiteers who thus central the life of every citizen by ever

December 1, 1978
Economic Policy
widening the gap between the poor and the rich. In a logical system, in a word, money must serve mankind rather than mankind be at the service of money, as we find today. In the face of such an aberration, Mr. Speaker, how could we possibly remain silent and passive? Yet, many others have denounced before us this situation where a few men at the head of large financial monopolies enslave 98 per cent of a working population which is running more and more into debt, poorer and poorer, while this monetary power is getting stronger and stronger.
The government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) in particular could cry out every day that we must get more into debt, that we must borrow more and more to get richer, they will not convince us, Mr. Speaker, that today debts are beneficial. I do not believe that everybody has become that mad. The one who takes the cake this week is the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien): I heard him challenge personally the Quebec representatives saying they should increase their deficit. Your deficit is not high enough, he said, it should be increased. That is the ultimate in stupidity, Mr. Speaker. Still, there is wisdom in his madness, for he knows that the more one goes into debt, the more of one's freedom is given up to one's creditor; and that is probably how he hopes that some day Quebec will be dependent on the central government, by reducing constantly its obligations towards the provinces while hanging on jealously to its right of taxation. The government keeps on increasing its revenue while stripping the provinces more and more, of their wealth. The government therefore does the same dirty work as the big financial monopolies do with the population.
Some may say that in the last few years we have made progress socially and even economically, Mr. Speaker. As far as we are concerned, there is only a semblance of progress since in fact we are taking away from those who could lead a comfortable life to help the neighbours who have nothing, either because they can no longer work or because they have been robbed, literally, of everything by loan institutions whose rates of interest are exorbitant.
Today the government tries to apply a few of the reforms we have been advocating for 30 years, but by taxing the workers even more, while overlooking big business, monopolies, those who really have the power in this country since the governments are only their lackeys. As I said a few weeks ago, the national budget is paid for by 75 per cent by the workers while the big financial trusts, including the chartered banks, finance barely 25 per cent of it though they rake in the wealth of the country.
If the country's wealth were distributed equitably in Canada, that is if the revenue were distributed fairly among all Canadians instead of going to about a dozen profiteers, we would be able to pay old age pensions, family allowances and the guaranteed annual income to all those who are entitled to them without having to tax the other workers for the money to

pay those benefits since the country makes over $40 billion in additional new production each year.
The Prime Minister tells us, Mr. Speaker, that there are only two ways to run a country: taxes and borrowings. But what about the $40 billion surpluses we have every year and the people's savings? He lets the big financiers take the largest part of the pie, while the government taxes the taxpayers and borrows money.
Let us have a look at the statistics for July. Those who want information need only to examine the statistics for July 1978. As for the amount I referred to earlier of a $40 billion surplus on new production, we find in the statistics an amount of $207.63 billion for the gross national product in Canada, whereas our gross national income, that is our expenses, amounts to only $163,663 billion, that is a $43.4 billion surplus over the country's total spending. Is it not true that with $40 billion we could easily undertake the social reforms proposed by our party, the Social Credit Party of Canada? We cannot under the present system because these $40 billion are monetized by the private banks which siphon everything right out of the financial monopoly, to the detriment of Canadian workers who are responsible for this new production. They are the ones who create these new products, yet only about ten multimillionaires profit from this production, while the people are clamouring, unemployed, and up to their neck in debt.
That is why this crazy system will only lead to one thing, a worsening of the workers' condition, because the more they work the more they increase the financial power of the large monopolies.
This double standard maintained by the government will help large corporations fatten their profits. Someone asked me the other day: But how are we going to stop our debts from increasing? The answer was: The only thing to do in this crazy system is to stop working because the more you produce, the more you get into debt, because you are forced to borrow for your own production. The impact of this attitude is felt not only at the individual level, Mr. Speaker, but also at the family level.
Since 1965, the unevenness of income distribution among Canadian families has been getting worse. This gap is generally said to be due to the very structure of the system. It is true that several behaviour changes in people have increased the number of women in the working place and the number of double income families. The ratio of single people has gone up significantly from 21 per cent in 1965 to 28 per cent in 1975. That of childless couples rose from 21 per cent up to 25 per cent whereas the percentage of families including more than six persons dropped dramatically from 15 per cent down to 7 per cent.
When relating that phenomenon to the gradual deterioration of the purchasing power of Canadian consumers, we can easily
December 1, 1978

understand why people alter their social habits. Also we can presume that women who are not the breadwinner in the family are interested in working because they want to earn an additional income and thus improve the standard of living of the family. Women decide to work not because they are attracted by the labour market as such, especially since it is often pointed out that there is discrimination between men and women as far as income is concerned.
At present, females earn annually an average of $5,884 against $12,611 for males. Thus the difference amounts to $6,727 and this scandalous injustice alone should encourage women to stay at home. Generally speaking and for the reasons I mentioned earlier, it appears that most married women who join the labour force do not do so because they choose to but rather out of necessity. They wish and need to increase the family income which in 1978 was not sufficient to provide for a decent life. That is why we keep on fighting and we will keep on fighting for a salary to the mother who wants to stay home. We must make it possible for her to stay with her family.
Mr. Speaker, I have already given this example in the House before, if we accept to pay generously the members of our armed forces, all their expenses, their uniforms, for the protection of our country, are we going to shrink from the obligation to support those women populating our country, giving life to those service men? That is something I cannot understand when we reject the concept of a mother's salary. If anyone is working for the country, I believe they are. Ironically, while single people are facing increasing financial problems forcing them to change their old way of life, the commercial and financial community is thriving on workers' misfortune. In one year, from 1976 to 1977, while the average family income rose by less than 3 per cent, the real purchasing power of Canadian consumers was considerably reduced by a real drop of approximately 5 per cent.
The Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity recently criticized the inability of this government to efficiently control soaring prices while managing on the other hand to efficiently curb salary increases. In fact, this new agency of the Economic Council of Canada blames both the government and the food processing industry for the inflationary situation prevailing in Canada. The profit margin of this industrial sector is 63 per cent per production unit for the first, second, third and fourth quarter of this year. These profits have resulted in an excessive and unwarranted increase of food prices. In their report, those same analysts from the study centre pointed out that such irresponsibility on the part of employers prompted employees of the brewing, packing and processing companies to demand higher wages when bargaining for new collective agreements. Workers consider that their purchasing power has been seriously eroded.
The competitive positions of Canadian businesses on international markets was materially improved by the fall of our
Economic Policy
dollar. We were, of course, in a better position on foreign markets. However, some companies are said to continue raising their prices on products which are now competitive in order to counteract the support prices on foreign products. This petty attitude of the established industry in Canada is not sensible because in spite of temporarily larger profits, its mid-term consequence will be to jeopardize considerably the competitive advantage gained at such a cost, at the expense of consumers. In fact the spiralling inflation which has been created by the industrial selfishness of corporate leaders will inevitably reduce our favourable position on world markets, achieved as it was through unconditional exploitation of small wage earners. The Prime Minister of Canada has even expressed his intention of going back to mandatory wage and price controls should that ever become necessary in the next few months.
But on a short and mid-term basis, the policy of the government will not be changed. It still aims at making the small earner pay for the consistent ineptitude of the government in economic matters. Mr. Speaker, there is nothing new here and this attitude has been demonstrated clearly during the ten years of political domination by the Prime Minister in opposition to the prevailing attitude of industrial and economic circles. The research centre warns the industry against any position likely to affect the national interest. According to them the industry must prove its good faith and show some social conscience by voluntarily reducing its prices on Canadian products. If the present trend continues, we could see a new surge of prices, particularly food prices. This shows a double standard which has been used by the government in the following manner: on the one hand the purchasing power of the workers has been deliberately reduced through a series of social and economic discriminatory measures, including the Anti-Inflation Act which controlled rising salaries, several amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act in a few years, and changes in old age security and family allowances which have been made to reallocate the funds saved on these programs and taken off old people's pensions and family allowances payments to be transferred to industry.
Have we not done enough for big business without providing them with further incentives at the expense of our children and old people? Even in the last budget, the Minister of Finance made several concessions and granted several advantages to big Canadian and foreign entrepreneurs, and that despite the egotistic and at times anti-social behaviour of those same companies towards the average taxpayer. We have reached a point where in the future companies must assume their responsibilities towards Canadians, or least must not hamper the productive efforts of the workers. In order to do so they will have to reduce their profit margin and tighten their belts, in their turn, for the same reasons as salaried Canadians. The report of the Centre for the Study of Inflation and Productivity illustrates perfectly the questionable objectives of big busi-

December 1, 1978
Economic Policy
ness which exploits our resources and our work, and reaps the greater of part of the benefits at our expense. The experience of the last ten years shows full well where the interests of our governments be when they have to choose between guaranteeing the interests of the workers or those of the industry.
Repeatedly, the government has chosen to listen to the recommendations of industry and big business, instead or showing concern for the fears and claims expressed by groups of citizens and consumers. Besides, when it made cuts in the budget last August the government proved clearly that it intends to reduce to a great extent the help it has been granting various consumer groups. The government took away hundreds of millions of dollars from family allowances, depriving thousands of children of their cheques, just as it slashed into unemployment insurance benefits. Why did the government not cut interest rates, which are the primary cause of inflation and the troubles befalling the workers? Double standard always, Mr. Speaker.
Let us now consider the constant increases in interest rates and their impact on the Canadian economy. The 1967 revision of the Bank Act gave rise to several controversies in the House. The Social Credit Party of Canada had necessarily taken part in that important debate which was quite lively. 1 know something about it, as 1 was personally involved. One of the provisions of the bill which had then caught my attention was the removal of the ceiling on interest rates. Such a step, it was suggested, would make chartered banks more competitive with one another and with other financial institutions. Dealing with this matter, I had suggested that the ceiling should be maintained at 6 per cent and if some assistance was to be provided to contractors, small businessmen, consumers and small industrialists, a ceiling on interests was essential. Well, I should add that my suggestion was to no avail. It was overlooked along with many others by the Department of Finance. Today with a rate fluctuating around 11.5 per cent, my suggestion seems more than ever appropriate.
Before proceeding further on the subject of interest rates, let us dwell a little longer on the banking reform. I was not the only one who participated in that debate, even the Minister of Finance did. The minister, who at that time was the parliamentary secretary to the then minister of finance, made a speech on July 6, 1966, in which he said, and 1 quote:
This decennial revision will certainly be welcomed by the newspapers and the public as the most radical measure since the institution of the Bank of Canada about 30 years ago. It will likely increase the confidence of the public in our banking institutions and in any future decisions of the government concerning the monetary policy of our country.
A few moments ago, I heard the Prime Minister say almost the same thing about foreign banks which will come to Canada to compete with our banks. But there never was and never will be any competition in banking; it is a perfect monopoly, and the government makes fun of us saying: competition is good indeed. Oh, come on. The least one can say is that in those days the minister was overly optimistic. He had no doubt

decided to ignore the old saying that no one is a prophet in his own country. The predictions that he made some twelve years ago never came close to come true. After a succession of increases in the interest rate, we may well wonder whether Canadians should trust this government's monetary decisions. As a matter of fact, at the time of that review, I had warned the government in committee that if it removed the ceiling on interest rates, Canada would be faced with its highest rate of inflation ever. Well, we are faced with this inflation rate right now and we will be stuck with it as long as the Canadian dollar keeps floating and there is no ceiling on interest rates.
1 intend therefore to consider briefly the impact on the Canadian economy of these constant increases in the interest rate. We shall see that such a monetary policy is undermining any confidence Canadians may have in their economy and, what is more, is detrimental to our economy. As to the minister's prediction that the Canadian people have more confidence in their banking institutions, other members who will speak after me will deal with it.
I shall deal now with the effect of regular increases in the interest rates. Up until 1967, the interest rates officially charged by chartered banks would not exceed 6 per cent. I say officially, for banks always found a way to charge more. They always came up with unsuspected tricks. But let's not go into it. When later on that ceiling was removed and the over-all bank reform took place, greater competition was to follow as was already mentioned. Moreover, they were intended to avoid further increases in the interest rates and to stimulate banking activities. There was therefore an attempt to strike a balance between banks and other financial institutions. Ten years later we find that we have gone from an extreme to another. From a ceiling rate of 6 per cent which, at the time had apparently a restraining effect on the banks, interest rates today have reached 11 per cent and even 12 per cent in certain banks.

Somebody on the other side said that there is no hurry. We, on this side, are in no hurry either. While successive increases in the interest rate have allowed the banks to make tremendous profits, their impact has been a totally different nature on the economy. Let us examine step by step the various effects of rising interest rates on our
December 1, 1978

economy. Generally speaking, they have resulted in an economic slowdown. How has it come about?
When the cost of loans climbs, it follows that the cost of investment increases accordingly. In fact all businesses, large and small alike, get their money supply from the banks to support their expansion. Large businesses can choose to borrow at higher rates to meet their financial needs and to pass the cost on to consumers through their products, thus creating an inflationary pressure. As for small and medium businesses, they will probably decide to postpone their expansion plans, thus depriving many persons from jobs that are so vital to our economy and increasing unemployment. The Conference Board in Canada had predicted for the year 1979 a 5 per cent increase in the investment at the level of business and equipment. However, such an increase was dependent upon stationary interest rates. These figures are outdated and hope for economic revival is vanishing.
And what about the housing sector? In the building, office and apartment construction industry the excessively high interest rates makes this kind of investment less attractive to contractors. But for an individual the purchase of a house, because of higher mortgage rates, becomes more often than otherwise a dream. As a result, there is stagnation in that area of the economy. Jobs that could have been created are not. It is worth noting that for the three-month period ending September 30, the number of anticipated housing starts in Canada stood at 217,000 compared with 249,000 last year, and according again to the Conference Board in Canada, an improvement in this area is not about to happen, at least for the moment.
We have been asking for many years that owners of single family homes be given the same justice as owners of apartment buildings. That seems to me easy to understand. An owner who builds houses for rental does not even use his money. His money is lent at 10 per cent or 10.5 per cent and he leaves it there because he would suffer a loss. He borrows the money and he is sure of being able to deduct from his income tax two-thirds of the interest on that borrowed money. Whether he borrows the money at 9 per cent, basically the money is costing him 3 per cent because he can deduct 6 per cent from his income tax. The same thing goes for somebody who builds-yes, it is true, I know something about it because I have built houses. He can write off two-thirds of the interest on his mortgage. He can deduct two-thirds of his municipal taxes, two-thirds of his school taxes. He can deduct the maintenance of that house. He can deduct the depreciation, 10 per cent or 15 per cent, on that same house.

I am told a 10 per cent depreciation every year. But that is fantastic. I made inquiries. 1 know people who build projects worth millions of dollars since they
Economic Policy
do not have to use a single cent of their money-they are right. Taxes pay all the expenses of their houses. They only have to collect the rents. You do not have to be a millionaire to build a one million dollar apartment building today, you have to be a financier. They call them financiers. I am not against the advantages they get-no, we need them-but 1 want the head of a family to get the same advantages for his single family home. It has been suggested that the owner of multiple unit dwellings builds for other people. I would like to tell something to the House. The head of the household also builds for others. He builds for his wife, he builds for his children, and he must therefore be entitled to the same deductions; he must be entitled to deduct the interest on his mortgage on his income tax return.
Recently I heard a member of the Progressive Conservative party talk about this, and I was pleased to hear him because it means that a party will finally take a position on this issue. The Liberal party has never done so. For the last 20 years, we have been asking for justice for the owners of single-unit dwellings so that the head of the household can be entitled to deduct the interest on his mortgage, as well as municipal taxes, school taxes, maintenance and devaluation. It is very simple. This is quite fair. What we ask is not so fantastic; simply that the head of the household be treated the same way as the financier who had the money to build large rental projects. It is very simple, but the strong have always been favoured while the weak have been left to fend for themselves. If they cannot pay their taxes, their house will be sold to make up the money of their taxes. Let us look at what happens. A big developer builds rental housing and the government endorses him so that the loan company will not lose one cent. The government stays behind him and says: Go ahead and lend money, we will protect you. The government would never do this for the head of a household. This is why our laws are anti-social.
When we start looking at our statutes, as I have already said in this House, we can see that 75 per cent of them are anti-social, and I can prove this any time. Everything we do is based on financial resources, but there is never any mention about what should be our main consideration, that is human resources. However, the main objective of the Social Credit party of Canada is to see human resources triumph over financial resources. As long as we cannot do this, Mr. Speaker, we cannot tell ourselves that we have a healthy economy or that there is peace in Canada*and that Canadians are happy. You could say that today everyone is committed to finance and has to produce for the benefit of finance. If someone is not useful to financial interest, he is left behind.
Well, Mr. Speaker, I believe that in this area as in all others, there is need for reform, and I hope that the government, that is the Liberal party, will include in its next electoral program what the Progressive Conservatives have already started to introduce in their policy, even though they have not gone far enough yet.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion placed before the House today by the Social Credit party refers to interest rates, inflation, and the burden of the public debt of Canada. I would like to deal in the opening part of my remarks with the subject of the net public debt.
Critics of the government, in fact of any government, are always quick to criticize the size of the public debt and the annual charges arising from that debt as an example, in their minds usually, of poor financial management. It is important to keep the extent of the public debt in its proper perspective.
If we look at net debt, which is arrived at by deducting from gross public debt the return on the interest component of government revenues, the amount in our case is in the area of $40 billion.
Taken as a percentage of gross national expenditure, commonly referred to as g.n.e., the net debt works out to about
19.3	per cent. It is interesting to note that in 1962, and I hope members opposite are listening, when we last had a Conservative government, Canada's net debt was equal at the time to
33.4	per cent of g.n.e. As I mentioned, the figure today under a Liberal administration is 19.3 per cent.
The percentage of g.n.e. required to meet public debt charges this year is estimated at 1.3, the same level as in 1962. The figures also show that public debt on both the net and gross basis has escalated sharply in the last four years. This has been the result, in substantial part, of the economy operating at below average levels of activity, something that has been an international phenomenon. The government has been compelled to incur larger deficits to offset in part this slowdown.
Moving next to the subject of inflation, there is, quite understandably, continuing concern in Canada and in other industrialized countries of the world about inflation. It is clear that, no matter what kind of figures are used, Canada has had striking success in turning the inflationary trend around during these past few years.
In his budget speech two weeks ago, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) said that he expects the consumer price index next year will average 6'/2 per cent above the level of this year, and that year over year increases between the current fourth quarter and the fourth quarter of 1979 will indeed be under 6 per cent. That was highly encouraging news for our Canadian economy.

It is worth while reviewing the factors that have contributed most significantly to Canada's most recent high rates of inflation. In the long run, inflation is primarily a monetary phenomenon. Increases in the rate of growth in the money supply will eventually lead to corresponding increases in the rate of inflation. In the short and medium term, however, increases in the money supply do not translate into proportional increases in the rate of inflation. Nor do decreases in the money supply necessarily imply proportional reductions in the rate of inflation. Because of this, trade-offs between inflation and unemployment will exist in both the short and medium terms.
The short-term relationship between the unemployment rate and changes in wages depends fundamentally on the flexibility of real and money wages. There appears to be a fairly high degree of inflexibility of wage change to changes in unemployment.
For many goods and services labour costs make up the largest part of total production costs and are the primary determinate of prices. Even in these cases, however, the relationship between labour costs and prices may be unstable and may change in response to other factors. There are, as well, many markets in which prices may be determined independently of wage behaviour. For example, in the case of agricultural products, demand factors and supply constraints may be more important than wage costs in determining ultimate prices. Government charges are also not closely related to underlying labour costs. Increases in the prices of internationally traded commodities or changes in the exchange rate can also lead directly to higher rates of inflation. Price increases stemming from these sources contributed significantly to the higher inflation rates of the 1970s. It is thus possible to have rising rates of inflation for a period of time despite a deceleration in wage increases.
The response of the rate of wage change to changes in the unemployment rate will depend not only on the degree of wage flexibility but also on the speed of adjustment of inflationary expectations to changes in the rate of inflation. It is not possible to state precisely how price expectations are formed. There seems little doubt, however, that they are influenced by past price behaviour. Further, inflation expectations may be influenced by government policy initiatives. In other words, if individuals believe government policies will reduce price increases, they may act as if the rate of inflation were going to fall.
In the period up to 1973 there were a number of domestic factors working toward worsening inflation. These included strong aggregate demand growth, which was partly the result of strongly expansive aggregate demand policies, increasing inflationary expectations, and rising public sector wages. Important changes were also occurring in the labour market. The increasing participation rates of women and youth, the growth in multi-earner families, and the 1971 Unemployment Insurance Act revisions raised the level of the unemployment
December 1, 1978

rate at which inflationary pressures were likely to emerge. These factors combined to generate a momentum leading to inflation rates in the 3 per cent to 5 per cent range. In the absence of the external price shocks of 1973 to 1975, however, the inflation rate would not likely have reached double-digit levels, and most likely could have been contained by less expansive aggregate demand policies.
The major increases in food and energy prices which occurred after 1972 had an immediate and direct impact on the rate of inflation. This led subsequently to higher wage and salary demands, partly because of attempts to maintain real wages and salaries and partly because of expectations of future high rates of inflation. The result was a secondary wage-price spiral and further support for the inflation momentum.
The rate of change of wages and salaries has been declining steadily since 1975, partly because of the anti-inflation program and partly because of high levels of unemployment. Consequently the rate of increase of prices of goods for which domestic wage costs comprise the most important part of total costs has been declining, and significant gains have been made toward restoring Canada's international competitive position.
Figures indicating our position internationally have been put on the record here in this current session on a number of occasions to show that in terms of the seven major countries with which the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and the financial critic of the official opposition were comparing us, we were indeed in first and second place by many important economic indicators. We were not in seventh or eighth place where those hon. members were attempting to place us. In this regard it is very important that those price increases in 1978 which were essentially temporary in nature not be built into Canada's cost structure through fully offsetting wage and salary settlements.
1 would like to move on to the subject of interest rates. An attempt to achieve a short-run reduction in interest rates through highly expansionary monetary policy would likely be of limited effectiveness in the short run and self-defeating in the long run. This is especially true given the importance of international flows of capital into the Canadian market.
It is questionable how far Canadian interest rates could be made to diverge from international tendencies in the short run. In the longer run, as higher money supply growth is reflected in high inflation, the outlook would be for still higher interest rates. We would generally accept the view that the high interest rates are primarily an effect rather than a cause of inflation.
The root of the troubles that the Canadian economy has been experiencing in recent years can be traced back to the problem of inflation, and in particular to the period of intense inflation Canada suffered in the early 1970s. Inflation in Canada peaked in 1975 with prices and wages rising very high in absolute terms, but also rising in a significant way above wages and prices in the United States which was then, and remains today, our main trading partner. This led to a serious impairment of our international competitive position, a large deficit in the current account of the balance of payments and a
Economic Policy
falling off of foreign capital inflows into direct investment in Canada. Such developments inevitably led in turn to a large downward adjustment in the external value of the Canadian dollar.
Canadians have worked hard to extricate themselves from the grip of inflation, but at the same time we want to maintain a moderate rate of growth in the economy. There is no easy way to achieve this. It can only be done over a long period.
We must also focus on monetary policy, which is playing an important role in slowing inflation in Canada. The Bank of Canada for the past three years has been operating within publicly announced guidelines of declining targets for monetary growth. There have been three successive downward revisions in the bank's target range to a current level of 6 per cent to 10 per cent a year. This policy has been acclaimed as what is needed for ensuring a continual gradual reduction in our rate of inflation.
As we are now very close to ending the decontrol period, it is important to set rigid monetary growth rates. In the event that the inflation rate should not decline, monetary policy will come into play to dampen any renewed acceleration of inflation. In such circumstances there is no alternative but to set interest rates high enough to prevent undue monetary expansion, which in turn could only feed still higher rates of inflation. Of course higher rates of inflation cancel out the benefits of the recent exchange rate adjustment on the Canadian dollar and our improved competitive position which is providing fresh stimulus to economic activity in Canada.
The major objectives of our monetary policy are clear and, indeed, impose a financial discipline on the economy and on all Canadians.
On the subject of monetary policy and interest rates I would like to draw attention to a recent speech given in Vancouver by the governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Gerald Bouey. Some of the observations he made in that speech were included in an excellent presentation made by the governor early last month in testimony before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
In my remarks today I would like to include one or two excerpts from the speech of governor Bouey because I think it is important, as we discuss an opposition motion such as the one put forward today and as we react to the kinds of comments that are being directed to us and to the Canadian public by the Leader of the Opposition and by his chief financial critic, that we place on the record, whenever there is an opportunity, the positive kind of news that is coming over and over again, not only from Canadians but from international figures of repute.
One of the things that has been of particular interest to me in the month or two that I have been Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, has been attending sessions at which international bankers and industrialists who have come to Canada for those meetings are praising us for the kinds of policies we have been implementing to cope with the problems

December 1, 1978
Economic Policy
with which we have been faced in recent years. I think that kind of news does not get out of this chamber unless we on this side say it. It will certainly not be said by hon. members opposite who are attempting to convince the Canadian public of the philosophy of gloom and doom which they think might help them and might have been of some small assistance to them in the few by-elections conducted in this country a month or two ago. They feel that kind of thing will be bought by the Canadian public at a major general election. This is indeed not the case.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext:
I would like to come back to my earlier point and read into the record some of the comments made by governor Bouey in his speech earlier this month, made in Vancouver to the Men's Canadian Club of Vancouver. He said in part, the following:
Monetary policy has had an important role to play in the slowing of inflation in Canada. For more than three years the bank has been operating within a framework of publicly announced and gradually declining targets for monetary growth. These targets specify the upper and lower limits of a range within which the bank will endeavour to keep the trend rate of increase of the money supply. The bank's initial target range for monetary growth back in 1975 was from 10 per cent a year to something less than 15 per cent a year. As monetary growth and inflation have slowed over the intervening period, there have been three successive downward successions of the bank's target range to its current level of 6 to 10 per cent a year. The bank had made it clear on numerous occasions that further gradual reductions in its monetary growth targets will be required over future years if monetary policy is to be consistent with the longer-run objective of ensuring a continuing gradual decline in Canada's rate of inflation.
He went on to say:
In setting its targets the bank's objective is to choose a range for the near-term growth of the money supply capable of accommodating a reasonable rate of economic expansion provided that this is accompanied by some continuing decline in the rate of inflation. The fact that we have been successful in meeting our targets for three consecutive years now provides, I hope, convincing evidence that we are serious about them. If as we come out of the decontrol period the rate of inflation should not decline, or worse still, if there should be a renewed acceleration of the rate of increase of wages and prices, the bank will not for that reason allow its monetary growth targets to be exceeded. In such circumstances interest rates would have to be high enough to prevent undue monetary expansion, and that in turn could lead to slower economic growth until inflation subsided again. That risk cannot be avoided unless monetary policy is simply to underwrite whatever rate of inflation turns up. Given more responsible wage and price behaviour, of course, economic growth need not suffer in this way. Indeed, if we do not let inflation cancel out the benefits of the recent exchange rate adjustment, our improved competitive position will itself provide fresh stimulus to economic activity in Canada.
Because of the importance of this major speech by the governor of the Bank of Canada, I would like to quote a little further from some of his comments. Later in his speech he went on to say:
The downward adjustment of the Canadian dollar from November 1976 to the early part of this year was reasonably orderly and was not a cause for particular concern. At the beginning of this year it seemed to me that Canada's underlying balance of payments situation was better than it had been for some time. A large downward adjustment in the Canadian dollar had taken place about as smoothly as could be expected, and this had much improved our competitive position in international trade.
Again we hear over and over again about the benefits that are accruing to the Canadian economy and to industry generally as a result of a lower exchange dollar. I go on to quote Governor Bouey's comments as follows:
Our costs of production were no longer rising significantly faster than those of our main trading partner, as rates of increase in money wages had come back down to about the same range as in the United States. The expenditures of governments in this country had slowed considerably and the money supply was under good control.
I might say that the federal government had been very much in the lead in this current endeavour to control expenditures under its management.
Governor Bouey went on to say:
The merchandise trade surplus was increasing and prospects for a decline in our over-all current account deficit seemed reasonably good. Although rising U.S. interest rates in conjunction with a lowering of Canadian rates had reduced the incentive to borrow abroad and there had been a lull at times in the pace of foreign borrowings by provinces and corporations, it looked as though these forms of net capital inflow would come close to financing the current account deficit.
I could go on to quote a number of sections of this speech that I think are pertinent, but perhaps I may just conclude these remarks by quoting an additional excerpt from governor Bouey's speech. Again I emphasize that it is extremely important at this time that Canadians understand the positive features of our economy, and that we on this side of the House do all we can to place on the record here, in our ridings and wherever possible, the fact that Canada's position, particularly as compared to other western industrialized nations, is second to none.
I will quote an additional section from Governor Bouey's speech wherein he says:
I have heard a certain amount of unhappiness expressed because of a feeling that our interest rates are tied to those of the United States. My reply to this is that to the extent they are so tied it is at our own choice. After all, we have had the choice of not following U.S. rates up and thus allowing the Canadian dollar to fall faster and further, with the risks that I have just referred to. We always have the choice of ignoring movements in U.S. interest rates if we think we can live with the consequences; in some circumstances it may be wise to do so, but in others it is not. In a situation where we are heavily dependent on inflows of foreign capital and when confidence in the Canadian dollar is still rather fragile in foreign exchange markets, opportunities to be able to ignore movements in U.S. interest rates are likely to be limited.
I would like to conclude my comments today by referring once again to the motion put forward by the Social Credit party, and to say that when we talk about the average Canadian and his situation ten or 15 years ago, or during the period of Conservative government-which seems to have been so many years ago that people have forgotten all about it-in some instances we find the situation much improved. When I go to my constituency in Scarborough on a Friday evening, as I will be doing tonight, I find it is not easy to get into a restaurant for a meal because of the large line-ups of people waiting to go in, often with their families.
The fact is that many Canadians today, the majority of them, are enjoying a standard of living that is substantially better than the standard which was in existence prior to the time that this government came to power. We realize and understand that indeed there are continuing pockets of serious

December 1, 1978

unemployment across the country. In my remarks today I have made that clear, as I have done on many occasions. The government is doing all it can with its measures and leadership to come to grips with those pockets of unemployment. The recent budget addressed itself to regional disparities by providing increased incentives for companies to establish and invest in areas where unemployment is the highest, and by providing tax credits of up to 20 per cent for investment in those particular areas.
We are hearing more and more irresponsible policies from members of the official opposition, such as two or three platform positions recently taken in terms of providing tax reductions. They would add a conservative estimate of $5 billion to $6 billion in total to the deficit. We on this side know that a substantial deficit exists at the present time. We are attempting to come to grips with it, but members on the other side would see it enlarged if they had their way. Yet the financial critic, the hon. member for York-Simcoe (Mr. Stevens), has the nerve to rise and continually criticize the government for not doing more to bring that deficit down. He knows full well that the hon. Leader of the Opposition and other Conservative members are travelling across the country recommending the immediate implementation of policies, if they were to become the government in power. Those policies would increase the deficit by as much as 50 per cent. They cannot have it both ways. Canadians will never accept the completely opposite positions they are taking: one day they say one thing, and the next day they say another.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wanted to take this opportunity to discuss with the House a couple of matters of particular concern raised by the motion of the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier). The first issue is the question of interest rates. 1 have debated this matter with the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Martin) on the late show, and I am glad to have an opportunity to follow him and deal with some of these important questions today.
Often my party is accused of living in the 1930s. Often it has been said that my party looks to the past too much, is too concerned with welfare, is preoccupied with the problems of unemployment and how bad things are, and is not sufficiently optimistic or aware of the fact that we are living in an affluent society. These are misconceptions. The parties which seem to be living in the 1930s are the Conservatives and the Liberals.
The parliamentary secretary indicated this afternoon that because so many restaurants in Toronto were full, we were living in a time of unprecedented affluence. The existence of a bread line, instead of a waiting line for a restaurant, does not demonstrate economic hard times. A great many people in major cities are unemployed, not simply a few pockets of the population. These people are facing extreme financial difficulties, and I should like to refer to two aspects of these difficulties this afternoon.
Economic Policy
The first matter is the question of the interest rate, and related to that is the question of the housing situation. Housing is an important aspect of our cost of living and is a fundamental part of the financial obligations which Canadians have. At the present time the prime rate is 10.75 per cent, and there is a spread of 1.8 per cent between the prime rate charged by the Bank of Canada and the rate charged by banks. The government has engaged in a policy of high interest rates. The parliamentary secretary quoted the words of the governor of the Bank of Canada, that it is a matter of choice. Thus, we can only assume that the government has chosen to go that route, or the government has been forced to go that route, because it is determined to keep the dollar at 85 cents, regardless of the cost in terms of interest rates.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext:
It is true. In the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, the Governor of the Bank of Canada made it perfectly clear that the government and the bank are not prepared to see the dollar go below 85 cents. That is why the interest rate has been kept at its present rate and will continue to rise in response to developments in the United States. At that time the governor created a spectre by referring to the horrors of the dollar going below 85 cents American. Also he said that we had succumbed to something terrible, the British disease. As I understand it from listening to the governor, the British disease is that we would depreciate our currency and import inflation, thereby setting off a spiral of wage demands and so on, which would exceed what we are experiencing at the present time.
It is a very old debating trick, not unknown to some lawyers, to parade a spectre of horrors before a jury so that it will come up with another alternative. In accepting the reality of that spectre-it is a spectre; it is not a reality-the government and the governor of the Bank of Canada succumbed to a disease which is much worse than a potential and unreal fantasy alternative, the Canadian disease. They have succumbed to the Canadian disease. The interst rate is at 10.75 per cent, and there are tens of thousands of houses on the markets of major cities which cannot be bought because people cannot afford them, and there is no market.
The United States has a different and lower unemployment rate of between 5 per cent and 6 per cent. Its industrial capacity is different at the present time, as well as its history respecting the economic problems which that country faces. The United States has increased its interest rate in response to internal developments. We have simply followed along in lock step with the economy of the United States in adopting a high interest rate policy. The government appears to be carrying out a financial policy, but if one looks at its internal implications they are dramatic, social and economic implications for Canadian consumers.
The high interest rate policy also provides for windfall profits for banks. Let there be no illusions about that. I addressed questions to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) today concerning the figures published yesterday which

Economic Policy
revealed that bank profits were approaching $1 billion and had risen 33 per cent from last year. The president of one of the major banks said that the main reason for increased profits is that the margin between the prime rate and the rate charged by banks has been increased, and that spread accounts for a large portion of the increased profits. That spread is at the expense of the ordinary person, the one who wants to borrow money or buy a house. The banks are taking advantage of those people.
If I may say, with respect to my friend, you do not have to be a Social Crediter to recognize that our large financial institutions are taking terrible advantage of our people. The amendments to the Bank Act which the government has proposed do not deal with that problem. They do not even address the problem.

speechtext: Be specific.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext:
An hon. member has asked me to be specific. All right, I will be quite specific. Let us accept the government's position that for external economic reasons, financial reasons, or for reasons of protecting the currency, we need an interest rate that is locked into the interest rates of the United States so that if American rates go up ours goes up. Let us accept that for the purposes of argument. If that is the case, it is the responsibility of the government to address itself to legislation in respect of banks which does two things: legislation which guarantees that banks will not make excess profits as a result of the fact that interest rates fluctuate and go up; and, second, that banks set aside a portion of their profits to be used to create what I would call subsidized interest rates for specific purposes. In other words, we should have legislation which provides for lower mortgage rates for first-time home buyers, to be subsidized by excess profits from the banks.
Alternatively, the legislation should address itself to another economic necessity relating to the concerns of small businessmen, particularly those in the Atlantic provinces, or even in downtown Toronto. Those concerns relate to their credit needs which cannot be met or cannot be satisfied if the government persists in following a policy of high interest rates because of external requirements.
That is the Canadian disease and the Canadian dilemma. We have high interest rates allegedly because of external constraints which have an impact on the internal economy, what I call the social economy of the country, which is quite out of line with requirements or external demands.
The classic example, as I said today, is that bank profits, which some people are able to take advantage of through high interest rates, are not available to the working people of Canada, but rather to the people who own shares in banks and who work in the banks. The Bank Act does not address itself to this problem. The Minister of Finance said he hoped we would propose amendments to the Bank Act, and I can assure him that we will.
I hope the government will address itself to that aspect of the interest problem. As the interest rate goes up because of external demands, there is a dramatic effect on the internal market, but there is no direct, intelligent or sensible relationship between those two things.
The second thing I want to deal with in the few minutes left to me is the matter of housing, particularly housing in our large urban centres. I represent a riding in downtown Toronto, so obviously I am speaking from that perspective.

The fact of the matter is, according to the government's own statistics, that about one-fifth of all metropolitan householders pay more than 25 per cent of their income on shelter, and, of those, about 180,000 pay more than 40 per cent of their income to secure and maintain their dwellings.
The important point to remember out of this is that renters have an even greater affordability problem than do the owners of houses. When the time comes for the next election and for the people of Canada to take a very hard look at the scheme which has been proposed by the Conservative party, I am sure they will recognize not only that it will not solve the financial problems of the Canadian people in regard to the size of our deficit, but that it is a fundamentally inequitable proposal from the point of view of our taxation system, and from the point of view of social justice.
It is important to remember that every time we give somebody a tax credit, somebody else is paying for it, and it is important to remember that the vast majority of the revenues of Canada come from the working people of Canada. It is the guy or the woman who is paying income tax every week and sees it knocked off the wage cheque who knows that this will be used to subsidize this scheme of the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext:
They would like to own homes, but we are also looking at a system which does not provide for their ability to own a home, but rather provides a subsidy to the people who own homes at the present time. You cannot sacrifice these wages for some future dream five years away. You are selling the people a Hollywood fantasy which is not going to work.
The reality of the fact is that there are a great many people living in our urban centres who are apartment dwellers and renters, and who will be renters and apartment dwellers until the day they die.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext: We will look after them too.

speechtext:
I am sure you will when your time comes, but until that time comes we have to address ourselves to the inequities
[Mr. Rae.)
December 1, 1978

of the tax system and to the inactivity of the government in respect of the housing problem. I think the degree of concern this government has accepted in respect of housing has been demonstrated by two recent events. First of all, this government chopped $260 million from the CMHC budget and, secondly, it is abolishing the ministry of urban affairs. We know full well that when the urban dweller in Canada wants to look to a government for the solution to his problems he will not be looking to the government in Ottawa, and I suggest that is a very sad day for the people of Canada. When the day comes that the Government of Canada says, "Don't come to us with your problems, go back to the provinces from which you came," that is the day we no longer have a country of which we can really be proud.
It is an abdication of political and social responsibility for this government to say that problems of urban dwellers are no longer to be a major preoccupation of this government. This government had the opportunity in 1971 to set up a ministry of urban affairs which would genuinely co-ordinate government policy in respect of our cities. This government has not fulfilled one aspect of that policy in respect of urban planning, urban growth, and urban transportation. The government's answer now is to abolish the ministry of state for urban affairs. The hon. member is supposed to agree with me, but he will not. That is why this government has bought the entire Tory package of restraint, the effect of which has been to reduce the total amount spent by this government on social measures, and reduce the ability of the government to provide for the housing needs of urban Canadians.
In the few minutes left to me I simply want to say that if this government thinks that by stumbling from pillar to post in response to what it sees as the vagaries of public opinion, and that by reducing the level of socioeconomic spending on its part, it will endear itself to the working men and women of Canada, it is in for a shock at the next election, and certainly it should be in for a shock. The fact of the matter is that the level of social spending by this government in terms of housing, in terms of urban transportation, and in terms of the needs of our inter-city Canadians dictates the level of the standard of living of those people. Those are not people who can rely entirely on the market for their standard of living.
In a civilized and decent society we should not have private wealth and public squalor. What we must have is wealth distributed throughout our society, providing a satisfactory living in respect of housing and transportation. We must have public investment that guarantees a satisfactory standard of living for all Canadians. That is why the matter of the interest rates is directly tied to the question of the standard of living, and I am glad that our friend has brought it up. As long as you have a government which relies entirely on a private market and a standard of high interest rates for the provision of its housing, there will be a housing market that will be unfulfilled and depleted in the inner cities of this country. We know that there are not only affordability needs but physical needs in housing that are not being met by this government.
Economic Policy
The abolishment of the ministry of urban affairs-and I see that we have a former minister of state for urban affairs in the House-is typical of the lack of concern that this government has shown for the housing situation in Canada.
