speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of items in this motion that have already been discussed by previous speakers, such as interest rates, inflation, fiscal and monetary policy, and so on. I intend to make reference to those subjects during my remarks, but there is a phrase in the motion to which reference has not been made. The phrase is "double standard" and I can understand the government not mentioning it because it reads, "this House deplores the double standard applied by the government. ..".
The parliamentary secretary gave some indication of that double standard when he talked about the striking success this government has had. 1 am sure a great many Canadians must view that statement as something of a double standard. He talked about how good things were for Canadians. Those who are out of work must regard that as something of a double standard. He referred to pockets of unemployment. I suppose that next the government will be telling us that there is no unemployment, that it is just a nasty rumour started by a lot of people who are out of work.
The parliamentary secretary also referred to the size of the government debt in relation to gross national expenditures. He seemed to draw enormous satisfaction from the fact that the debt was a higher percentage of g.n.e. during the last year of the last Conservative government than it is at the present time. That is a double standard, because if government g.n.e. doubled tomorrow he would then boast to us that the government managed to reduce the debt, when it is clear that one is simply expressed as a percentage of the other.
He also said that the opposition party has been attempting to convince Canadians of doom and gloom and how terrible things are in the country. We do not have to convince the Canadian people of anything. The results of the October 16 by-elections, when I and a number of my colleagues on this side had the honour to be elected, indicate that they already understand what things are like in this country. We are simply pointing out what a disastrous job this government has done managing the affairs of the country over the years it has been in office. If we preach doom and gloom we preach it to the government, and only in the sense that if its policies continue then we face disaster. We put sensible policy alternatives before the government, many of which it adopts, but as I pointed out before, it gets the words right and the music wrong. Ministers opposite did it in 1974 with wage and price controls, and they are likely to do it again with some of the things that are in the current budget.
It must also be a double standard to Canadians when this government talks about restraint. 1 believe the phrase the parliamentary secretary used was "leadership in restraint." 1 am sure that those same Canadians have noted that during the entire period of wage and price controls when wages, profits
80067-37'/2

December 1, 1978
Economic Policy
and prices were restricted, the spending increases of this government never fell below 10 per cent, never got down into the single digit figures, and soared as high as 16 per cent. That is a double standard of major proportions.
For the last three months this government has been talking about spending cutbacks and what a wonderful job it is doing in that area. Yet, even if you believe that the restraints it predicted for next year are actually going to take place-and based on the record of this government it is very difficult to believe anything it says-it will still have a 9 per cent spending increase next year. It will be the largest dollar spending increase it has had since 1974. And that is supposed to be some form of restraint? There are so many examples of double standards, playing with the figures, and misrepresentation on the part of this government that they are difficult to deal with adequately in the time we have today.
1 would now like to comment on a document that appeared before this House in concert with the budget. It is a report on a study by the Department of Finance of the tax systems of Canada and the United States. The government in printing that study did not go into great detail about what precisely it was purporting to prove. The message seemed to be that things were pretty good here because this study purports to show conclusively, according to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien), that the Canadian personal tax system compares favourably with the United States and, therefore, we are doing all right. I suppose we are to believe that the people of the United States are doing all right too, which is not the case.
This study does not show that the conclusion by the Minister of Finance is correct at all. For example, he says that "our business taxes are fully competitive." That is a highly arguable point and I intend to argue it later. The study itself is so highly qualified that it does not provide the conclusive demonstration he suggests. It notes five difficulties with the comparability of data, and two difficulties with the interpretation of tax burden, and it consistently confuses the differences between the tax burden and the tax rate. Finally, it concludes that the Canadian and U.S. tax systems are competitive but only in a general way. It makes no attempt to provide a conclusive demonstration.
Several of the conclusions in this study are misleading, particularly when they are used to claim that the Canadian tax system is competitive. 1 would like to point out five or six specific examples of the kinds of misleading information contained in it. For example, on page 57 of the study the second paragraph reads:
The paper leads to the general conclusion that the Canadian tax system compares favourably with that in the U.S. In aggregate, while tax revenues of all levels of government were 1.8 percentage points of GDP higher in Canada than in the U.S. in 1977, Canadians had the benefit of publicly provided health care services and demogrant transfer payments in the form of family allowances and old age security pensions.
There are two points here. In the first place, the study clearly concedes that the aggregate tax burden as a proportion of the total economic activity is higher in Canada than in the United States. That concession alone is enough to make the findings of this study less than conclusive.

Secondly, it argues that if you exclude the cost of certain services provided by the government without cost-health care, family allowances, etc.-then the Canadian tax burden is lower. That argument is ridiculous. It does not hold water because the study deals with the tax burdens of the two countries, which is conceptually different from the study of the services provided by the two governments. Also, if one subtracts the cost of social services provided by the government, why should you not subtract other services? For example, why do they not include the higher spending on defence in the United States, which is a much greater portion of their national budget, in the comparison?
The common theme of the two reasons for disputing the study's argument is that the issue is tax burden and not spending habits. No one doubts that U.S. government agencies spent tax dollars on different items than Canadian government agencies. Surely the issue is the tax burden that is required to finance those activities, not what the activities are. That is part of a different argument that takes place in this chamber also, but at a different time.
Another item in this study concludes that non-income taxes form the same proportion of total revenues in both countries. In the United States there is greater emphasis on social security taxes than in Canada, and Canadian non-income taxes have their primary impact through indirect taxation, specifically the manufacturers' sales tax. The study maintains that this tax has little effect on international competitiveness as these taxes apply only to goods produced or imported and not to exports. It is probably true that it has little effect on international competitiveness but it is also a fair conclusion, although it is not mentioned in the study, that United States social security taxes probably have little effect on international competitiveness either.
On page 57, the study notes:
(iii) Aggregate personal taxes (personal income taxes, social security taxes levied on persons and estate and gift taxes) are lower in Canada, as a percentage of personal income, than in the U.S.
On the next page it states-and this is the important part- as follows:
In Canada, personal income taxes are a higher percentage of personal income than in the U.S. but this is more than offset by lower levels of social security and estate and gift taxes.
Even if we assume that these facts are correct, although there are a number of reasons to question the study, not only for the conclusions which seem to be used for political purposes, but in the way-

Even if we assume that these facts are correct, what is of interest is that Canadian unemployment insurance contributions are treated as a tax in this study. According to this document, the Department of Finance considers UIC contributions to be a tax. Surely, then, the government should cease referring to them as insurance premiums, as they do consistently. There is quite a difference between tax and insurance.
Another point in the study is that total exemptions and deductions are higher in Canada than in the United States. That may be true but it is irrelevant. The study has already conceded that personal income taxes are a higher percentage of personal income in Canada than in the United States. That being true, exemptions and deductions should also be higher.
On page 58 the study makes comparisons of disposable incomes as follows:
(v) Comparisons of disposable incomes (gross income plus family allowances where applicable, less income tax and employee social security contributions) of typical taxpayers in Canada and the U.S., indicate that most lower and middle-income taxpayers in Canada have higher disposable incomes than their American counterparts.
That is an extremely misleading statement for at least four reasons, Mr. Speaker. First of all, it includes family allowances. While family allowances are fairly included in disposable income, the spending of the government should not enter into calculations of the tax burden of the government. To do so creates a distortion which would allow industrial subsidies to be deducted from the tax burden of industry.
Second, the comparison deals with disposable incomes, not real disposable incomes. Several of the comparisons in the study deal with the period from 1972 to 1977. Over that period, while consumer prices in the United States increased by 44.9 per cent, in Canada consumer prices increased by 53.4 per cent. The 1972 United States consumer dollar was worth 69 cents in 1977, while the Canadian consumer dollar was worth 65 cents. A comparison of real disposable incomes might therefore tell quite a different story.
Third, unless the comparison is made over the period of a business cycle, it will be misleading. This government has been very cute over the last several months in carefully picking periods when restraint or accomplishment on economic fronts or on government spending fronts seems to have been present, but in fact has not been present in many of those cases, and certainly not over a full business cycle.
Fourth, the fact that Canadian incomes are higher should come as no surprise to anyone, especially the government. The parliamentary secretary referred to this already this afternoon. It was the imbalance in incomes and wage rates that led this government to impose wage and price controls in the first place. That is a suggestion that was made by this party and
Economic Policy
rejected categorically by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in the 1974 election campaign, when he said, "We will never ... etc."
That same imbalance in wage rates led to the devaluation of our dollar. The government is speaking out of both sides of its mouth. Out of the one side they claim that because Canadian disposable incomes are higher than those in the United states, there is no problem with our tax system and everything is dandy. Out of the other side they claim that because Canadian disposable incomes are higher than those in the United States, there is a need for wage and price controls and a devalued dollar. Wage and price controls fortunately are coming to an end, but until this government comes to an end there is no end in sight for the devalued dollar. They cannot have it both ways, Mr. Speaker.
On page 59, in paragraph (vii), the study states:
-the over-all effective corporation tax rate in Canada was some six percentage points lower than the U.S.
That is nothing new but you cannot fairly proceed from that to conclude that the over-all corporate tax burden is lighter. What the comparison leaves out primarily is the federal manufacturers' sales tax payable in Canada which has been reduced in the last budget by 3 per cent. It still exists, however, and it has a major effect on economic activity.
The economic theory of pricing suggests that all taxes-not only direct corporate income tax but indirect taxes and sales taxes paid by business-have to be reflected and are reflected in the price of the product. The product is priced to provide an after tax return on investment. If that applies, then both income tax and sales tax enter into price calculations. That is one reason that automobile prices, for example, are higher in Canada than in the United States despite the auto pact. Canadians pay a federal sales tax indirectly that United States residents do not. While the federal sales tax does not affect export competitiveness, it does affect domestic prices and thereby affects corporate income. In assessing comparative corporate tax burdens as this does, it must be included. Statements about the corporate tax rate completely ignore this.
Mr. Speaker, this is but one study that compares the tax systems of Canada and the United States. 1 have already indicated that 1 think its timing is suspicious, its conclusions dubious and its logic arguable. I should therefore like to quote from some other studies, particularly one done in 1976 by the private sector. It was prepared by the senior tax partner of Price Waterhouse and Company for a conference sponsored by the The Conference Board in Canada. As everyone in this House knows, this is a very effective, very professional, highly proficient and certainly unbiased organization. The senior tax partner of that firm said in the first paragraph of this study:
Making any sort of comparison of tax burdens between countries is a very complicated matter. By an appropriate choice of figures, it is possible to arrive at virtually any answer that you might desire. It is therefore possible to draw only very general conclusions from most international tax comparisons: in one set of circumstances, one tax system may appear more favourable than the other, but a change in the assumed circumstances can readily change the conclusion.

December 1, 1978
Economic Policy
The thing that is wrong with the kind of comparison or statement that our interest rate is good because the United States interest rate has done thus and so is that it does not deal with where Canada is and where Canada is going.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and, I thank hon. members for their indulgence.
Comparisons that dwell on how well we are doing in relation to the United States or any other nation are not ultimately useful. Over the past few months the government has made considerable reference to the fact that Canada is a healthy country in a difficult world. The government have said that all the problems we face-inflation, unemployment and son on- are essentially caused by factors outside our borders and outside our control. They have said that inflation comes from the Arab oil price increases, unemployment comes from Hong Kong and Taiwan, and presumably our weather comes from Alaska! Nothing can be done by this government.
We have done much by way of argument against that theory of the government. However, we are not doing well compared to other nations. The figures are there and they are clear. Given our favoured resource picture and a well distributed and educated population, we are not doing even equally as well as other nations in the world with which we are compared, we are doing worse. It is not how well or how poorly we are doing in comparison to some other nation, it is how well we are doing on our own that is important. It is how Canadians regard the management of the economy and the effects of the policy that this government puts into operation that counts.
One should not point to other nations in the world with an equally high unemployment rate and then say our rate is not our fault. Every time things go well this government takes credit for it, or tries to; but every time things go badly the government blames somebody else. We were told by the Prime Minister that we in the opposition are enemies, that the provinces are enemies, and certainly the media are enemies for reporting all of this. "It is someone else's fault" is what the government says; "we are doing what is right" 1 do not think that doing what is right, if that is the case, would lead to one million people out of work. It would not lead to a 9 per cent inflation rate, to a devalued dollar, or to the kind of messing with figures that we have seen in this particular study that I have indicated, throughout the speech of the parliamentary secretary, and indeed throughout the speeches of most members on the government side.
The motion presented by the Social Credit party this afternoon reads:
That this House deplores the double standard applied by the government in deliberately reducing the buying power of Canadian workers and families while allowing an increase in the interest rates which will result in higher revenues for financial institutions, an increase in the inflation rate, as well as a heavier public debt.
Although I agree with some parts of this motion, I think that the motion is too long. It could come down to a very few words; for example, "That this House deplores this government."

speechtext: A rose by any other name-

speakerposition: Minister of State for Economic Development
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles).
This motion before us has had some comments made about it, and I will continue by adding mine. It manages to combine a number of misconceptions, as the previous speaker has said, in a very long sentence. First, I would like to respond to the concern over interest rates which has been expressed in the motion. Then for a few moments I would like to turn to the question of how Canadians are faring in terms of real income, and finally I would like to make some observations on the profit picture of our corporations.
None of us welcome increases in interest rates, but sometimes higher interest rates are a bit like old age-they are not so bad when one considers the alternative. What is the alternative in our present circumstances which have led the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates, admittedly several times this year, to their current levels? The governor of the Bank of Canada has set out the considerations we face in a clear and forthright way in recent speeches. He has stressed that the bank is very much aware of the concern over high interest rates.
Canada is currently importing more goods and services than it is exporting. Therefore, an inflow of money must be attracted from abroad to cover this deficit. We are indeed making progress on a number of aspects of this balance of payments deficit. Looking at trade in goods alone, we are in a surplus position. The surplus in the first three quarters of this year is running more than $1 billion higher than it was in the corresponding period last year. As the positive effects on trade of our lower dollar continue to build and we maintain our much improved domestic cost performance, particularly relative to costs in the United States, I think we can look forward to further improvement in our trade surplus and to a further reduction in our over-all deficit on goods plus services. But for the present, as I have said, we have to face the fact of that deficit and the necessity of attracting inflows of funds to cover it. If financial conditions in Canada are not such as to attract sufficient funds from abroad, we can expect further deprecia-

December 1, 1978

tion, quite possibly substantial further depreciation, of our exchange rate.
We all know and recognize that depreciation of the dollar is not always a bad thing. It was also recognized that Canadian costs had become significantly out of line with costs in our trading position, particularly with our major trading partner, namely the United States, over the years up to 1976. We have to acknowledge that there has been a downward adjustment of the dollar, which was bound to occur sooner or later and had to occur if the conditions for growth of employment, output and investment in our manufacturing industries and many of our other exporting industries was to be re-established.
We also know that the devaluation or depreciation of the dollar has increased our rate of inflation. Unfortunately, that price had to be paid. Instead of the pessimism that is around for whatever reason or motivation, there is reason to believe that we have re-established a reasonably favourable competitive position which, with time, will allow us to move into a more sustainable balance of payments position.
We are also in a very critical period as temporary price and income controls come to an end. If we can continue to bring down the underlying rate of inflation our prospects for growth in employment and real income in the 1980s are very promising. If domestic inflation starts to flare up again, those prospects will fade.
The critical nature of the period immediately ahead and the recent pressure on prices because of devaluation which has already occurred, together with food prices, has led the government to provide some offset to immediate pressures on prices through the sales tax reduction which my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) announced the other night, through the earlier gas excise tax reduction in a previous budget, and indeed in our hope for deferral, if it comes about, of the oil price increase on January 1, 1979. That has led the bank and the government to be a little concerned to moderate any further pressures on costs and prices that could occur through exchange rate fluctuations. Thus there has been action to moderate the pace and scale of further exchange rate adjustments and to moderate the danger of a serious overshoot in that adjustment.
Foreign borrowing to supplement our exchange reserves has been part of this action, as have the actions of the Bank of Canada. In the governor's words, "we must give priority for a time to the need to maintain confidence in the Canadian dollar in foreign exchange markets". Faced with rising interest rates in international capital markets, this has required increases in our domestic rates. Hopefully, the need to maintain rates at current levels will be of relatively short duration. With further progress in reducing inflation we should be able to look forward to one of the rewards of lower inflation: lower interest rates on average. The government supports the policies of the Bank of Canada, including the interest rate response to the current situation. The alternative for our exchange rate and for inflation would be still less desirable.
Economic Policy
I would like to turn to the second part of the motion before us, which alleges that the government is deliberately reducing the purchasing power of workers and families. There is a short and very justified response. It is simply: Nonsense! In saying that, perhaps it would be wise to state for the hon. member who put forward the motion a little more detail.
First let us look at government actions this year. A special personal income tax cut took effect last January to give an extra boost to purchasing power. The federally-financed retail sales tax cut provided a further boost.
In August, at the same time that I was announcing severe cuts across a wide range of government expenditures, the government rearranged the family allowances and child benefit system so as to give more assistance to lower income families. The real purchasing power of older Canadians with modest incomes is already protected by the full indexation of the old age pension, the guaranteed income supplement, and the Canada pension plan. But as part of a general policy of reallocating our admittedly limited resources to where they were most needed, and in recognition of the above average share which food occupies in the expenditure of lower income retired individuals and couples, the government also provided an additional increase, over and above full indexation, in the guaranteed income supplement.
Two weeks ago my colleague the Minister of Finance introduced his budget which, through the sales tax cut and the increase in the employment expense deduction under the personal income tax, will further assist the purchasing power of Canadians, and in particular working Canadians, in 1979. These measures come on top of full indexation of our tax system which is a very important form of protection against one of the ways in which inflation can reduce real purchasing power. This is a type of purchasing power protection which citizens in most other countries do not enjoy.
We must recognize that the counterpart of the very rapid growth in our real incomes which took place from 1970 to 1976 was that our competitive position got rather badly out of line. A pause in real income growth was an inevitable part of bringing our competitive position back in line and re-establishing the conditions for employment growth. The government's actions have been designed to help ease this aspect of the adjustment. Our expenditure restraint has allowed us to make major cuts in taxes which have cushioned this adjustment in real incomes.
As we go through this difficult period of adjustment to income levels which are sustainable given our productivity and competitive position, it is important not to lose sight of the fact that Canadians are still faring very well in terms of increases and the improvement in their standard of living compared with a few years ago. As the Minister of Finance noted, real after-tax income per employee in Canada increased by 7 per cent in the last three years, whereas it decreased by 2 per cent in the United States. This is a difference of about 3 per cent per year in the annual rate of increase. I am talking about real income.

December 1, 1978
Economic Policy
Some critics have responded that Canada has had higher real income growth for an extended period, and that no special significance should be attached to the result for the last three years. The fact is that during the preceding ten years, the amount by which the average annual increase in real after-tax income in Canada exceeded the increase in the United States was only about half as large as during the last three years. Therefore, those figures and the significance of them represent a very current and immediate period.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to make a few comments on criticism about profits. Corporate profits have shown substantial rates of increase over recent quarters. Of course, profits typically vary a good deal up and down. In 1975 total corporate profits actually decreased 1.8 per cent whereas total wages increased by close to 17 per cent. In 1976, profits increased by almost 3 per cent whereas wages increased by almost 16 per cent.
In this period, when our costs were becoming increasingly out of line and the exchange rate adjustment had not yet occurred, profits were experiencing much of the initial squeeze which these adverse developments implied for the economy. If the squeeze had continued, we could have expected even less employment and invesment growth than has occurred, and much poorer prospects, in terms of the platform from which we now go forward. Last year the rates of increase in total profits and total wages were very similar, but this year the increase in profits is running ahead of wages, in part because profits tend to receive much of the initial benefit of the exchange rate depreciation. The share of profits is now back up to something like normal levels, though well below levels reached in 1973 and 1974.
Concern has been expressed that profit increases may worsen price performance, and also that high profits may be a target for wage negotiations-contributing in this way as well to a new inflationary spiral. In its report to the First Ministers Conference at the beginning of this week, the Centre of the Study of Inflation and Productivity noted the improved profit position of corporations, the moderation in labour costs and the recent reduction in federal sales tax. It expressed the view that corporations should be exercising a substantial degree of price and profit restraint, and urged firms to use the depreciation of the exchange rate to expand their markets rather than just raise their prices. I would add that the reinvestment of the improved profits is also critical to our short and longer-term prospects. Indeed, the budget has increased the encouragement provided by the tax system to such reinvestment.
Mr. Speaker, I hope Canadians in business, in the labour movement and in this House will read the report of the Centre of the Study of Inflation and Productivity very carefully. 1 hope they will quote it in context and not out of context. They will find in that report the concern about profits and prices to which I referred and which has already been raised in this House. They will also find that recent developments regarding profits are treated by that report in what I call the proper
perspective. The report notes, for example, that while it appears that profit increases may have contributed somewhat to the rapid increase in food prices over the last year, they were by no means the major cause.
Given the problems we face and the shifting international economic conditions under which we must operate-and there is no rhetoric which will convince Canadians that there is not reality to the recognition that we do not live as an isolated community and that conditions in other countries do affect us-policy decisions in that context are difficult. I do not care who has to make them; the responsibility for making policy decisions in economic matters these days is not a simple thing. I think the actions of the government and of the Bank of Canada are best suited to encouraging sustained non-inflationary growth in employment, output and incomes.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to take part in the debate on the excellent motion moved by my colleague, the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier), and show the House how the government applies the double standard policy with regard to Canadian financial institutions.
The government is responsible for the extraordinary increase in the the revenues of banks and financial institutions in two different ways. First, when the government allows the Bank of Canada to raise its interest rate, it indirectly allows the institutions affiliated to the central bank to pass the increases on to the consumer. Naturally, the new interest rates allow chartered banks and other financial institutions to extend their profit margins. However, the small wage earner must suffer from those new interest rates and carry a heavier debt load.
It is not rare these days to meet people paying 20 per cent interest on their loans. Since wages do not go up as often as interest rates do, the difficulties occurring at the time of the loan prove insurmountable. The consumer must generally pay the original amount of his loan several times over. Second, the federal government must be held directly responsible for the exhorbitant increase in the annual revenues of financial institutions because, in a sense, the government sets the rules. Indeed, the federal government is responsible for the amendments made every ten years to the Bank Act, loan companies, trust companies and co-operative credit associations. So. the government sets the broad rules of the game of financial markets. Unfortunately, the government and its Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) accept the expansionist aspirations of large Canadian banking institutions and draft the legislation with those big bankers in mind. In this way, since the Bank of Canada was set up as a regulatory body the government has been the agent of big financiers by increasing their powers which are normally reserved for banks. The ordinary man must control his frustrations as he watches the big banks get richer while his purchasing power gradually shrinks.
Let us look at a few facts concerning those big institutions. Chartered banks take the larger part of the revenues coming

December 1, 1978

from the financial sector. It is not a surprising statistic as the ten major chartered banks have 7,000 branches. Furthermore, the five major chartered banks alone control approximately 90 per cent of the Canadian financial market. This centralization of the financial sector accounts for the excessive concentration of financial power in the hands of a small minority of individuals and the enormous share of revenues they draw every year from various sources. The total assets of the chartered banks have increased at a rate of 400 per cent during the last ten years, a period which coincides with the last bank reform. The present government was already in power at that time. Banking revenues have therefore increased by 400 per cent while the purchasing power of workers and Canadian families was being constantly eroded by an ever rising rate of inflation and not too surprisingly, since the banks were one of the prime factors behind the increasing costs of production.
The assets of chartered banks were $31.7 million in 1968 while their total assets went up to $162.4 million in May 1978. This means then a $130.7 million increase over a period of ten years. When one considers that these institutions get a sizable part of their rollover funds through the deposits of low and medium income workers, it is sad to note that the excessive profit margins were not reflected at all in the interests paid on deposits and savings accounts. The total assets of banks have increased from 1972 and 1975 at the same rate they had increased during the entire previous century. These were the results of the 1968 bank reform. The Liberal government allowed the ceiling on interest rates to be removed when that review took place. The Social Credit Party of Canada then predicted the dangers such a measure held in store for the Canadian economy.
The hon. member for Roberval who moved this motion today also mentioned those risks in the debate on the antiinflation act, when he said on October 20, 1975, in the House of Commons, and I quote:
What, in my opinion, is more fantastic yet, Mr. Speaker, is the fact that all through his long speech, the minister did not refer to today's inadmissibly high rates of interest. The true inflation spiralling started when this government removed the chartered banks interest ceiling.
I said so the day after that decision and I said here that Canada would experience its worst years of inflation ever. The first serious step should have been to freeze the Bank of Canada's discount rate at 4 per cent.
And the hon. member for Roberval was perfectly right. We have proof of it today. After discussing the performance of banks by reviewing their liabilities and assets, we should look at the revenues and expenditures of those institutions which reflect more or less the same conditions. Between 1968 and 1977, total revenues of banks increased by some 424 per cent, from $2,209 billion to $11,569 billion in 1977. The major part of these revenues comes more and more from accrued interests on bank loans. In 1968, the percentage of total bank revenues from interests on loans represented 70 per cent. In 1973, that percentage reached 80 per cent, while in 1977 it reached 84
Economic Policy
per cent. During the same period, from 1968 to 1977, bank revenues from stocks, shares and other operating revenues went down from 30 per cent to 16 per cent, which means that chartered banks are progressively earning a larger share of their income from the public while the people get more and more into debt.
I feel it is unfair for the federal government to support a bank system that takes openly advantage of the people, but it is also a fact that banks pay interest rates on deposits and mortgages bonds and that the percentage of money they pay back to the public in interests is rather low. In fact, the increase in expenditures paid in the form of interests on deposits or mortgage bonds has been significantly lower than the percentage of revenues earned by banks as interest on loans. In other words, the average citizen gets ever lower returns on his investment while the banks ever increasing profits on the back of the small investor. The Minister of Finance feels that we save too much; the banks use children in their publicity, telling us that we are helping to increase the capital of the country, when in fact they are trying mostly to serve their own interests.
Let us now look at another aspect of banking operations. The percentage of expenses paid out by the banks in salaries, retirement funds and various other contributions, has decreased over the last ten years compared with their over-all expenditures, moving progressively from 26 per cent of their total expenditures to 20 per cent, and finally 19 per cent. So, as bank revenues increased, the money spent in salaries decreased. That fact proves clearly the present trend towards reducing the purchasing power of the consumers who work in the banking sector. That tendency is becoming even more alarming when one considers that during the years under study, the number of male employees in banks increased by 26 per cent, while that of female employees more than doubled. It seems, therefore, that the latter category of employees paid the bill for the prosperity of the financial sector, since women usually work for lower salaries. All those facts would explain, once again, why the purchasing power of the average consumer has decreased since the present Prime Minister came to power. Thanks to the elimination of certain limits during the 1968 Bank Act review, banks were in a position to gain a firm hold over the mortgage market and consumer loans, leading in these two areas to an extraordinary increase between 1967 and 1977. The mortgage market is one of the most profitable assets for banks. In 1967 banks held only $840 million in mortgages while in 1977, due to the government weakness towards chartered banks, their assets soared to $11.6 billion. Now chartered banks are threatening to control the mortgage market and reduce considerably the activities of other financial institutions such as trust companies which rely particularly on their own profitability on the financial market to go on making profits.
By adopting its irresponsible banking legislation, the government triggered off a reduction of competition on the mortgage

market. And when competition diminishes, it always has a negative impact on the people who are no longer free in their financial operations with banking institutions. Because of the banking policy of this same government, banks also captured an ever larger share of the consumer loans market. In 1967, banks had the equivalent of $3.6 billion in assets of this category while in 1977 they controlled $20.2 billion-a 461 per cent increase in ten years.
In recent years, other financial institutions have considerably added to their assets but with no obvious benefits to the general public. Compared to the chartered banks, trust and mortgage companies increased their assets by 310 per cent between 1968 and 1977. These companies had boosted their income on loans by 700 per cent between 1972 and 1977 while raising their assets in mortgage loans and sales contracts by 400 per cent. Finance or consumer loans companies and savings banks in Quebec increased their assets by 164 per cent and 150 per cent respectively between 1967 and 1977. Fortunately, during the last ten years the assets of financial institutions such as caisses populaires and credit unions also rose by 480 per cent. Since the assets of this type of institution increase even faster than those of powerful chartered banks, it is easy to see why the public sees in them a people-oriented organization which is more likely to meet the needs of average citizens. But because the five major banks control such a large share of the financial market-90 per cent-the public support given to the "caisses populaires" and the credit unions is not enough to compensate.
In any event, it is quite obvious that Canada's financial system, which was reviewed and regulated by the Liberal government, has allowed the chartered banks to keep the people under their control as far as consumer credit is concerned. Between 1967 and 1977, the total amount of credit granted by major lenders increased by 272 per cent. In 1967, the two major lenders were the chartered banks, with 44 per cent of the market, followed by finance or loan companies, with 41 per cent of the market. Ten years later, under the aegis of this government's fiscal policy, the banks held 76 per cent of the total amount of consumer credit. The government was not satisfied with allowing the interest rate increase steadily and the Canadian people run deeper and deeper into debt. No. Moreover the national executive, thanks to banking regulations that show no concern for the needs of ordinary people, has let an increasing share of credit to be controlled by the banks. Such federal incompetence contributed to a decrease in the purchasing power of the Canadian people while allowing financial institutions to fill their coffers at our expense.
But the Social Credit Party of Canada is not only concerned with the increased revenues going in the financial system. We are also concerned, Mr. Speaker, with the fact that financial institutions and particularly chartered banks are getting more and more control over the market. All financial organizations should base their operations on the needs of the population as a whole, and this includes small and medium businesses, rather

than concentrating on the demands of the affluent and big corporations. The needs of the people must be filled, and to that end a healthy competitive climate is needed where fairness is the rule of the game. Hovewer in introducing certain pieces of legislation this government has shown that it had no intention whatsoever to give the average citizen a larger share in the financial wealth of the country. 1 am referring of course to the proposals which are found in the omnibus legislation, Bill C-15. We were really looking forward to see how the government, in introducing the ten-year review of the Bank Act, would implement their stated intention to increase competition within the banking system. Until control of that system is returned to the people, under the leadership of a Social Credit government, an even minimal decentralization of financial institutions would have been welcome. But we had been waiting in vain. When the Bill passed, we saw once more that the government had one law for the rich and another for the poor. Their speech changes according to whom they are speaking to.
Let me take a few moments to elaborate on this, because that part of the legislation in the long run will affect the financial well-being of every Canadian. This is relevant to our motion because financial market structures and the way their contents is regulated influence the growth and profitability of financial institutions. This is why financial operations should be shared on fair basis by all institutions accepting deposits, in order that consumers may reap the benefits of a free market system. However, the government has gone against its stated intention and has introduced legislation which grants more power to chartered banks and does not attempt to defend the interests of average Canadians. Moreover, these same banks have convinced the government to reduce other limitations on their business powers. In fact, they will be invited to corner an even greater part of the housing mortgage market, even though this authorization will threaten the existence of consumer trust and loan companies. It is tragic that this government has once again refused to listen to the Canadian consumers who have been requesting that a ceiling of 6 per cent be again placed on interest rates.
In the part of Bill C-15 which concerns the creation of a Canadian Payments Association, the government has shown once again its lack of concern for ordinary citizens. The Canadian Payments Association, which will be established under this legislation, will have a very great role to play in the development of an electronic payment system. However, our government experts have forgotten to include proposals to guarantee that consumers will be represented on the board of directors of this association. Since all monetary operations between financial institutions will be eventually controlled by the CPA, it is imperative that the public should be able to influence to a certain extent the policy of this association.
In Bill C-15, the government betrays its desire to create even more chartered banks by making it more easy for them to set into the market. The performance of these institutions must have a more direct application to the Canadian economy. It is up to the government to include in its review of bank legisla-
December 1, 1978

tion provisions which will force financial institutions to retain 15 per cent of their profits to create an investment fund. This money should be invested in the sectors of the Canadian economy which need to be stimulated.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, and I also thank the hon. members on both sides of the House. As 1 was saying, the funds earmarked by chartered banks for investment purposes should be invested in Canadian economic sectors which need stimulation. The development of such sectors should be designed to increase the general welfare of all Canadians. That kind of controlled investment would provide employment, increase production and support our external trade.
The lack of such a proposal is a great deficiency in Bill C-15. However, considering the past performance of this incompetent government, is it any wonder that it has always encouraged financial institutions instead of looking after the long-term welfare of Canadians?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this occasion is quite unique in that the motion of the Social Credit party raises the subject of interest rates. I was very concerned when I heard the budget speech and listened to the ensuing debate from both sides. At this time it is important to discuss the question of interest rates in our domestic monetary and fiscal policies, and we owe a debt to the Social Credit party for bringing this subject forward.
Earlier this afternoon the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Martin) participated in this debate. It was a rare occasion to hear a member of the government actually discussing the theory of budgeting and domestic monetary policy. Since 1 have been interested in the subject of monetary theory over the last 20 years, I could do no less than reply in kind.
The President of the Board of Economic Development Ministers (Mr. Andras) had recited a series of myths which have surrounded the government since the war. I will not go through the entire series but I should like to deal with just one, and that is interest rates. He suggested that interest rates were like old age: we must face up to them and accept them because of the alternative. That same attitude has been prevalent in the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance ever since I have been here.
I recall with great vividness the days of the Diefenbaker administration. At that time a new government, without a
Economic Policy
single person in cabinet who had previously been in government, attempted to face up to the realities of governing the country. The only advice it received was that which came from the Department of Finance and the Governor of the Bank of Canada. Even though the inflation rate at that time was approximately 1 per cent or 2 per cent, the department's officials and the Bank of Canada were worried. They began to push the idea that it was necessary to have higher interest rates in order to hold down inflation. Their idea was accepted by the government. In fact, businessmen flocked in and indicated that the idea was wonderful. Their job was to convert the debt.
Approximately $6.25 billion was converted to the higher rate of interest. The people in the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance deliberately set about raising the interest rate step by step. In a year and a half it rose approximately 20 per cent. Thus, the value of the bonds purchased by Canadians dropped by 20 per cent. Until this year, it was the greatest theft in the history of western civilization. I say that because a new record has been set today by the same mythology: if one wants to hold down inflation, one must raise interest rates. The same view is held by advisers to the American government. As I said in my budget speech two weeks ago, Canadians should not become involved in the same mess simply because the Americans have made such a fatal blunder.
I am not attempting to defend everything the minister said today. I realize the type of material which the nitwits in the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance put before every minister of finance. In view of the quantitative evidence we have today and which we did not have 20 years ago, it is thoroughly insulting when a faceless group of people advise the minister to stand up in the House and recite such a mythology.
Canadians are not interested in discussing theory. They know Canada is a strong country. They ask why we have been in a stagnant position for the last five years-when there is ample material wealth in our mines, forests and land, as well as wealth of human resources. The answer is in the fact that for the last 30 years the government has been receiving the same type of advice as the government of the United States. As the evidence develops, it is apparent that what Canadians thought was the truth 30 years ago is no longer the truth. The people we pay to run the Bank of Canada and advise the Minister of Finance should think more along these lines.
A little over a year ago, the economists of this nation met in Montreal in order to look at this problem. These disciplined economists who have been running this country for 30 years in business and in government finally faced up to reality and admitted publicly that they do not know where we have been, do not know where we are and do not know where we are going. These economists have now said this publicly, but economists have been saying this for four or five years in the United States. Yet still those who advise the governments of Canada and the United States are pouring out the same pap to those who are elected to govern the United States and Canada as they have for the last 30 years.

December 1, 1978
Economic Policy
Let me get down to some details. In my budget speech I referred to interest rates. I will not take too much time, but I want to quote four lines as follows:
-I am simply saying, as bluntly and as candidly as I can, that to move along the road of raising interest rates as a device to keep our dollar from dropping- is going to be costly for the people of Canada over the next year or so.
1 went on to make an exhortation. I was not the only one who attacked this mythology that if you raise interest rates you will check inflation. The new member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. de Cotret), who has risen to high places among economists in this country, in making his maiden speech used these words, and his language is much better than mine. 1 do not know how to use all these words correctly, but 1 think he does. Let me quote him as follows:
In an environment in which there is rampant excess demand, inflation, shortage of manpower, shortage of goods and in which we are facing bottlenecks, certainly a higher level of unemployment traditionally has led to a decrease in inflationary pressures. But in an environment in which no such pressures exist from the demand side, in an environment in which there is ample excess capacity, in which demand is weak, and in which unemployment is hovering between the 8 per cent and 9 per cent level, the economic and social costs of unemployment, far from decreasing inflation, are fed right through the line, add to the over-all cost pressures on the economy, and contribute to a higher rate of inflation. At that point the policy prescription is clear: we can fight both unemployment and inflation at the same time. I remain firmly convinced that that is an objective which we should set for ourselves.
Let me emphasize that phrase "cost pressures", because that is something I do understand. The hon. member for Ottawa Centre has put into the language of the intellectual the precise words I would like to be able to say. What we have been saying in these last 30 years, and what we have been doing in that time in Canada and the United States, has been wrong. In other words, that you can help the unemployment situation and decrease inflation at the same time. But these people who advise the government keep standing up and saying, as we have heard here today, that you must keep a balance, because if you try to slow down inflation you are going to make more unemployment, and if you try to reduce unemployment you are going to create more inflation.
The fancy name for that is the Phillips curve. Every economist of any reputation at all today has admitted publicly that the Phillips curve is a myth, a false truth. Yet we have this government coming out at this late hour saying it must continue that type of thing.
Theory is all right, but I should like to bring this theory down to the subject of this motion, which is interest rates. To be able to draft domestic monetary and fiscal policy today, the government basically must accept the fact that we are not in a demand-pull type of inflation, which is all those experts based on Keynes learned 30 years ago. What we are in today is not a demand-pull situation. As the hon. member for Ottawa Centre explained, what we are in is a cost-push situation, and these cost-pushes are well defined. Number one is the growing cost of government in all countries, not just in Canada; number two is the money supply; and number three is interest costs. There are three more of them.

1 accept what the parliamentary secretary said today in a well reasoned speech, that the Bank of Canada is beginning at long last to grapple with the problem of oversupply of money. It set up in the last three years these targets, although in the last two or three weeks it has got off target. Generally speaking, the Bank of Canada has done a good job in respect of what it calls the Ml money supply, but not so good a job in respect of M2 and M3. At least the bank is trying on that one point.
While trying to control the money supply, which adds up to a cost, the bank has deliberately raised our bank rate six times in the last year. This means in dollars and cents a fantastic amount of money in cost, particularly when you consider cost of business expanding in what is termed capital intensive areas. Most of our business falls into that category. When you get through all the guff of discounting cash flow which business uses, and after looking at all the things government and private industries are doing, buying farms and homes, you will find that in this enterprise which is capital-intensive approximately 75 per cent of the cost is interest cost. With such a big proportion of our costs being interest, and interest being one of the main cost-pushes in inflation, any government that will allow the Bank of Canada or the officials of the Department of Finance to push a policy of raising interest rates should have its head examined.
This government in all honesty and conviction came out strongly this last year in favour of a floating dollar. The big reason for having a floating dollar is that it makes you independent of other countries in respect of handling your domestic monetary and fiscal policy. It is only when you have a pegged dollar or a dollar tied to the system of other countries that you take on the burdens of those other countries as well as the assets. When your dollar is floating, each country is able to get at its basic domestic problems of inflation and unemployment. As a matter of fact, it is by having a floating dollar that you allow the world system to come in and help. When we get into trouble domestically the results show up in the value of our dollar internationally, and that is when the world system provides an advantage so that we can recover from our troubles. When you try to fool around with a dirty float in order to control or protect the value of your dollar, either by borrowing big sums abroad as this government did, or by this horror of horrors of raising interest rates, you cut off these world forces from moving in to help.
I want to close my remarks with some figures relating to costs. Suppose we allow the dollar to float. There has been a great deal of discussion quantitatively about what this costs us. The minister said today that when our dollar goes down our inflation rate rises. But by how much? One statement from the bank through the Department of Finance was that every drop of one cent in the international value of our dollar costs us one-tenth of a point in inflation.
We have the quantitative analysis theory of Professor Mun-dell, a Canadian who moved to the United States and who says
December 1, 1978

that over the long run a drop of one point on foreign exchange increases inflation one point in Canada. As far as I am concerned, the cost is somewhere in between that one-tenth of a point and one point. Nobody seems to be able to say for sure-1 have talked to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) and other people about it-but the figure is probably halfway between. In other words, if our dollar drops one point our inflation rate costs go up half a point.
Let us now take a look at this in big figures. Let us suppose that this is applied to our total gross national product of over $200 billion. One per cent would equal $2 billion and half of one per cent would equal $1 billion. Therefore, if our dollar drops one point we can expect approximately $1 billion in extra costs for that year.
What would be the cost in interest rates? Our bank rate has gone up by roughly 50 per cent, from just over 7 per cent to 10.75 per cent, which means that our prime rate has gone up at least 30 per cent, from somewhere around 8 per cent to 11 per cent. It would be fair to say that the ordinary individual who borrows has had an increase of 10 per cent in his interest costs. If we take 10 per cent of this figure of $200 billion, we get $20 billion. On that basis, if the dollar had been allowed to float the people of Canada would have paid in a year's time $1 billion in extra costs, but by this monkeying around with extra interest rates it will cost this country in 1979 at least $20 billion. That is a fantastic burden for the people of Canada to carry. Even if you cut that figure in half and make it $10 billion, it is still a large burden because there is a great difference between $10 billion and $1 billion.
In my speech I have tried to emphasize, at my level of language, that by choosing the route of raising interest rates as a means of controlling inflation is a costly procedure, ten to one over letting the dollar float. The country is struggling to get out of a period of stagnation, but it is loaded down with the cost of interest which ultimately stops us from going ahead.
What happens in the next few months is very important to the government. They are gambling that the few measures in the current budget will keep the country moving along fast enough so they can say that the country is improving. If this load of interest ever takes hold, as it will, it will send us down into the pits again, and the government will have only themselves to blame. Surely there must be someone over there who takes the time to read what the evidence is. They have all heard of Mundell and Laffer, and they have all heard the Republicans of the United States saying the same thing we are saying. Common sense would indicate that what this motion says is not, as the government would have us believe, that the rise in interest rates is not inflationary, but that the rise in interest rates is inflationary; and therefore it is essentially sound on that point.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext:
1
am pleased, Mr. Speaker, to be able to participate in this debate today. I would like to look at some of the questions raised by this motion. I have listened with interest to all the speeches that have been made in this debate. Although there are conflicting philosophies, there is, 1 believe, on the part of
Economic Policy
all those who have participated, a sincere desire to contribute some worth-while suggestions to the economic problems which we face in the country in the dilemma which governments find themselves at this particular juncture in history. I refer to governments of all political stripes, because if we look at the different governments across the nation, where there are political labels different from that of the federal government, they are doing no better than we are, unless there are extraordinary circumstances such as is the case in Alberta or areas which are being substantially helped by the federal government.
One of the proposals in this motion is that the House deplores the double standard of the government. I have noticed that only one speaker referred to that today, and he did so facetiously. The motion also talks about reducing the buying power of Canadian workers. It can be proven that the buying power of Canadian workers is in fact not being diminished. Indeed, I know of few countries where it costs workers as little as it costs workers in Canada to buy food, shelter, fuel, and the activities of leisure. So, by whatever stand one wants to pursue the fact is that in Canada we are doing very well on a relative basis compared to the other industrialized countries.
I would like to put a few figures on the record to prove my case. If we take a look at the real disposable income per capita and per employee in Canada as compared to the United States over the period of time this government has been in power- excepting this year because the figures are not in yet-taking 1968 as the base year of 100 and going through to 1977 we find that real personal disposable income per capita in Canada has risen from 100 to 151.9, whereas in the United States it has risen from 100 to 133. If we look at the real disposable income per capita for employees in Canada, we see that it has risen from 100 to 124, whereas in the United States it has risen from 100 to 112.3.
In other words, between 1968 and 1977 real personal disposable income per capita in Canada rose by 51.9 per cent and only by 33 per cent in the United States. Real personal disposable income per employee rose 24 per cent in Canada and 12.3 per cent in the United States. The United States, of course, is the foremost of the industrialized nations and the standard by which all other nations are judged.
Using that standard, Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that we have done quite well in Canada. We have made much progress in distributing wealth but, of course, there is always more progress to be made. We have not solved all our problems and no one would suggest that, except, perhaps, some rightwingers who do not believe in distribution of the nation's wealth.
We have programs of social services to help those who are unable to earn their own living, to help the ill, the maimed, the abandoned. We have old age security and the guaranteed income supplement as well as the spouse's allowance, all of which combine to make one of the best programs of any nation in the world. We look after senior citizens, those who have contributed to the growth and development of our country. No one should apologize that we make these transfer payments to

December 1, 1978
Economic Policy
our senior citizens, because if anyone had earned that kind of security for their twilight years, it is those who have built this country.
We have mothers' allowances and the youth allowances which are now being refined. In fact, for those in need they are being increased by something in the order of $160 per child per year. That additional sum will be paid as a lump sum payment from the federal treasury at the end of each fiscal year.
We are redistributing wealth through two of the most ambitious social programs ever undertaken by any government. I refer, of course, to hospitalization and medicare. I cannot stress enough the importance and value of those two programs. I would be the last to suggest that there have not been abuses of them or that the programs do not need some fine tuning. The fact is, however, that in Canada today we are raising a whole generation that has no idea what it means to pay a security-destroying medical or hospital bill. Those have been valuable social tools. I am sure there are senior citizens who are receiving first class medical treatment today who would have otherwise died long ago because they could not afford to go to a doctor or hospital. There are children growing up to be strong, useful and productive members of society who might have died because their parents could not afford to give them needed medical attention. Those are only two of the benefits of hospitalization and medicare.
Going back just thirty years, 1 think of my own family situation. My brother had to go to hospital for an appendectomy and my father had to borrow the money for that rather simple surgery from a bank. I am not about to go on any great political or emotional binge attacking the banks. Obviously, everything is not right with them or, indeed, with other things; but at least the banks serve a purpose and I think we should be responsible in our criticisms of them.
In the list of social programs, two others must be mentioned. The first is the Canada Pension Plan which is providing a source of security particularly for workers who are unorganized and do not have strong unions to negotiate a pension plan. All workers in Canada can look forward to a guaranteed source of income at retirement and will not have drastically to reduce their standard of living or beg from their families for shelter, food or any of the necessities of life.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we have unemployment insurance which has already been mentioned. This is also a social program which has been abused somewhat by workers but there have also been abuses by employers. I will not say any more about that today as 1 have already expressed my views on previous occasions.
A negative motion such as the one before the House is symptomatic of the negativism that is rampant in the country today. I wonder why.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext: 1 wonder why!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58(11)-ALLEGED DOUBLE STANDARD IN GOVERNMENT'S ECONOMIC POLICY
speechtext:
One of the reasons is sitting over there, Mr. Speaker. There are people who

see advantage in poor-mouthing our country. There are people who have not said one positive thing about Canada in this House in the last two years, I am sure. That is their choice, but let us look at how Canadians live.
There are all sorts of amenities in Canada today that most Canadians did not dream of a quarter of a century ago or even fifteen years ago. By any standard we are better off than almost any other nation in the world. That is not to say there are no problems, but I suggest we will not solve our problems by failing to recognize our successes. A nation's successes are important to the nation just as an individual's successes are important to the individual. If there is no sense of accomplishment. of achievement, of pride, then the individual will wither and so will the nation.
I urge those who seem to enjoy going about wringing their hands and complaining about how awful things are and what a terrible state the nation is in to start thinking about how gifted this nation is, how gifted its citizens are to have the advantages that have been bestowed upon them through divine providence. I urge them to be more thankful and less inclined to poor-mouth our achievements.
In the debate today we heard many criticisms and not much of a positive nature. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Rae), for instance, suggested there were two things that the review of the Bank Act should do but is not doing. One was to guarantee that banks will not make excess profits. That is a very laudable objective and 1 do not think anyone would argue with it. I am not so sure that it is always the obligation of the government, however. I would expect the New Democratic Party to put forward that view, of course, but surely those great lip service proponents of free enterprise and the free enterprise system, the Tories, would not agree that government alone is responsible for that. Surely market forces must be responsible to some extent for making the banks competitive and for seeing that they do not make excess profits.
The second mandatory condition was that a certain percentage of excess profits be used to subsidize some types of borrowing. If there are to be no excess profits, then certain percentages of nothing is nothing. So there would be no money to set aside in subsidization of certain types of borrowings. His argument is in effect a self-defeating argument.
I listened to the argument of the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). I must say 1 always enjoy his speeches; he delivers them with such power and force and such experience that they are a joy to listen to. But when he starts talking about a false truth, I become confused. One would only expect to hear that from the official opposition. Indeed, I did enjoy his explanation of the floating dollar but I do not agree with it. The floating dollar, as he said, is a way to align our economy with the other economies of the free world. But there is certainly more to it than that.
I want to return more specifically to the motion, which talks about a heavier public debt, and I want to spend just a few moments dealing with that. I will deal with it by going back
December 1, 1978

over a period of 25 years. In 1952 the per capita debt in Canada as a percentage of the gross national product was 42.9 per cent. In 1968 when this government came to power the debt as a percentage of gross national product was 22.7 per cent, almost half the figure for 1952. But in 1977, Mr. Speaker, the debt as a percentage of the gross national product on a per capita basis was 14.1 per cent. In other words, it was one-third of what it was in 1952 in percentage terms. That indicates we have been doing pretty badly, doesn't it? It indicates the bottom has fallen out of our world and Canada will come tumbling down!
1 know my time is up and I do not want to take extra time. The party who proposed this motion has another speaker and I do not want to deprive him of his time. I will conclude by saying that although we have problems in Canada, we are not on the verge of bankruptcy and we are not on the verge of destruction. We are a strong, healthy country and Canada is still the best country of any in which to live.
