I was going to ask why the government no longer believes it necessary to have a full time independent representation commissioner. Can the job be handled adequately on a part-time basis? These are some of the question we will have to ask.
Another thing we are concerned about is research. I do not want to get involved in this particularly because other members of this party are eager to jump in and condemn the government for its tunnel vision approach to research and science. This has resulted in many talented young people and people with expertise fleeing the country. This is one of the least understandable and at the same time one of the most important of the government's measures and I condemn them for it. We all know what will happen as a result of this tunnel vision.
The bill allows the Medical Research Council, the National Research Council, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council and the Social Science and Humanities Research Council to appoint and classify staff without ministerial approval. That is a very significant step and a very significant statement and the government House leader says it is what he wants. I must ask, however, what mechanisms are being put in place to ensure that this appointment and classification authority will not be abused. We have already seen how classification has been handled in the public service when it
January 23, 1979

has been delegated. I am talking about waste, Mr. Speaker. Misclassification and particularly overclassification which this government has allowed to proceed year after year through neglect, costs $75 million per year today.
I would just say, Mr. Speaker, that during my absence the President of the Treasury Board laid on the table the findings of the classification study. He did not have the courtesy to follow the practice of his predecessor who indicated that he would not only table this report but would also give us the solutions which the government found it necessary to implement in order to bring about the savings which are sorely needed to reduce government waste.
We know that there are incentives in the present system which lead to consistent overclassification, and we will get into that area as soon as we get the minister's estimates. I do not think that we are going to get any answers from the government on how they propose to save some $75 million on overclassifications. Can the government assure us that this will not also happen in the appointment and classification of positions in the research councils? Once again they have delegated the authority.
We are now looking into the whole question of Crown corporations, their conduct, their thrust and initiatives. I hope that the omnibus bill dealing with Crown corporations will soon come before the House. I know it will not come before the election, of course, because the government does not care about this. They would let the Crown corporations carry on as they are doing even though some of them have a history of throwing the taxpayers' money down the drain and of pursuing questionable practices to the disadvantage of the public.
I return to my concern about the government's tunnel vision regarding these councils and its lack of understanding of them. Mr. Speaker, there are priorities and priorities. When it comes to the research and development that affects in particular the Medical Research Council and the National Research Council, we wonder whether government is on the right track in delegating its authority.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I must say that the bill makes an interesting change with regard to parliamentary secretaries. Subsection 2(2) of the Parliamentary Secretaries Act at present reads as follows:
(2) There shall not be at any one time more parliamentary secretaries than the number of ministers who hold offices for which salaries are provided in section 4 of the Salaries Act.
Clause 31 of the bill provides that this section shall now read as follows:
(2) There shall not be appointed more parliamentary secretaries than the number of ministers who hold offices for which salaries are provided in section 4 of the Salaries Act.
The purpose of the amendment is to clean up an anomaly in the act. At present the act requires that if a minister resigns then a parliamentary secretary must also resign. There cannot at any time be more parliamentary secretaries than there are ministers. The amendment does not allow for an increase in the number of parliamentary secretaries but rather fixes the number at the time of appointment.

An important point which 1 think goes to the root of the matter, Mr. Speaker, is that the resignation of a minister would no longer require the resignation of a parliamentary secretary and therefore, as a result of this amendment, there could be more parliamentary secretaries than ministers.
I think I have put the position of my party on several matters of concern before the House. I do not intend to speak longer because I know there are other members on this side of the House, including members of the New Democratic Party, who wish to speak on matters that they find either satisfactory or objectionable in the bill.
I cannot give the government House leader the assurance of quick passage that he is seeking for the bill, however. We do not intend to filibuster the bill, but I feel that if he were sincere about this whole matter he would have included the questions of the fisheries and the environment. It is my view that the government is not sincere and has thrown a lot of other things into the bill. We have no alternative in this party but to take a stand, having been given this opportunity to register our concerns on behalf of constituents in all regions of the country.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was my understanding that as lead speaker for his party and as lead speaker for my party, the comments should be fairly general. I understood his comments should point to his party's proposals and ideas as to how this bill should be written. That is what my comments were about.
I was saying that in the area of fishery development, if the Conservative party takes power after the next election, with their backward looking views in this area we may be back to the fishing admiral days. If anyone knows Newfoundland history, they will know that was one of the most repressive types of arrangements in our history. It went out with the end of the eighteenth century.
I am going to deal with Parts I and II of this bill. Part I sets up a separate department of fisheries and oceans. Part II establishes a fisheries and oceans research advisory council. As I mentioned, other members of my party will deal with other sections of the bill.
We in this party support the setting up of a separate department of fisheries and oceans. As has been pointed out, it reflects a campaign promise on the part of the government made in 1974 to set up a separate department of fisheries. It is interesting the government is getting around to it just before the coming election. The government has belatedly recognized the proper emphasis that should be placed on the fishery and the importance of the fishery to the economy of this country.
In Newfoundland there are some 27,000 fishermen prosecuting the fishery. In Newfoundland, fishery processing involves some 8,000 man-years of work. To give a further indication of the size of the fishery in Newfoundland, in 1978 some 430,000 tonnes were harvested with a value of $106 million. Nationally some 66,000 fishermen are involved in the fishery. The value to Canada nationally was close to half a billion dollars, representing a catch of 1 'k million tonnes of fish. This indicates that the fishery is of extreme importance to this country. By setting up this separate department the government is only now recognizing this fact by its actions and not just by its words.
This new department must be concerned with fisheries development. In fisheries development, the department has a very powerful tool to shape not only the fishing industry but the communities and the social structure of the areas where the fishing process takes place. Our contention is that the department must move toward three basic areas. First, there has to be local or Canadian control of the industry. Second, there has to be maximum benefit established on the east coast to coastal communities. Third, we have to manage the stocks and issue licences in light of the social requirements and social problems that must be solved in the communities where the fishing industry is located.
I will begin by dealing with foreign investment in the fishery. This is becoming a serious problem on the west coast of this country. Foreign interest now control over 10 per cent

of the industry's assets on the west coast. The bulk of these foreign interests are in Japan. The frightening thing is not so much that 10 per cent is foreign-controlled, but that this 10 per cent has been acquired almost overnight.
The cause of this has been the lack of proper planning of the industry on the west coast. The west coast fishing industry, as with the industry on the east coast, should be an integral part of an industrial strategy or plan based on Canada's resources. Our leader said this when he was on the west coast last week. He pointed out that the cause of the problem of foreign investment is the lack of an industrial strategy.
The reason for the influx of Japanese capital with its resultant control is the fact that it has not been available locally. Canadian banks and lending institutions have been reluctant to make loans to canneries, fish processors and fishermen for years. We feel the government should, within the framework of an over-all industrial strategy, make sure that capital is available so that fish companies and individual fishermen do not have to go to foreign sources in order to obtain capital to develop their industry.
On the east coast, the government's record is a little better in this area. At least in one case the government used its licensing powers to ensure that valuable fish resources did not fall into the hands of foreigners. I refer specifically to the proposed takeover of the Ocean Harvesters processing plant in Harbour Grace, Newfoundland, by the Nord See group of West Germany. I applaud this approach on the part of the government and I hope this trend continues.
In their approach to the fisheries, the Tories would seem to give us investment at any cost. Certainly they pressured the federal government and the provincial government of Newfoundland for this type of investment. They supported the takeover by the West German company and generally have supported this sort of foreign intrusion into this Canadian resource which, in the long term, would not do anything for us. I applaud the government's approach to this question and hope the new department continues on this route. I am sure the present minister will ensure that it does.
Another area of concern is how development of the industry takes place. In the sixties, proposals for development were very capital intensive. There were plans and proposals for large freezer trawlers plying the Grand Banks and the east coast fishery. That, of course, was before the advent of the 200-mile limit. It was at a time when foreign countries had their massive capital intensive fleets on our offshore and were reaping great benefits.
Fisheries development must be considered with social development as well. The midshore and offshore fishery, which is a sort of capital intensive fishery that was recommended ten years ago and beyond, requires a centralized development. It requires the establishment of large cities and towns, large centres from where the fishery can be serviced and prosecuted. This tends to reinforce the deterioration of the small coastal rural communities, especially on the east coast of this country.
January 23, 1979

On the west coast, the fishery is fairly well developed. It has set patterns. However, a change must take place on the east coast. If not done in a careful manner, this change could destroy existing living patterns which have gone on for centuries and create much disruption in lifestyles.
The trend has changed in Newfoundland over the past few years. I submit the fishermen's union was a major influence. The federal Department of Fisheries recognized that development of the fisheries has to take place while considering the communities from which the fishery takes place. The Tories do not seem to be sensitive to these needs. They would prefer development to follow the needs of the big fish companies, not those of the fishermen in the rural communities.
It is important to develop the fishery in a way compatible with traditional patterns of life. It is important that change should not come about too fast. We should recognize that most of the fishermen on the east coast are part-time fishermen. Part of their income, perhaps the major part, comes from fishing during the summer, but during the winter they cut wood or engage in some other part-time job. There are few full-time fishermen in the Newfoundland context and due regard must be paid to this situation.
If the department concentrates on full-time fishermen, the social impact will be profound, particularly on young people about to enter the industry. Traditionally, sons begin work in the fishery with the help of their fathers. Many part-time fishermen in my riding have found it difficult to introduce their sons to the fishery. I trust the department will recognize the problem and come forward with proposals for suitable compensation during periods of dislocation.
In recent years licensing arrangements have begun to change traditional patterns in the fishing industry. We recognize the need for a forward-looking, coherent policy for the development of the fishery, but while restricted entry to the industry might be desirable in the long term, such a move toward an elite corps of fishermen would cause tremendous dislocation in the short term and could give rise to a great deal of unemployment and hardship affecting individual fishermen in coastal communities. It is most important to consider the realities which exist in these communities when making overall fisheries policy, and I am confident the new department will do this.
The licence freezes of the past few years have caused hardship. I recognize there is bound to be dislocation, but we must surely minimize the extent of that dislocation. Certain licences have been frozen for some time; I have in mind, especially, those required for lobster and certain species of groundfish. The part-time fishermen, who constitute a majority in the Atlantic region, have been hit hard, new entrants into the fishery have been hit hard, and the future of young people has become uncertain. Should they stay in their communities with the expectation that they can enter the fishery, or should they go to Alberta or Toronto, for instance, to seek jobs there?

These are serious questions and they must be dealt with; I trust the minister will consider them very carefully.
The new department, through its licensing policy, could have a tremendous impact on local conditions along the east coast. It could also have an important impact on the size of fish stocks. It is necessary to balance the social cost to communities against the benefits of conservation. By varying the number of fishermen engaged in the industry we could change the recovery rate among fish stocks. If fishing were completely cut out for one year, fish stocks would probably recover in one year, but what would be the effect upon thousands of fishermen? It seems to me that if we allowed unlimited entry to the fisheries, stocks would continue to decline; so the need for some sort of balance must be recognized, always bearing in mind the needs of the rural communities.
I should like to turn my attention for a few moments to the seal fishery and its relationship to the fishing industry in general. What impact do the seal herds have on fish stocks? It is estimated there are about 1.3 million seals in the herd along the east coast. Each seal eats about 15 pounds of fish a day on the average. I have done the arithmetic and this works out to approximately 3.2 million metric tons of fish a year consumed by the seal herd off the east coast. Looking at the total fish landings on the east coast last year we see they amounted to less than a million metric tons, so seals are right now consuming three times as much fish as Canadian fishermen are catching off the east coast.
The figures I have given are, of course, approximate because it is impossible to ascertain just how much fish seals eat. Nevertheless, the information is very valuable in terms of the annual irrational debate and also because of the fact that the minister seems in part to have given in to the protesters. This year the quota for the seal hunt has been set at a level which would see a small increase in the seal population, thereby endangering fish stocks even more. So another thing the department should seriously consider is whether in the light of the continuing controversy over the seal hunt it is the fishermen or the seals which will get the fish off the east coast. If the seal stocks increase, as the protesters would wish, many fishermen will be unable to make a living because the fish just won't be there. This is a decision which the new department will have to approach with some care. I trust the minister will give this matter his consideration. His record thus far has been good and I trust it will continue.
I turn, now, to part II of the bill. Under these provisions there is a proposal to change the name of the Fisheries Research Board to the Fisheries and Oceans Research Advisory Council. I will not comment on the board itself or the work it has done, but in my view the new reorganizing bill has one substantial flaw. In setting up the council the proposal totally neglects representation by fishermen themselves or by their organizations. Clause 4 of part II of Bill C-35 provides:
4. (1) The Council shall consist of a chairman and not more than 24 other members.
(2) A majority of the members of the Council shall be scientists.

Now we come to subclause (3), the subclause I am most concerned about:
(3) The members of the Council shall include persons from
(a)	departments, boards and agencies of the Government of Canada that have a specialized interest in the marine sciences;
(b)	universities and other educational institutions;
(c)	the fisheries industries and industries that have a specialized interest in the marine sciences; and

Mr. Speaker, it could be said that the reference in subsection (d) to the general public having representation on the council might include fishermen and their organizations. But I suggest this is much too important a council to warrant the omission from its constitution of a specific reference to fishermen or their organizations. Let us face it, Mr. Speaker, the fishermen are the ones who will be directly affected by the recommendations this council will make. The council will be making recommendations in the area of quotas, fish stocks and so on, and it would appear to me to be essential that fishermen, fishermen's unions and fishermen's organizations should have a voice on this council, not just the industry or company representatives.
Over-all, Mr. Speaker, we support this move of the government to place the proper emphasis on the fishery by setting up this separate department of fisheries and oceans. There is much promise for the future of the fishery in this country, especially off the east coast, since the declaration of the 200-mile limit. Through this department the federal government in Ottawa has to provide leadership to the industry in two main areas, management and foreign relations. By properly managing and controlling fish stocks, quotas and the issuing of licences which permit entry into the fishery, the department can shape the whole face of the industry. It can have a big impact on the social fabric of coastal communities where the fishery takes place. This is something which I know the minister has approached before, and I think he is moving in the right direction on it.
However, the government has failed in the past with regard to the foreign relations aspect of its responsibilities involving fisheries. It took many years for the government in this country to match the efforts of small countries such as Iceland and Norway in extending our offshore jurisdiction. Iceland is a very tiny country with a population of probably not half that of the city of Ottawa, and it relies on fish perhaps even more than the city of Ottawa relies on government.

It took many years for this government to match the efforts of Iceland in extending jurisdiction over offshore fishery resources, and now that that has been done, I applaud it. But it came many years too late. Now, because of inaction in foreign markets, the Canadian fishing industry has been placed in a back seat position regarding a place in world markets. The problem is fairly simple: 85 per cent of our fish exports go to the United States, but Americans eat only about

nine pounds of fish per person per year. Europe and Japan, which are big fish-eating areas of the world, consume much larger amounts of fish, but we have a very small place in their markets. Part of the problem is tariffs. Part of the problem is that we cannot enter or find it difficult to enter markets because of tariff arrangements against processed fish. At this point in time we should be actively and aggressively pursuing new markets.
Right now we have an export advantage. As much as hon. members from time to time decry the devaluation of the dollar, with regard to export industries it is fairly evident that it is an advantage. The devaluation of the dollar of some 15 per cent in recent months is about the same as the tariff on processed fish entering the European Common Market, so at the present time we have an advantage. The devaluation of the dollar balances the tariff, so now is the time for us to be actively pursuing European markets. Because it is only by pursuing those markets and gaining a foothold in those markets for processed fish that we can have maximum benefit for the economies of the east and west coasts. In order to get maximum benefit for these economies there has to be the maximum amount of processing of fish at the local level.
I would like to quote from the report of the People's Commission on Unemployment. I have done this before. I want to quote from this report because I think it is a very good report. It contains a very good analysis of the Newfoundland economy in particular, but with regard to fisheries it applies to the industry nationally. One of the recommendations of the commission is found at page 103 of the report and reads as follows:
That a policy of total processing and packaging of our fish be implemented to provide more jobs here in Newfoundland, tariff restrictions notwithstanding.
Tariff restrictions are the main problem right now, but we can get around that by aggressive marketing policies, especially now when we have an advantage on the international market because of our devalued dollar.
I trust that this new department will look to the future of the fishery and will foster the future development of the industry in a way which will benefit people on the east coast- fishermen, processors, plant workers-and also fishermen on inland waters as well as on the west coast. Our party supports this move as a good reflection that the government recognizes the importance of the fishery to this country now.

Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome this opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-35. As the present minister is well aware, I think it is in the area of Marseilles, France, where people make a special dish. I believe they call it bouillabaisse. The minister will have to correct me on my pronunciation, but I think that is a rich fish stew which contains just about every type of fish which comes out of the sea. Bill C-35 could well be called bouillabaisse because it contains many words which apply to the Department of Fisheries and the Environment as well as many other items.
January 23, 1979

Nevertheless, I am pleased to note that the government has finally decided to re-establish a separate department of fisheries called the department of fisheries and oceans. The peril, however, in bringing forward this measure in an omnibus bill is that it could needlessly be delayed because of problems associated with other parts of it. In our view the part of Bill C-35 dealing with the establishment of a department of fisheries and oceans should have been brought forward separately and divorced from the other parts of the bill.
Actually, we should not be discussing the re-establishment of a separate department of fisheries at all. The fact that we are discussing this matter is a direct result of the Liberal government's having needlessly ended the existence of the department of fisheries in 1970. Having made that change, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) soon suffered some political remorse over what he had done because in the 1974 election campaign he promised to establish a separate department of fisheries. Five long years later it appears that this promise is finally coming to fruition. I add that this is somewhat typical of Liberal promises, especially campaign promises; they are long on words and short on action.
It should also be noted that this bill is very similar to Bill C-65, which was very hurriedly introduced on the second last sitting day before last summer's recess. Obviously, the Prime Minister wanted to place that bill on the record in case he decided to call a fall election. However, things then started to happen. We had a Gallup poll, we had a Goldfarb poll, we had the North Pole, the South Pole and the "roly-pol". All these polls seemed to frighten the Prime Minister out of his wits, and when he could not find the courage to call an election, what did he do? Did his government introduce his bill at the first opportunity? It did not. It delayed action for another five months.
In fact, further delays could result from the government's seeing fit to introduce an omnibus bill dealing not only with the re-establishment of a separate department of fisheries, but also with the employees of Canada Patents and Development Limited, the representation commissioner, the Medical Research Council, the National Research Council, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council, parliamentary secretaries and the Department of the Environment. I submit that these measures could well have been dealt with in a separate bill.
It should also be recognized that the establishment of the new department will not in itself be a cure-all for all the problems which presently plague Canada's fishing industry. The proposal by our lead speaker that this bill be referred to the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry is one that I endorse. I think various proposals in the bill would be more acceptable if the debate were carried out in that particular committee, since those members of the Commons who have expertise in fisheries and the environment generally are present at the meetings of that committee. So I think it would help bring forth a better bill. This is a proposal I endorse and throw out for consideration by the government.

The measure of success of any government policy cannot be based upon the government's view of things, but rather upon the view of others, especially those directly involved in the industry. This leads us to ask how the government's fisheries policy is faring. In the letter to the Prime Minister of September 22, 1978, the Fisheries Council of Canada stated:
We are deeply concerned that the potential of our industry will not be realized because your approach to the country's economic problems is not being followed in respect to fisheries. In fact in fisheries the government's approach is one of increasing intervention and opposition to the private sector.
To realize the opportunities, it is necessary to establish a continuity of investment. As Mr. Chretien has put it, encourage risk taking and willingness to spend in the private sector that is essential to get the economy growing faster.
But the council points out that this depends in turn to a large extent on the creation and maintenance by government of a favourable climate for future investment.
The letter goes on to say that the council regrets the government's approach to fisheries is not creating a favourable climate for long-term investment, and they itemize some of the main problems as follows. First is the refusal of the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) to issue to Canadians licences for freezer factory vessels. This is particularly difficult to understand when such Canadian vessels would replace only foreign effort and would not reduce by a single pound the existing catch of any Canadian fisherman. Second are the unclear and unwise policies in such areas as ownership of vessels; and third, the ad hoc manipulation of the fisheries resource instead of forward planning for development.
It is my understanding that this letter was almost completely ignored by our Prime Minister. He sent only a pro forma reply thanking the fisheries council for its views. I submit that the time is long past for nice words of gratitude. I submit that what is needed now is action, or otherwise the Canadian fishing industry will lose the optimum benefits of the 200-mile limit which we on this side have originally proposed.
The fisheries council points out that the federal government has the complete responsibility for the management of the fisheries resource and that lack of jurisdiction over the stocks in the past has handicapped the ability of Canadian scientists and resource managers to carry out their mandate. However, the council makes the point that the scientists are now in a position to manage properly, but they have much to do in gathering knowledge of stock size and population dynamics. This is the area where the federal government has the responsibility and the expertise, and it is here that it should be directing its efforts rather than in commercial activities which must be the responsibility of the private sector.
I endorse those views of the council on behalf of the fishermen. What was the government's response to this important recommendation? Almost at the same time that it was being made, the government announced its decision to close down the Halifax fisheries laboratory, effective April 1, 1979, and its plan to discontinue all programs involved in research oriented toward the secondary fishing sector; that is, fish processing. The stupidity of this move became evident finally

January 23, 1979
Government Organization
even to this government, and on December 21, 1978, the minister, in a press release containing the kind of double talk to which we have become accustomed from this government, stated that he had completed his review of cutbacks in fisheries technological development programs and said he had no intention of reducing essential fisheries research. I ask the minister, when he replies in this debate, as I am sure he will, to define to the fishermen of Canada and to the people of Canada his interpretation of the meaning of the word "essential".
He has stated that the fisheries technological laboratories at Halifax and Vancouver would not be closed down, which I submit is comparable to telling the crew of a ship: "Have no fear, your ship will sail, the only difference being that there will be a few changes; there will be no captain, mate, cook, bosun or engineer." At Halifax, where there was a total staff of only 79, some 23 scientists will be laid off. On the west coast, where there is a staff of only 31, some 11 scientists will be dismissed. The only place where no changes are contemplated is in Newfoundland where, as I understand it, only seven scientists are employed.
At the Halifax laboratory, for example, there are at least four divisions. In the resource utilization division, 11 scientists, including the division chief, will be dismissed. This minister and this government have destroyed the division, which leaves us to ask: Just what were these scientists doing? They were studying and developing processes for utilizing fish for human consumption which would otherwise be turned into fishmeal or thrown overboard, completely discarded. They were developing new processes for mincing and flossing saltfish, new storage techniques, such as hypobarric or reduced pressure storage so that fish could be stored for longer periods. All of this important work now goes by the board.
In the chemistry division where studies were carried out on the nutritional value of fish, among other things, ten scientists will be displaced. Perhaps their most important work was on the value of marine oils to mankind. But this work is considered unimportant by this government and by the minister so three research scientists, three chemists, a biologist and three technicians will be dismissed.
The industrial development division remains untouched, but in program management two out of four of the key men presently employed will be laid off. So much for the minister's announcement.
The minister in his statement of December 21, 1978, said:
With the resurgence of the fishing industry in the past year or so, companies should now be in a position to meet these development costs themselves.
The minister seems to forget, for example, that lobster fishermen are individuals, that they generally do not own large companies and they are therefore not in a position to continue the studies of the fisheries laboratory on wet storage for lobsters, or the studies on the relationship of offshore and inshore lobster stocks, or the studies on an acceptable substitute for artificial baits for lobsters so that valuable mackerel and herring presently used for lobster bait could be sold for human consumption, thereby increasing the fishermen's income.

The actions taken by this government will seriously affect our fishermen and our secondary industry. They are in direct contradiction to the advice given to the government by the industry. I submit that this policy, which the minister stands by so firmly, should be changed. In fact, when making these changes in our scientific staff, no mechanism whatsoever has been established for the transferral of the 54 years of basic research expertise either to the provincial governments or to private industry. Some of these scientists have ten to 15 years or more of experience, and this type of know-how once lost cannot easily be regained. Some of these scientists already are planning to go to the United States out of necessity and the need to obtain employment. Their knowledge will soon be aiding our competition. These scientists were showing our individual fishermen and our secondary industry how to upgrade their product.
Therefore, we view this section of the minister's fisheries policy as a retrograde step which should be reconsidered. Following the next election, when we on this side form the federal government-

The year 1979 will mark the third year since the declaration of our 200-mile limit. Consequently, the industry believes that a policy should be established now for controlled expansion of inshore and offshore fleets, and providing for the selection of licences to be unfrozen in a fair, equitable and orderly manner. By establishing such a policy now, some unnecessary uncertainty would be removed as vessel licence owners would know the order in which licences would be unfrozen, and along with shipyard operators they could plan for the sizeable investments which will be required.
Instead of following this course, on December 4, 1978, the minister announced a six-month freeze on new entries to the inshore fishery in most Atlantic coast areas. Canada cannot reap the potential benefits of the 200-mile limit if its fleet does

not have the capacity to harvest the fish stocks available during the next decade. Many of the vessels in the present fleet are technologically obsolete.
Much of the fish allocated by Canada to foreign countries is of non-traditional species, such as squid and silver hake. These species cannot be landed in good market condition by present Canadian trawlers. Rather, they are caught by foreign freezer trawlers. He said: Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to ask this House to pass Bill C-218, to amend the Canada Shipping Act. Perhaps the easiest way to explain this measure would be to read from the explanatory notes in the Bill itself:
This bill recognizes that modern bulk carriers can carry millions of dollars worth of oil or other potential pollutants and that the damage from a massive oil spill can run into the tens of millions of dollars. Its purpose is to make the penalties for operating a vessel in such a way that it poses a threat to the environment commensurate with the damage such action can cause. It is hoped that the significant deterrent provided in this bill will more fully ensure that Canadian regulations designed to prevent pollution are obeyed completely.
All too often Canada has neglected her maritime heritage and minimized the importance of the seas to the nation. "From sea unto sea" is not motto which restricts us; the seas do not hedge us in; rather they are our highways to the world. While we can all mouth such bold phrases as "the world's longest coastline", "coasts on three oceans", these have been homilies often repeated but seldom acted upon.
Perhaps we need to look at these situations in new ways if we are to realize again the importance of our maritime commerce. Consider the fact that eight of the provinces have ports which handle international cargo. Moreover, and somewhat paradoxically, the two land-locked provinces, Saskatchewan and Alberta, are heavily dependent upon ocean transport for shipping grain, one of Canada's most important exports.
Just as too many of us have failed to realize the vital importance to Canada of maritime commerce and of our ocean resources, this government has allowed the Canada Shipping Act to become outdated. It is, sadly, an act which was written for earlier times. It is an act which needs to be amended so that its provisions will be relevant to today's shipping. It is for this reason that I propose these amendments to the Canada Shipping Act.
I should make it clear at once that I do not expect that the specific element of this bill-an increase in the fines which can be assessed under the act-will solve the problems created by this government's lack of concern with maritime affairs. Similarly, I am familiar enough with the ways of this house to know that extensive modifications of an act as complex as the Canada Shipping Act cannot be expected to be realized through the mechanism of the private member's bill. Rather, I have introduced this bill to point out one of the particularly simple ways in which the government has allowed the act to become outdated. It is my hope that this will prompt the government to amend the act to bring it into reasonable accord with today's situation in shipping.
Of particular concern to the residents of coastal communities is the potential for disastrous pollution posed by today's supertankers. Twenty years ago, when tankers of 40,000 tons were the largest to be seen and oil was cheap, fines of $100,000 may well have seemed Draconian; now with tankers of 400,000 tons and cargoes of oil worth tens of millions of dollars, those fines pale into insignificance. Supertankers have indeed forced a complete rethinking and re-evaluation of the seas and shipping and the relation that these bear to society as
January 23, 1979

a whole. Ships which may take half an hour and four miles to stop, which have a turning radius measured in miles, and which have the colossal momentum required to do significant damage while barely moving, are not the ships which the shipping act was designed to cover.
What we must admit is that these ships force us to re-think the nature of freedom of the seas: that is, the relation between littoral states themselves. These changes have been made necessary by the changed nature of the ships; they have been made urgent by the scale of damage which a mishap can now cause. The changes being wrought in these areas fall into two major categories: changes to ships, the way they are built, maintained and manned; and, secondly, changes to the ways in which ships may be operated.
Let us begin with the first category. In some ways this is the easier group to deal with as the problems are largely technical-matters of design and reporting procedures. Even these changes are not straightforward, however.
The 1973 conventions of the Inter-Governmental Maritime Consultative Organization, known as IMCO, were not ratified largely because of difficulties with the drafting of the technical articles. Now that the errors of the 1973 conventions have largely been rectified by the 1978 conventions, it is time for the Canadian government to ratify these protocols. That these protocols require amendments to the Canada Shipping Act is all the more reason for the government to sign the protocols, as they could use the opportunity to bring about other improvements to the act.
In looking over these protocols it is apparent that much of the concern of the convention has been with the pollution caused by current habits of dumping the oily residue left after flushing tanks which have been unloaded. While such pollution is certainly not as spectacular as that created by tanker founderings, the cumulative effects of such minor incidents are far more severe, and it is with the consequences that we must be concerned. If stopping two hundred gallon spills or one hundred flushes lack the high profile politically of swinging into action after a disaster, that is too bad. We must concentrate on what does the most good, no matter how mundane the continual inspection of radar, steering systems and clear segregated ballast may seem to be.
The tendency of this government to go in for big, splashy programs, often at the expense of effectiveness, is of particular concern to me. I should like to relate to the House a particularly frustrating example, one which was the result of oil leakage or tank flushing, the major source of oil pollution.
Some five years ago the municipality of Oak Bay, which is in my constituency, suffered a small oil spill offshore. The municipality was made aware of this before the oil came to shore and they set about with an emergency crew to mop up the damage before it became worse by drifting on to the sand and rocks of the foreshore. They were able to complete the work within hours at a cost of S430.
They started very quickly trying to recover this money from the government, which has assumed the responsibility of
Canada Shipping Act
paying the claims of people who are not covered or not able to claim against the ships involved. This is accomplished by application to an unusual little organization which looks after the maritime pollution disaster fund. This may have started off being a small organization, but with claims of 15 cents per ton for every ton of oil that is shipped into Canada, or from one point in Canada to another, over several years this has amounted to some $48 million or $49 million.
From time to time I have put questions on the order paper concerning this maritime pollution disaster fund. The last question was answered on December 15 just over a month ago. At page 2178 of Hansard for that date we find the following question:
What is the total amount accumulated in the maritime pollution claims fund?
The answer was $48,997,810.93. The second part of the question, which might be even more interesting, was:
How many payments have been made from the fund in each case (a) in what amount (b) to whom (c) on what date?
The answer to the question what had been paid out of this $48 million was that there had been two claims, one for $345.90 to a Mr. William Guimond, a fisherman at Pointe au Pere, Quebec, on October 23, 1975; and a second payment of $300 to a Mr. Eudore Boudreau, fisherman, Carleton, Quebec, on January 5, 1977. So we have managed to pay out $645.90 of that $48,997,810.93 in the fund. I would also point out that they quit contributing to that fund according to last year's report of this organization. The report reads:
The payment into the fund of 15 cents in respect of each ton of oil-was cancelled as of September 1, 1976-
I suppose it is of interest only to people in this House that there seems to be a slight difference in the balance of the fund at the present time. The current report which was tabled today shows a balance of $46,936,174, whereas according to the order paper answer which I received in December it was $48,997,000, an extra $2 million which must have come from somewhere. It may be interest accrued on the $46 million which they had last spring.
I took the occasion to get in touch with these people regarding the Oak Bay problem. I eventually found that the government has a set of reasons as to why one cannot qualify for these funds. One qualification which Oak Bay did not meet was that they did not have previous Privy Council approval for cleaning up the oil spill. How ridiculous can an act get, when it expects a municipality with a three-hour time difference and faced with an incoming small oil spill at midnight to wake up the Privy Council?
We cannot wake them up during question period, so how on earth is Oak Bay going to wake them up at three o'clock in the morning to get approval to clean up the oil spill before it drifts ashore? I would hope that some minister of transport some day will be able to find out just what the reasons are as to why no money ever comes out of the maritime pollution disaster fund and why the fund does not satisfy the ordinary means of the
2480

January 23, 1979
Canada Shipping Act
small communities which run the most danger from such disasters.
I think that this example demonstrates, Mr. Speaker, that legislation in this area must be flexible, but, above all, responsive to the immediate problems, not just the spectacular problems. Similarly, the technical changes which need to be made to Canadian shipping regulations-such as back-up radar, twin screws, segregated ballast, properly trained crew and careful inspection-are vital, though perhaps not overwhelmingly exciting. We must ensure that in these areas the appropriate authority, in most cases the coastguard, has the resources required to do a thorough job as well as sufficient authority to ensure full compliance with the regulations and sanctions such as those proposed here.
Earlier I referred to another type of change which will have to be made if maritime shipping is to be made safer-changes to the human side and the way the ships are operated. I realize that these questions are often harder to deal with than the seeming complexity of technical changes, and I certainly approach this end of the problem with some reticence. The fact remains, however, that the best designed ships will not of themselves prevent accidents; much also depends upon the maintenance of the ship and the diligence and training of the crew. Unfortunately, time after time when spills are investigated it is found that the crews were overworked, undertrained, and that basic equipment was not up to par. In this regard I would like to refer to the findings of Dr. McTaggart-Cowan's inquiry into the Arrow disaster. He found that the radar had ceased to function an hour before the ship struck, the echo sounder had not been in working condition for two months, and the gyrocompass had a permanent error of three degrees. I read now from the conclusions of that committee of enquiry:
We are well aware of the fact that no form of transportation can be 100 per cent safe but from the record available to us, the standard of operation of the world's tanker fleets, particularly those under flags of convenience is so appalling and so far from the kind of safety which science, engineering and technology can bring to those who care, that the people of the world should demand immediate action.
As Dr. McTaggart-Cowan points out, one of the primary obstacles to realizing significant change is the refuge offered by flags of convenience. It is impossible to believe that Liberia makes even the most perfunctory effort to ensure that ships registered there are competently manned or in proper running order. In this regard I would like to quote from a report tabled today by the administrator of the maritime pollution claims fund where he speaks of an incident when the Island Spruce broke adrift from her tow, resulting in a suit to recover the cost of an action to prevent oil pollution:
The ship-owner, the Cayman Islands corporation, does not appear to have been insured, nor, at the moment, to have any apparent assets upon which to realize.
Of course not, it is a one ship company. The world is plagued with these one ship companies which have as their sole asset one single ship, and if it runs aground they simply abandon it. This effectively shields the actual owners from any responsibility. While the Canadian authorities have had to try to deal with this problem by inspections after the ships have

docked, this is clearly an after-the-fact approach, as the ships have already made their oil-laden journey. What seems to me to be needed is tighter international licensing regulations of both men and machines, as well as more uniform international inspection. This may seem impractical for some. However, I am drawn to compare the situation in international maritime trade with that of international civil aviation. In that field, the International Civil Aviation Organization, ICAO, has been highly successful in imposing technical and personal standards and in facilitating the adoption of uniform standards in guidance systems.
Let us consider ICAO's success to see whether we can learn from it any lessons which could be used to strengthen bodies like the Intergovernmental Maritime Consultative Organization, IMCO. The universality of ICAO regulations seems to stem in part from the fact that countries use them as basic regulations for all planes landing there. The locus of enforcement or initiative is shifted to the nation of registration. As well, many countries, particularly among the advanced industrial states, have registered supplemental accord raising their standards above the basic ICAO levels.
The conclusion should be clear, that even in the absence of sufficiently stringent IMCO regulations, the oil consuming nations could band together to enact stricter rules for ships using their ports. As these ports represent an overwhelming percentage of the trade for oil tankers, market forces would soon make these the effective minimum standards. By enacting such standards jointly, Canada, Japan, the United States, the EEC and Scandinavia could effectively set the standards for world oil shipping.
There is another aspect of this subject, Mr. Speaker; I would like to compare our approach to shipping with that of aviation. This facet of the question concerns the control of ship movements and knowledge of those movements. While in aviation there is a ground control which knows of the movements of all commercial aircraft in its area, no such mechanism exists in even heavily-used, major waterways such as the English Channel. Similarly, while an airplane pilot must keep ground control closely informed of any problem, no such imperative exists for ocean commerce.
One of the particularly upsetting features of the Amoco Cadiz foundering was that the French coastguard was not informed until after several hours of negotiation and then an attempted rescue by a German tug. This neglect of the public interest, despite the fact that the damage to the shipping cargo may be dwarfed by the damage to the coastline, is a relic of older times and must be changed.
I see that my time has just about expired. I would simply say that we must open up the shipping act one way or another. I am not foolish enough to be optimistic about the passage of this bill, Mr. Speaker. I have proposed these amendments to the Canada Shipping Act because I fear that the act has failed to keep pace with the rapid changes in world shipping, particularly with respect to the transportation of oil and products such as liquid natural gas. Canada should be pressing strongly
January 23, 1979

for better ships to transport these commodities, and for tighter controls over the manning of these vessels.
To these ends we should ratify the IMCO accords of 1973 and 1978 and continue to press for tighter regulation of crew training. Unilaterally, Canada should continue to inspect ships closely and demand high standards of ships using Canadian waters. We must make sure that the coastguard has sufficient resources to do this as well as perform the increased duties brought on by the 200-mile limit. In addition, there must be sanctions sufficient to deter those who would ignore Canada's attempts to protect her maritime environment.

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh A. Anderson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subsubtopic: INCREASED PENALTIES FOR POLLUTION OF WATERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, apparently the intention of Bill C-218 is to set the maximum fine for certain offences under the Canada Shipping Act at three times the combined value of the ship and its cargo, thus acting as a much greater deterrent in case of massive oil and other pollution spills. The present maximum fine is $100,000.
As a member of parliament from British Columbia representing a constituency on Vancouver Island, I must say there is a great deal of basic sympathy for the remarks made by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon). I think many of his statements are fitting and correct, but regarding the proposed provisions for three times the combined value of the ship and its cargo, while I think the basic idea is both commendable and interesting, upon closer scrutiny the proposal begins to show some serious weaknesses, not the least of which is a scatter-gun philosophy which fails to take into consideration other forms of penalties. The end result could be harshly punitive and far out of proportion to the offence committed. What the proposed bill does not do, Mr. Speaker, is take into account the differing nature of offences specified in the Canada Shipping Act and its regulations.
The bill would, in effect, result in a maximum fine of three times the combined value of the ship and its cargo applicable to: failure to comply with a pollution prevention officer's orders or directions; sections dealing with evidence of financial responsibility by the owner of the ship or its cargo for civil liability purposes; regulations dealing with fitting, maintenance, testing and use of electronic and other navigational equipment; infractions and maximum quantities of pollutants; loading procedures; navigation practices; records to be kept on ships and certificates showing compliance with the act and regulations, and on and on. The proposed bill, containing one single nucleus of a deterrent, would presumably hope to cover this wide variety of possible offences. It would encompass everything.
There have been a number of major pollution incidents over the past decade which have focused international attention on marine spills, such as the one involving the Arrow, the Argo Merchant, and in 1978, the incident where the Amoco Cadiz oil spill drenched the holiday coastal areas of France. These
Canada Shipping Act
events were accidental in nature and mainly the result of human error or abnormal or unusual conditions.
Unless evidence is produced showing that these types of disasters were due to criminal negligence or acts on the part of the master of the ship or other persons, action to obtain compensation for pollution damage must be taken through procedures other than the act, or other regulations and provisions, since the latter exclude accidental spills due to stranding, collision and foundering, or discharges to save lives or the ship itself.
When one considers the scope and nature of the Canada Shipping Act and the regulatory provisions which relate to oil pollution or other types of spillage, plus the types and variety of vessels subject to these provisions, it becomes quite obvious that a maximum penalty of three times the value of the ship and its cargo is not only inappropriate but excessive. As an example, this bill could mean that a ship's master who failed to keep proper records on pollutants could forfeit a $1 million cargo and a $5 million ship upon conviction for a comparatively minor offence.
The penalty could obviously be disproportionate as well where the master, owner or member of a crew has committed a minor offence, or in instances involving offences by small ships, tugs, fishing boats or pleasure craft.
There is yet another consideration, Mr. Speaker, and that refers to the possible escalation of fines implied in the proposed bill. In 1957, when the first regulations to prevent oil pollution from ships were promulgated, the penalty was a maximum $500 fine or six months' imprisonment, or both. This was raised to $5,000 in 1965 and to the present $100,000 maximum level in 1971. It is interesting to note that over this period the actual fines imposed have risen from a few dollars in 1957 to the average level today of $4,000, with the highest individual fine being $20,000. This bill would alter the current maximum $100,000 fine and introduce new levels of monetary punishment inconsistent with what is generally accepted as an effective deterrent.
With respect to the maximum fine being set as the combined value of the ship and its cargo, it is felt that problems would be encountered by the court and Crown counsel. It would devolve on the Crown to submit evidence of the combined value of the ship and cargo in order that the court know the limit of the fine that could be assessed. While this may not be an onerous process in the case of a minor infraction involving a large ship, it could be so in the case of a major infraction involving a small ship against which the court desires to impose a more severe penalty.
While it cannot be denied that, in the case of massive oil spills, the coastal state affected is not only highly concerned in protecting its resources but will of necessity seek adequate compensation for clean-up costs, nevertheless a reasonable degree of objectivity which takes into account the magnitude and nature of the offence, the circumstances surrounding it and the persons or ships involved, must be maintained.
80047-16 (4

January 23, 1979
Canada Shipping Act
1 believe, Mr. Speaker, that a key point that must be borne in mind is that the penalties to which this bill addresses itself are specifically for cases where deliberate and wilful contravention of regulations and directions of a pollution prevention officer occur. The penalties are not intended to provide any form of compensation against pollution damage to property, resources or costs of clean-up.
Another interesting point, Mr. Speaker, is that part XX of the act provides that the owner of a ship carrying a pollutant in bulk is liable for the costs and expenses of any action authorized by the governor in council to repair or remedy any condition resulting from pollutant discharge by the ship.
Such liability as referred to in this clause is not dependent upon proof of fault or negligence; but no person is liable for costs and expenses where he can establish that the discharge was caused by another person or where the cause was through an act of war, hostilities, or was of an exceptional, inevitable and irresistible character.
In addition, Mr. Speaker, this serves as a reminder that the maritime pollution claims fund, established under provisions of section 737 of the act, operates as an unsatisfied judgment fund, similar to that established in most provinces covering damages incurred as a result of automobile accidents where the driver at fault is not insured.
The proposals in this bill are, in my opinion, too general in nature to cover the national and international requirements for pollution control. If the bill should become law, it would be unfair. The bill as proposed fails to take into consideration the present diversity of legislation which has so far demonstrated its effectiveness in Canada as a deterrent. While I said I have a general sympathy for the direction in which the hon. member is going, the proposals contained in the bill are neither practical nor desirable amendments to the Canada Shipping Act at this time.
In British Columbia there is a great concern about oil spillage on the Pacific coast. One issue which has united most members from the province of British Columbia in this House is the opposition to the creation of an oil port at Kitimat. I think it is fair to say that the people of British Columbia do not want to be involved in the possibility of an oil spill in the transshipment of American or other foreign oil that would be transshipped through Kitimat to the northern tier states. This government has taken the position that it opposes the development of Kitimat on that basis.
It is interesting to note that a consortium of companies has apparently started a further drive to have Kitimat opened as an ocean-going port for transshipment of Indonesian, perhaps Arab and certainly Alaskan oil. I also understand the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle) has supported the policy of the development of Kitimat as a port of transshipment of oil. He has stated he is in favour of this proposal and that if the Conservative party is elected as the government in the next election, it will proceed with this port.

I raise this because the hon. member for Victoria, for the very best of reasons, is concerned about oil spillage, while another member of the same party would support the transshipment of oil, realizing the dangers of a spill in that area.
It is all very well to talk about changing legislation and increasing fines. However, I hope the hon. member for Victoria will agree that in this situation the way to solve the problem of pollution, especially on the west coast of British Columbia, is not to increase the fines, but to not allow the port of Kitimat to go into operation in any sense, regardless of who supports it in the United States.
The reason Kitimat is being proposed at this time is the fact that by going from Alaska to Kitimat you go from an American port to a foreign port. The shipper therefore is not bound under the Jones act to use American carriers. By going from Alaska to Kitimat he can, as the hon. member mentioned, use flags of convenience. For that reason alone I have great fear about Kitimat being opened as an oil port, as well as the dangers because of the topography, because the entrance is too narrow for huge oil tankers.
Increasing fines is not the answer for the port of Kitimat. Members on all sides of this House should state that we will not develop Kitimat for the use of the United States which would have all of the benefits but none of the ecological or environmental problems. I hope the hon. member will agree that the solution to problems such as Kitimat is not increasing the fines for oil spills but by not allowing it to happen in the first place, and ensuring that the United States and the consortium interested in developing Kitimat are clearly told that members on all sides of this House will not tolerate development of the port of Kitimat.
