speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Lapointe (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: INCREASED PENALTIES FOR POLLUTION OF WATERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) for his proposal to increase fines in the case of water pollution caused by oil spills, and since I am aware of the love of the hon. member for his region and the natural beauty of Vancouver Island, I understand that he must be very concerned about the possibility of pollution.
At the present time, section 752 of the Canada Shipping Act provides a maximum fine of $100,000 for any person or any ship discharging a pollutant in contravention of any regulation made pursuant to section 728. The suggestion of the hon. member to set the amount of the fine so as not to exceed three times the combined value of the ship and its cargo is certainly interesting, but its application could present many problems, and I shall try to explain some of the difficulties that could result from such an amendment.
The present legislation aims at producing a deterrent effect in the cases of massive discharge of oil or other pollutants. Such cases result in extremely high cleaning costs as well as possible and often major damage to the maritime environment and the coastal regions. In this regard, I would refer to the
January 23, 1979

accident of the Amoco Cadiz on the coast of Britanny which discharged 200,000 metric tons of oil which then spread over more than 100 kilometres along the Britanny coast. As everyone will recall, this catastrophe not only destroyed marine life forms, but also chased away summer vacationers. This is one of the many such cases which greatly concern us, and such an accident could well occur along the Canadian coastline despite the action that has already been taken.
Maritime pollution is therefore a major problem and a risk that we must recognize. In this regard, these amendments would extend the penalties not only to the sections of the legislation which provide for the interdiction and control of oil spills, to the directives given to pollution prevention officers, to the proof of financial responsibility that ship owners must provide, but also to the violations of the regulations provided under the sections of part XX of the act, which concern such things as the good condition, the maintenance and the use of electronic navigation equipment, the maximum quantity of pollutants which can be shipped and the means and facilities provided for storage.
Those regulations apply also to the supplies and equipment the vessels should have for the treatment of pollutants, the storage of oil residues, to the supply, keeping and use of maps and nautical publications, to the number and qualifications of officers and crew members, to navigation practices and procedure, to the records, the process for loading and unloading the pollutants and the possession of certificates required by the law and related regulations.
I wish to say that if we apply more severe sanctions for contravening the provisions of the law and related regulations we would not take into account the different nature of offences described in this legislation. In most cases of oil spills, be it the Amoco Cadiz I mentioned earlier or the Arrow or the Argo Merchant which have been the most important oil spills in recent years, those are accidental disasters resulting most of the time from human error or abnormal or unusual conditions. Unless we have proof that such disasters are due to criminal negligence or imputable to the captain of the ship or other people, to claim a compensation we must follow procedures other than that of the law or the regulations mentioned earlier. In fact, those provisions exclude accidental spills due to leakage, collision and so on.
Compensation for damages caused by oil spills is provided by the legislation through provisions other than those I mentioned earlier. Section 734 holds responsible the owners of a polluter vessel and they have to pay all cleaning costs and expenses as established by the governor in council and the losses or damages incurred by the Crown or other individuals. In no case must there be proof of human error or negligence to establish the responsibility of the owner of a ship or cargo.
Canada Shipping Act
In addition to the preceding considerations, the Maritime Pollution Claims Fund, established under section 737 of the act, provides for unsatisfactory findings. This fund can be drawn upon where shipowner claims for cleaning expenditures and other pollution damages are not fully satisfactory.
In this connection, I followed with great interest the remarks by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) concerning the fund's inefficiency-or operating difficulties. I also regret that Oak Bay could not get the $300 or $400 compensation due because of regulations that are somewhat too stringent in my view, or too narrowly interpreted.
I am certain the comments made by hon. member and the bringing of this matter to the attention of the House can bring improvements and those charged with the administration of the fund will have a more open mind and somewhat less literal in their interpretation of the regulations.
As stated by my colleague the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Anderson), the act and the regulations apply to a wide variety of ships, either supertankers, tankers, bulk carriers, dry good carriers, general cargo or bulk carriers, containerships, passenger ships and what not, private yachts, tugs and other small boats registered either in Canada or abroad. It might then make for heavy administration if the penalties were extended to all such classes of ships that do not always fall into the same category, as supertankers or tankers.
When the type and variety of ships subject to the act and regulations are considered, and also the nature and scope of the regulations section, it seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that a fine three times the value of the ship and its cargo are considered highly excessive in a number of cases by many people in the maritime field.
Although it cannot be denied that in the case of major oil spills, the province affected is deeply concerned for the protection of its resources and claims adequate compensation for cleaning costs, a reasonable degree of objectivity that takes into account the nature and the extent of the fault as well as the related circumstances and the persons involved must nevertheless be maintained.
When minor offences are committed by small vessels, or by the captain or the crew, in such a case, Mr. Speaker, the fine would definitely be out of proportion. Although the ruling concerning the amount of the Fine ultimately remains the responsibility of the court, a higher maximum penalty could indeed result in raising the fines now imposed.
I think that my colleague from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Anderson) also raised that point when he said that in 1957, when the first regulations for the prevention of sea pollution were established, the maximum penalty then was $500 or six months in jail or both. And yet at that time the maximum fines imposed by the court ranged from a few dollars up to about half of the maximum amount. In 1965 the maximum penalty was raised

January 23, 1979
Canada Shipping Act
to $5,000 and fines up to this maximum were imposed until 1971. During this period, the average fine was approximately $1,000. Since 1971, with the enforcement of Part XX of the act, while the maximum fine is now $100,000, the biggest fine that was imposed was only $20,000 and the average has been only $4,000.
The number of investigations and the number of court actions finalized each year have not increased. While the ideal situation would be of course a total lack of violation of the law, it can be considered, Mr. Speaker, that the present level of fines is a major dissuasive factor. However, Canadian courts clearly have wide latitude to impose higher fines, should the need arise, since they use only one quarter of the maximum available.
As regards the proposal to establish a fine representing three times the value of the ship and its cargo, one must consider the problems that the court and the Crown would be facing in any action. According to the size of the ship as well as to the type and nature of its cargo, the Crown has to prove the combined value so that the court can know the limit of the fine to be imposed. If such a calculation can be approximate, it is nonetheless a complex process, particularly where the cargo is composed of different commodities.
Although the investigation should not be too costly in the case of minor offences involving large ships, it could however be expensive where smaller ships are involved in major offences for which the court could wish to impose a higher fine. Furthermore, in the case of actions against people, some of them having possibly no relation with the accused ship, as in the case of longshoremen for example, the proposed penalty seems altogether disproportionate.
According to the considerations mentioned earlier, it does not seem that the proposal in Bill C-218 is at the present time a desirable amendment to the Canada Shipping Act.
Again, the bill would increase the limit of the fines, which is presently $100,000, applicable for failure to comply with the act and its regulations in all areas. What does it mean exactly? It means for example that if there is discharge of one or several pollutants such as specified in the regulations, except for two which are authorized under part XX of the Canada Shipping Act, in all waters covered by the said part and regulations, that penalty could also apply to any person falling under the provisions who fails to give some evidence of financial responsibility such as insurance, salvage bond or any other kind of evidence of financial responsibility which satisfies the Minister of Transport, in the case of civil liability resulting from oil spills. In case of failure to comply with any reasonable requirement of a pollution prevention officer or to provide some information concerning the condition of the ship, its machinery and equipment, the nature, quantity and location of its cargo; as well as failure for a ship that is within waters

described in part XX of the legislation to comply with any order or instruction of a pollution prevention officer about its route, the manner it should proceed to anchor and moor, if the pollution prevention officer has reasonable grounds to believe that the ship fails to comply with any regulation or that such an order is warranted to avoid pollutant spills.
Penalties are also levied in case of failure of a ship to comply with any order or instruction of a pollution prevention officer to report its position.
Mr. Speaker, in addition the higher penalties would apply for failure to comply with the regulations established under section 730(l)(c) to (l)(o) of the legislation and then it would become a little more difficult to levy such penalties respecting the fitting, maintenance, testing and use of electronic and other navigational gear.
Penalties could also be levied under section 730 for other classes of ships and the maximum quantity of pollutants that may be carried aboard such ships whether as cargo or otherwise, as well as the method of stowage of the cargo or fuel in such holds and tanks; respecting the supplies and equipment and the fitting and installations required for the handling of pollutants and dealing with any discharge thereof; respecting the method of retention of oily and other wastes by ships carrying pollutants; respecting regulations applicable to the maintenance and use of appropriate charts, tide tables and other nautical publications; respecting the number and qualifications of navigation and engine room personnel, including pilots and lookouts required to be on duty aboard; respecting procedures to be followed when pollutants are loaded or unloaded from a ship; respecting procedures and practices to be followed by persons on board ships in order to ensure safe navigation; for the supplies and equipment to be maintained by the operators of loading and unloading facilities for ships for use in the event of any discharge of a pollutant; and finally for records to be kept on board of any activities which result in or may result in the discharge of a pollutant as well as for the persons by whom such records shall be kept.
There are still other cases, Mr. Speaker, such as the prevention of the pollution of the air by ships, the establishment of compulsory traffic routes and of other shipping traffic controls considered necessary for safe navigation in waters to which part XX applies, the issue to the owner or master of any ship of a certificate that, in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, is proof of the compliance of such ship with the requirements of the act. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, because of all these considerations, as I was saying, I do not think it would be wise at the present time to amend the Canada Shipping Act by passing Bill C-218 proposed by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon).

subsubtopic: INCREASED PENALTIES FOR POLLUTION OF WATERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1979, it is an unquestionable fact that pollution of all kinds, be it air, water or even sight pollution, is increasingly worrying the people of all countries and more
January 23, 1979

particularly the people of Canada. Bill C-218, proposed to the House by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon) reflects all the concerns expressed by the Canadian public, concerns which the hon. member wishes to still-and I can understand that-by means of his amendment to the Canada Shipping Act.
The hon. member for Victoria should be commended for his initiative although I, like the previous speakers, have some doubts about the possibility of implementing the propositions he made to the House.
Mr. Speaker, water is much too vital an element in the life of a nation to let anybody use and abuse it with impunity and inconsiderately. Water serves not only to generate electricity, which is indispensable for the economic development of our country and creates a great many jobs for our labour force, but it facilitates the transport of goods or makes sailing and canoeing possible; it contains resources which are a source of food and make it possible for thousands of Canadians to earn a living.
When one thinks of the enormous problems the fishing industry has been faced with over the past few years, one can easily appreciate that water pollution resulting from the discharge of oil, gas and other pollutants from ships in our waters is a very important cause of the deterioration of our marine resources.
Mr. Speaker, I can remember at least two instances of the consequences of oil spills by ships in my riding. Naturally, those accidents could perhaps have been avoided; I really do not know. Perhaps, from the technological angle, the ships involved might have been built to ensure more security, but in one case there was an accident: the ship struck a rock and unfortunately spilled gallons of oil which polluted not only the water but the beaches of the Magdalene Islands among others. In 1974 or 1975, there was a case similar to the one mentioned a while ago by the hon. member for Victoria, along Chaleur Bay, in my own parish of Carleton, and over roughly a 30-mile stretch. There was a cleaning operation, but even now traces of residue can still be found of the pollution caused by the Golden Robin. That was the name of the ship involved in the accident.
Since it is almost six o'clock, I should like to make a few remarks on the speech of the sponsor of the bill to the effect that what he is suggesting is intended to remedy the neglect of the present government. Mr. Speaker, to my mind, no federal government has ever done as much as this one to help prevent water pollution. I could name all the bills introduced by the Minister of Transport and the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment: the Clean Air Act which states, the legislation which indicates what to do with wastes spilled in the water. I think one can say there was no negligence. True, one could go to extremes, but in a society where private enterprise is expected to participate to such a great extent, restrictions must not be too numerous. I am surprised that the hon. member for Victoria, whose party supports private enterprise, should come
Government Organization
and suggest such a fine, though I can understand that, in some cases, it might be reasonable where there was gross negligence. But when, by sheer accident, a ship spills oil or other pollutants without any fault on its part, I think it would be imposing a little too much constraint on this ship's owner. If we impose payment of up to three times the value, we will not see many ships navigating in our waters.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. MacEachen (for the Prime Minister) that Bill C-35, respecting the organization of the Government of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House adjourned for private members' hour at five o'clock I was debating Bill C-35 which deals primarily with establishing a separate department of fisheries and oceans. I pointed out at that time that there are many grave concerns within the fishing industry at present, and now I suggest that the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) should become acquainted with them.
The Canadian fishing industry can compete in world markets, but I submit it should not be handicapped by unfair competition and by a federal government reluctant to show leadership in attaining fair competition for our fishing industry. An integral part of any successful fisheries policy, I submit, must be consultation. In this matter, the road which the federal government has travelled has been paved with failure.
In 1975, for example, changes were made in the Atlantic lobster industry. Only after the recommendations were drawn up were the fishermen involved and concerned invited to participate; and then they were invited to the Citadel Inn in

January 23, 1979
Government Organization
Halifax for one day and asked to digest some 160 pages of regulations drawn up by the minister and his bureaucrats here in Ottawa. No wonder that the fishermen claimed there has not been a real chance to participate in the decision-making process.
The lobster fishing policy of the present government is frightening-that is the only word I can use. It is frightening to read some of the letters that I receive from my constituents, men who have been fishing since they were 12 years old, and because they decided they could not make a living as lobster fishermen they had to participate in some other form of fishing. The minister and his bureaucrats have stated that the fishermen's lobster fishing licences will not be renewed, that they cannot follow two forms of fishing. The minister is saying in effect that they must starve as lobster fishermen. Let me point out that the same edict does not apply to defeated politicians. For example, we have one in Nova Scotia who was defeated, namely, the premier of that province, and they made him a Senator. He now draws senatorial pay, which is sufficient. He is also serving as president of Dalhousie university. It seems there are no restrictions on moonlighting for defeated Liberal politicians, but let a fisherman decide that he is starving as a lobster fisherman, and when he asks the minister to please renew his licence even though he must do some other form of fishing, the minister says, "No way, you cannot hold down two jobs. You must make up your mind." Those are the words he used when the scallop fishermen came here from Digby, Nova Scotia. When they came before the committee, what did the minister say? He would not even appear to meet with them right here in Ottawa, and yet he talks about consultation. The minister should hide his head in shame-

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
-because he refused to consult with the people who were being legislated against by him and his department, when they came here to the capital at their own expense to meet with him and his associates. They were refused any right to discuss their problems.
We submit there was no consultation. This was evident during the committee's hearings last session on the bill to amend the Fisheries Act. At that time province after province came forward to testify they had not been consulted despite the fact that the bill dealt in part with pollution and environmental control, areas of shared provincial responsibility. Consequently, a Progressive Conservative government, which we hope to have soon in Canada, would do its utmost to maintain a close and continuing liaison with the fishermen, the industry and the provinces so that their viewpoints would be taken into account in the drafting and implementing of present and future fishery policies. No more do we want to hear the following complaint, as expressed by the Halifax Chronicle-Herald:
The federal officials appear disposed these days to think only in terms of handouts when it comes to maritime needs.
Thus, it is with some regret that one measures the success of this Liberal government's fisheries policies. The potential brought forth by the declaration of the 200-mile limit is enormous, but federal government inaction in fishery development could negate the achievement of optimum benefit from this limit.
Canada now has the opportunity to become the world's largest exporter of seafood products during the next decade. Because of changing factors in the industry, it should be able to increase substantially the degree of processing of fisheries products. However, without a planned and positive approach to the major policy issues facing this industry, which issues 1 outlined in my remarks earlier today, and the elimination of present uncertainty, many of the available opportunities may not be realized. A realization of these opportunities is critical to the creation of additional jobs and the establishment of a solid economic base for the fishing industry so that it can compete in all world markets in the years ahead.
We need a policy which would encourage investment in the fisheries by any and all Canadians. The minister has made public statements to the effect that only practising fishermen could and should invest in fishing vessels. He is on record as stating this. I cannot understand where the minister obtained such a policy. For example, does the minister believe that only bankers should own shares in banks, that only miners should own shares in mines, that only architects should own shares in buildings? The minister's proposal is ridiculous and just does not make any sense. While we on this side agree that fishermen should be encouraged to invest to a greater degree in their own ships, the fact remains that the present fleet will require a great deal of capital for replacement and expansion when appropriate. Rather than restricting the classes of investors, the government should be encouraging a broadening of the investor base. This is the concept on which private industry is based. It is the only concept which assures the greatest participation of Canadians in the growth of this important primary industry.
The minister cannot continue on his present course without bringing disaster to our area. It does not take an economic genius to realize that one cannot substantially inflate prices and costs, ban production, as the minister has done by freezing licences for the inshore fleet, the lobster fishermen and the scallop fishermen, increase taxes, and expect vigorous, healthy production. They are just not compatible. Only intellectual basket cases in the realm of economic reasoning would follow the course the minister is pursuing at present. For example, in the United States, with a population of 235 million people, the deficit this year is predicted as being $29 billion. In Canada, with a population of only 23 million people, we are facing a declared $13 billion deficit which may end up at $15 billion. This course can lead only to the total disruption of our productive capacity.
In conclusion, when the minister is free of his joint responsibilities as Minister of Fisheries and the Environment and is able to devote all his energies to our fisheries problems, I hope

January 23, 1979

he will give some thought along the lines I have mentioned toward its greater progressive development.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the party to which I have the honour and good fortune to belong has long been urging the establishment of a separate department of fisheries. To that extent we welcome this bill. We would welcome it with more open arms if it were confined to the division of the Department of Fisheries and the Environment into its two component parts, environment and fisheries. But this bill is a grab bag. It has many other components with which 1 do not propose to deal at any great length.
The hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) has spoken with experience as a background, with knowledge gained from that experience, and from close study of the problems. He spoke about the fishing problem on the east coast. I propose to deal only briefly with some of the fishing problems on the west coast. In due course some of my colleagues from the west coast will wish to make their contributions to that particular area.
In beginning my comments, I hope-and this is something of a more general nature-the minister will be able to provide the House and Canadians with some account of where we stand in our bilateral talks with the United States on the matter of fisheries and boundaries. One hears conflicting rumours as to what state the boundary talks are in, and it may very well have been decided that they should go to arbitration on the east coast. According to an announcement made approximately two weeks ago, it was decided by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson), I hope in conjunction and collaboration with the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc), to leave the west coast problems aside for the time being and deal with the east coast. They are both difficult problems, and no one will deny that.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext: What about the north coast?

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
Of course there is the north coast as well and the Gulf of Alaska. 1 do not really think the government is capable of handling these complex problems. It cannot handle our economy. It has run us into the ground on that. What sort of results will we receive out of these discussions, even with the best negotiators in the world? With the political direction they have, I doubt very much we will receive what we ought to receive out of these talks. Before the debate on second reading terminates in the House, I hope we will have some indication from the minister as to where the talks on the boundaries, fisheries and other resources stand.
On the subject of fisheries on the west coast, I will deal primarily with the environmental aspect. I feel I have an obligation to mention some of the problems on the west coast. They are current because within the next six weeks there will be a large fishery opening on the west coast, and there is utter confusion among the trailers and the gillnetters. Only today I received a telegram from the gillnetters concerning the new regulations which were issued after the gillnetters had re-equipped their vessels to go out and fish. They spent thou-
Government Organization
sands of dollars to bring their gillnet equipment up to date in order to go out and fish, and now the new regulations have [DOT] been issued. The same situation is hanging over the heads of the trailer men.
I have a feeling that both trailer men and gillnetters are small business men. Sometimes they are pretty big business men, but they are independent. These are the people this government should be encouraging rather than discouraging, and that is what is happening as a result of these regulations. Our trailer men are being regulated out of business. Our gillnetters are being driven out, so that all we will have left will be employees or hands working for the companies owning the ships. They will be hands on board the ships, recruited in the recruiting halls. This is only part of the fishing industry, but an important part, made up of independent fishermen who operate trailers, and the gillnetters. They must not be regulated out of existence, but they fear for the extermination of their kind. 1 hope there will be a re-examination of the regulations which have been drawn up and which are condemning them to extinction.
I have in the past made a number of comments about the forestry aspects of this bill and I should like to do so again this evening. I will leave the better part of that to my colleague, the hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle). I am sure he will draw on his experience to bring to the attention of the House and the Canadian public some of the disasters brought on by this government through its neglect of the forestry industry, and particularly by its attack on forest research programs of the current department and the department that will be taken over by the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand).
I am sure the government will be bound to reply in the usual way by stating it has done wonders for the forestry industry, yet it cuts back on a number of important forestry research programs in the interest of so called economies, short run economies, I might add.
The same can be said, of course, about cutbacks in fisheries research programs run by the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment. Again, these are short-term economies. It defeats me how this government can rationalize cutbacks in research programs aimed at increasing productivity in a particular sector. I just do not and cannot understand that. I am sure the Canadian public, particularly those who have devoted their lives to these programs, will ask themselves similar questions.
If these cutbacks were related to research projects in areas where they may or may not contribute in the long run to the economy, I could understand the government taking no risks at a time of restraint. Anyone can understand that attitude. However, there are many programs at this time of restraint which could have been cut as they are not productive and do not contribute in the long term to growth and development in our economy. Yet this government chose to cut back on productive research programs. What I am saying is that when

January 23, 1979
Government Organization
research is virtually certain to add to the GNP we should not have cutbacks, as has been the case in respect of fisheries research programs on both coasts.
Let me make one final comment on the fisheries side now that I have found out, according to this bill, that "whales is fish." They ain't, Mr. Speaker, but according to this bill "whales is fish."

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext: They are mammals.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
I know they are mammals, but for the purposes of this bill and this minister a whale is a fish. This minister is going to be responsible for the Canadian attitude in respect of the whaling community of the world. For the time being, and only for the time being, he will be speaking for Canada at the International Whaling Commission. I wondered for a time whether whales would fall on the environmental side or on the fisheries side, but I discovered after looking at the small print that they fall within the purview of the Minister of Fisheries. That being so, it is no wonder, at the International Whaling Conference in London recently, Canada's attitude caused a certain amount of dismay.
Although we are no longer a whaling nation-we have not been for years but at one time we did have a great whaling fleet-Canada regularly argues in support of and votes with Japan, which is a whaling nation. Canada supports the taking of whales, that largest of the earth's mammals, although it is a fish as far as this minister is concerned. It is the largest of the earth's mammals and is on the verge of extinction. There has been practically a universal call for the cessation of whaling on the high seas. I see the minister shaking his head. Obviously he just has not been listening. He has plugs in both ears. The fact remains that Canada, although not a whaling nation, is supporting and contributing to the taking of whales on the high seas in a manner which is completely inexplicable. I will now leave the minister with his whales which he does not know are mammals, and will turn to the purely environmental aspects of this bill.
It seems to me that the department of the environment created by this bill will not really have the responsibility commensurate with the name. What the bill says is one thing, and what it does not say is another. I would draw to your attention, Mr. Speaker, the throne speech of October 8, 1970, in which the Governor General, in outlining the programs of the government of the day, said:
There will be proposed the establishment of a department to be concerned with the environment and the husbanding of those renewable resources that are a part and dependent upon it, with a mandate for the protection of the biosphere.
I would draw your attention to that final phrase, "with a mandate for the protection of the biosphere."
That legislation was brought forward that year also in an omnibus bill. The bill eventually became Chapter 42, 1970 Elizabeth II. Like the present bill it was cited as the Government Organization Act of 1970. It did set up on that occasion, as it appears at page 847 of the Consolidated Statutes of 1970, 1971 and 1972, the Department of the Environment. Among

the things that department was intended to do, and in conformity with the undertaking given in the Speech from the Throne, and included in its duties and powers, was the protection and enhancement of the quality of the natural environment. At that time the department covered fisheries off our sea coasts and inland fisheries.
Let me draw your attention again to that phrase "protection and enhancement", because that will come up again as we continue our consideration. First let me deal with this mandate for the protection of the biosphere. I must ask myself where the mandate is for the protection of the biosphere when the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is responsible for the Arctic Waters Pollution Prevention Act and the Northern Inland Waters Act? Where is that mandate to protect the biosphere when the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources is responsible for the Atomic Energy Control Act and, I believe, nuclear waste, a matter which we considered in the standing committee on national resources, not in the committee on the environment? The disposal of nuclear waste is an environmental concern. Is that the mandate which this minister will exercise?
I would ask also where that mandate is when the Department of Transport is responsible for the Canada Shipping Act and, more important, the oil pollution prevention regulations stemming therefrom? The Department of Transport also names a delegate to the International Maritime Co-operation Organization where pollution, among other things, is not very high on the agenda. Is this the mandate that the Department of the Environment is going to exercise?
The Department of Agriculture is responsible for the Pest Control Products Act. Is there no pollution there, and is it not an environmental concern? The Department of National Health and Welfare is, ironically, responsible for the Environmental Contaminants Act. What is the Department of Environment doing? All its responsibilities have been farmed out or have been assumed in the past by other departments. Where then is this mandate to protect, as indicated in the Speech from the Throne and as the original bill says-"the protection and enhancement of the quality of the natural environment"?
If the word is protect in accordance with the terminology in the Speech from the Throne, why was the word "protection" deleted in this particular bill and another word presented in its place? The word here is "preservation". The original bill which was passed in 1970 provided that the minister shall be responsible for "the protection and enhancement of the environment." Now we find that among the duties, powers and functions of the Minister of the Environment is the "preservation and enhancement of the environment."
I wonder if the minister understands the difference between these two words, or is there a difference in his mind? Is this just a drafting error? To my way of thinking the preservation of something as distinct from the protection of something means that we are pretty well satisfied with the way it is and we are going to preserve it as such. That is the role of the
January 23, 1979

Minister of the Environment, to preserve it the way it is and, on occasion, to ensure its enhancement.
I find that particular change in terminology unusual. It occurs in both the English and the French portions of the bill. In the earlier bill on the French side it reads:

-the protection and enhancement of the quality of the natural environment-

In the new bill it reads:

-the preservation and enhancement-

This occurs not just once, but twice. It occurs not only under clause 14 which is a rewriting of section 5 of the original act, but also in clause 6, the revised version of section 6 in the original act. The Minister of the Environment in exercising his powers shall, "promote and encourage the institution of practices and conduct leading to the better preservation"-not protection, but preservation-"and enhancement of environmental quality". This may appear insignificant, but I hope the minister will be able to explain why the wording has been changed, because preservation has a static ring about it whereas protection is a more aggressive activity, to my way of thinking. I am sure that some of us will be watching very carefully to see whether he does in fact explain the distinction which must be there, or will this be another cace of 74 amendments as occurred in the Bank Act?
How many amendments to the bill is the government going to bring down before we get through the committee? On many occasions we have had bills drafted and brought down hurriedly. I do not know why that is the case with this bill, but I will bet you-

speechtext: Hurriedly? Five years?

speechtext: How many?

speechtext: Five years.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext: And still there will be amendments brought down by the government, and it may even change that word "preservation" back to "protection".

speechtext: You can't trust them.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
No, you cannot.
Another matter I would like to draw to the minister's attention deals with pollution control. I notice among the responsibilities of the minister the responsibility for drawing up objectives and standards relating to environmental quality and to control pollution. That is in the revision of section 5. If one sets that against the mandate stipulated in the Speech from the Throne in 1970, to protect the biosphere, is the establishment of objectives and standards going to be the only role of the Minister of the Environment?
Government Organization
Will the minister be able to enforce the standards or will he get other departments to enforce them? How will the minister be sure that other departments will follow the objectives and standards set down by his department unless he has the whip hand in this particular bill? I understand from his little gesture that he is not too sure. If the role is simply to establish objectives and standards, I wonder where in this bill or in the original act the minister finds the power to enforce conformity to those objectives and standards.
In almost every bill that we consider we have a "shall" or a "may". Here we have a "may". Clause 6(2) of the bill reads as follows:
For the purposes of carrying out his duties and functions related to environmental quality, the Minister of the Environment may, by order, with the approval of the governor in council, establish guidelines for use by departments, boards and agencies of the Government of Canada-
This is a "may" proposition. Will the minister introduce an amendment to change that "may" to "shall", or is he content with the "may"? Is this to be a wishy-washy department that only has the power to exhort the other departments, and will it produce guidelines only if it feels so inclined? It may-it is not mandatory that they should do so.
In 1970 we learned that a ministry of the environment would be established with a mandate for the protection of the biosphere. That cannot be done with a "may"; the only way it can be done is with a "shall".
I must therefore ask how effective these guidelines are likely to be even if they are produced? Was this "may" intended or was it a slip of the drafter's pen? In French it is "peut". There is no obligation involved to draw up these guidelines. I do not know whether we have created a department without teeth, or have taken the teeth out of a department that was already there. It would take a longer comparison than is permitted to us of the original bill of 1970 with the bill before us today to find out whether those components of it which relate to the environment are stronger or whether they are the same and have merely been transferred. Are there any "shalls" in the 1970 bill?
I see, Mr. Speaker, that the Department of Transport is responsible for marine pollution. In committee 1 asked the minister if he could produce for me a list of locations of all the pollution-fighting equipment on the west coast. He was good enough to do that, and the result was a thick print-out from a computer under the name NEELS, I think it was, giving an indication of the placement of clean-up material for oil spills. The equipment listed, however, was in the hands of Esso, to clear up their particular oil spills around their off-loading docks, or of Shell or of Texaco. Despite the size of the document it was apparent to me that the extent of the government's foresight to deal with any pollution that happened on the east coast or the west coast was practically nil.
This government will not even assist those people doing research into clean-up procedures. There are two of these in my area, one related to woodchips. It is a very good system if

January 23, 1979
Government Organization
the woodchips are dry and, of course, woodchips go up and down the coast all the time. It would require a command structure to divert those woodchips over to the spilled area. They would absorb, they would agglomerate, and they could be set on fire. Of course it will require research to prove that- I do not know whether it would be the Department of Transport or the Department of Fisheries and the Environment- and to permit some authority to divert some of the woodchips coming down the coast to the oil spill area and to see that they are spilled.
The problem of spilling them, getting them out over the oil spill, has not been solved. I do not know whether you would pull up the sides. It has been suggested that a helicopter could probably blow a lot of them off, and that is probably right. One system that is being worked on is a grab bucket which would be lowered from the helicopter. These things do not grow on apple trees, Mr. Speaker; they have to be developed, but no assistance is being given to the man who is working on this. The Department of National Defence is prepared to take him out and allow a small research project to be carried on within a boom in a contained area. He has appealed to the Department of Fisheries and the Environment and to the Department of Transport, but he does not really know where to go.
These are real problems, Mr. Speaker. Petroleum products are being shipped up and down our coast every day of the year, and one day there is going to be a disaster. There is no question in my mind about that, and we are not ready for it despite the NEELS.
Another type of experiment is being carried out. Someone has developed a form of sponge-polyurethane I think it is- which is specially treated to absorb oil and resist water. I have seen the experiment on a small scale. It is called "grab oil", which is self-explanatory. The product looks like sponge rubber. Within a matter of seconds of being dropped into a substance with oil floating on top, it sucks up the oil, leaves the water, and then the oil can be recovered. It can absorb 17 to 20 times its weight in oil, depending on the specific gravity of the oil. There is, of course, the question of storage of this sop-up equipment and the developer has put his mind to this question. It should probably be stored in Comox where it could readily be picked up and then dropped on site. The material is fairly bulky, so a system of compacting it would have to be developed to ensure easy storage.
These experiments are worthwhile, Mr. Speaker. The two people who have developed them to this point are anxious for assistance in research but they are not getting any, except from the Department of National Defence. If the cost of such research is compared to the cost of cleaning up of the Amoco Cadiz, the Torry Canyon, the Arrow and Van Lean spills, obviously it would be money well spent.
The minister may be charged with drawing up guidelines or establishing norms and procedures, but he is not charged with implementing any of this. This is the great defect that I see in the creation of the Department of the Environment as set out in the bill. 1 do not even see that it would be charged with

responsibility of ensuring that research takes place in the areas to which I have referred. There is no indication in the bill that it is reponsible for research into the standards it sets, and for making sure that the standards are reasonable.
Another question is the standards in respect to domestic storage of nuclear waste, and I stress that, Mr. Speaker- domestic storage of nuclear waste. Are they to be developed in the Department of the Environment and submitted to the Atomic Energy Control Board for application? Does the Department of the Environment supervise the implementation of these criteria for the disposal of nuclear waste, or is that left entirely in the hands of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources? Does the Department of the Environment have any responsibility for the environmental aspects of the external sales of CANDU reactors and the disposal of the nuclear waste generated from those sales? I suspect not. Therefore I feel that the Department of the Environment as developed here, set up and put in charge of this particular minister, is not really a very effective department.
We also heard criticisms of the application by Norlands Petroleum for exploration drilling in Lancaster Sound. The hearings were held in October and November of last year. These criticisms were legitimately made by those who participated in hearings at Pond Inlet. Is the minister going to put to rest the misgivings of those concerned interveners? Why must financial limitations be placed on those who wish to intervene? Why were not some of the hearings held here in Ottawa? Must all interveners go into the area of Pond Inlet for their interventions?
The short notice and failure to disclose full information within the time limits are another criticism. Is the minister going to satisfy those who have levelled these criticisms? I am sure the minister has had letters from a variety of sources outlining, specifying, and setting forth these various criticisms.
There was also the pervasive feeling, and this is a strange one, among those who intervened that the applicant was going to be allowed to drill in any event unless the interveners could prove that the application would endanger the environment. Surely this is a reversal of the process of natural justice. Is it not? Surely the applicant should have to prove that his activities are not going to damage the environment. These are answers the Minister of the Environment will have to give. If not, he will certainly be asked these questions in committee.
The whole principle needs to be restated that the applicant must be required to prove that his activity will not offend any of the laws of Canada or any of the criteria, standards, or objectives set up by the ministry of the environment, and not the other way around. The interveners should not have to prove that the applicant may or might. Damage is always possible. Both sides recognize this. The burden of proof lies with the applicant.
There is another criticism. It became apparent during those hearings that some government agencies wished to appear during the second hearings. However, they could do so only if
January 23, 1979

invited by the Department of the Environment. Why should they not be permitted to appear as other interveners? Possibly it is because it would destroy some of the mystique, the powers of the government, if a government department had the effrontery to interfere.
I would also like to speak about the Oceanographic Institute at Pat Bay and Bedford. I think this also falls within the Ministry of Fisheries. It could create problems. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to take part in this debate
Government Organization
tonight on Bill C-35. As far as the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. LeBlanc) and I are concerned, this is a very important step forward.
I tried to listen very carefully to the points made by the various speakers in the debate today. I will note them very carefully. Undoubtedly I will not be able to answer all the questions raised by the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich (Mr. Munro). As he knows, we will deal with those in committee in the greatest of detail. If I were to deal in detail with the questions he and other members raised tonight, there would be no time left.
Eight years ago the government affirmed its concern for Canada's physical environment when it proposed to parliament the creation of the Department of the Environment. That department brought together for the first time concern with the quality of the environment and concern with the sound management of our renewable resources. Today, in the light of eight years' experience, and looking ahead to the problems and the opportunities of the 1980s, the government is seeking the creation of separate departments for the environment and fisheries and oceans. This change is, first and foremost, a recognition that each of these areas is of such importance to the present and future well-being of Canadians as to require the full-time dedication of a minister of the Crown and of a distinct department.
My colleague responsible for fisheries will tell the House what has been done and what awaits to be done in the exciting areas of fisheries and the oceans. Therefore, despite a temptation as a British Columbian to speak of the great prospects for the salmon fishery, I will not speak about fisheries other than to assure hon. members that my colleague and I, and our respective departments, will continue to work in closest collaboration because of the inseparability of the fisheries resource and the health of the physical environment at large.
The past year since the decision in principle was taken to separate fisheries and environment has been an opportunity for us to think afresh about the mandate, the orientation, and the responsibility of an environment department at the federal level. We have done so in recognition of the changing environmental problems which face this nation, of the greatly enhanced capacity of the provinces to deal with the environmental concerns within their jurisdictions, of the changing nature of federal-provincial relations, of the finite nature of so many of our resources, and of the growing recognition of the need to have our economic development take place in a manner consistent with a sound physical environment. Thus, what this bill proposes is not just the division of a department but the creation of a new department of the environment to provide leadership which will enable this country to meet the environmental challenges of tomorrow.
The bill before the House would charge the minister of the environment with the formidable and positive task of preserving and enhancing the quality of the Canadian environment for the benefit of present and future generations. Three goals

Government Organization
spring from this task. First, through his knowledge of the physical environment, and his authorities, the minister has an important responsibility for contributing to the quality of life of all Canadians, based on a society in harmony with its environment; second, he is expected to safeguard man's health and property from harmful substances and environmental changes, whether natural or man-made; third, the minister must encourage resource productivity through the conservation and wise use of renewable resources-our forests, our water, our wildlife.
There is often a perception of dichotomy, of opposition between protection of the environment and development, Canada is a growing and developing country. We need jobs for our people and we need many-though not all-of the things which jobs create. But development is not indiscriminate growth. Development must, by definition, respect the base on which it is built, since otherwise it cannot be sustained.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I see it as my responsibility to contribute to the environmentally sound development of this country; the three objectives I have stated come together in harmony around that theme. Without sustained productivity and use of our natural resources there is no development possible for this country. I am thus concerned with the use of our resources, now and in the future.
My responsibility is to help make the difficult choices, which can only be done on the basis of sound knowledge of the present and longer-term effects of man's activities on his physical environment. That knowledge lies to a considerable extent within Environment Canada, and the good judgment which comes from such knowledge will be brought to bear on all the decisions of government. The Department of the Environment will thus contribute to the economic development objectives of this government and of this country. It is the repository of data and knowledge which others fail to take into account at their peril.
An environment department with a strong environmental policy is an essential element in the whole social and economic well-being of Canada and Canadians, and it is to be strengthened by this bill.
How is this to come about? Mr. Speaker, you will see in the bill that the Minister of the Environment, in addition to his existing responsibilities, will be empowered to co-ordinate "the policies and programs of the Government of Canada respecting the preservation and enhancement of the quality of the natural environment." More specifically, we are setting forth in legislation, rather than cabinet decision, that an early assessment must be made of all new federal projects, programs and activities for their potential adverse effects on the quality of the environment. The federal environmental assessment review office, whose executive chairman reports directly to me, now has panels set up on some 20 federal projects to scrutinize their environmental acceptability. With the passage of this legislation, I propose to re-examine the environmental assessment and review process to ensure that it continues to play an ever more effective role in screening federal activities.

Earlier in this debate the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander) said, in effect, that proposed drilling in Arctic waters would not be subject to environmental assessment under this bill.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
I listened to what the hon. gentleman said. I can assure the House that this is not the case. Federal projects are considered to be those which are initiated by federal departments and agencies, those for which federal funds are solicited, and those involving federal lands or waters. Since the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development would bear responsibility for seabed drilling in Arctic waters, any such proposals are subject to the review process.
It is evident that actions and regulatory activities undertaken by other departments and agencies can have a profound effect, for better or for worse, on the environment. Emissions from motor vehicles, for example, which account for half our urban air pollution, are controlled by means of the Motor Vehicle Safety Act, administered by the Department of Transport. The Canada Shipping Act governs discharges from vessels. I do not propose to take that over; perhaps that is what the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich was suggesting. The Atomic Energy Control Board regulates the nuclear industry.
A section of the proposed act empowers the Minister of the Environment, on the basis of his knowledge of the physical environment, to establish, with the approval of the governor in council, environmental guidelines for use by other departments, boards and agencies of the government. This constitutes a second important lever for ensuring that the actions of the federal government itself, and of those whose activities it regulates, are taken in an environmentally responsible way.
Not all our forward-looking activity, by any means, is dependent on the new bill, but because it is relevant to a new department looking ahead to the eighties I would like to tell the House that we are re-examining in a very fundamental way our whole pollution control strategy. This examination involves a rethinking of the federal role and responsibility in environmental protection, taking into account provincial capabilities, the strong desire expressed by all jurisdictions to avoid unnecessary and costly duplication of work at the federal and provincial levels, and the requirement to look to the socioeconomic impact of all pollution control proposals. My officials will begin to discuss the new strategy with their provincial counterparts in the next few months. Depending on the outcome of those discussions, which I am confident will be welcomed by the provinces, I expect to propose to my cabinet colleagues a number of significant amendments to the legislation on which our environmental protection activity depends.
Let me say a word about federal-provincial relations in the environmental field. While the federal power is clear in respect of certain of our environmental and resource activities, such as the management of fisheries, and uncontested in others on the ground of common sense, such as the provision of weather
January 23, 1979

services, a large part of the work in which we are engaged falls into that difficult area of shared or even unclear jurisdiction.
The government is determined to work out with the provinces the appropriate goals for the two levels of government in the environmental field. This re-examination should be unfettered by past positions and differences or by narrow interpretations of jurisdictional rights. We are prepared to examine what is the best division of responsibilities for today's needs, based on the criteria of common sense and economy. The basic question should be who can best do the job needed to ensure the health of the Canadian environment for the present and future enjoyment of all Canadians, and if the answer is that both the federal and provincial governments must do a particular job in shared fashion, as is often the case, we shall work out an equitable sharing of that work. I am confident that my provincial counterparts welcome this approach and will make it work.
Were time to permit, I would like to draw the attention of hon. members to many other activities of my department. I think particularly of the work of the Canadian Forestry Service, on which I had occasion to comment at some length last November 24 during the budget debate. The Canadian Forestry Service is one of the oldest and most renowned components of the Canadian government. Because of the importance 1 attach to the federal role in forestry I have set out new directions for the service so that it can make a direct and essential contribution to the economic development and sound environmental management of the forest resource. It is therefore very much a part of the new approach which the new department of the environment will be taking as it faces the challenges of the decade ahead.
The bill before us reaffirms the government's commitment to the preservation and enhancement of environmental quality in its broadest sense. It gives the minister of the environment a clear mandate to provide leadership and direction on environmental matters within the federal structure. I am happy to accept this challenge, and I hope this bill will receive speedy passage.
Early in his remarks the hon. member for Esquimalt-Saanich talked about forestry disasters. I would like him to spell out those disasters. He talked about research in forestry. I am very committed to research in forestry. If the hon. member were to examine the record he would find that not one of the research establishments across the country has been touched. We have six regional laboratories across the country. There is one very near Victoria, as the hon. member knows. There is one in Edmonton and another in Sault Ste Marie. There is one in Quebec city, one in Fredericton and another in St. John's, Research has not been touched.

system. We know where every piece of equipment in this country is. We know where every piece of equipment in the United States is. There is no country in the world which really has the wherewithal to handle a major disaster.
The hon. member talked about the Amoco Cadiz and the disaster involving that 153,000 ton tanker. There is no country in the world which singularly has the capability to handle that kind of oil spill. With the talent and equipment that we have in Canada we are in as good a position as any country in the world to handle major disasters, things with which I have been concerned since I have taken the job of Minister of State for the Environment. subtopic: GOVERNMENT ORGANIZATION ACT, 1978 DEPARTMENTS AND AGENCIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-35 may be called in short the Government Organization Act, 1978. As we all know, no doubt, from listening to a good deal of the debate today, it has ten parts. I wish to make some remarks on the first three parts which deal with the new department of fisheries and oceans. I am really glad that finally the minister got around to doing this, something for which we have been asking for a long time and something which, as I recall, the government had promised in 1974, namely, the establishment of a separate department of fisheries.
The second part of the bill deals with the establishment of the fisheries and oceans research advisory council. I should like to say, as did my colleague, the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Faour), that there is nothing wrong with changing the title to read the establishment of the fisheries and oceans research advisory council. It is a good thing. It is a realignment of what has been done in the past in this field. Perhaps I am naive in this because fishermen are a small minority of the total population in my riding, nevertheless they constitute one-industry communities, that is, fishing communities. Fine and decent people have to live off this hazardous occupation. Naturally such a body should be primarily dominated by scientific people.
Obviously the minister has agreed to become involved in more consultation with the fishermen to some degree. But I find it difficult to understand that the fishermen's unions or co-operatives on either coast are not represented in the 24 people who will comprise this advisory council. Also it is difficult to understand that clause 2 of the bill contains no room for fishermen from these organizations, or independent fishermen as such.
The two coasts of Canada are as different as night and day. The only common elements are the word "fishery" and the species or genus of fish. The minister should give more consideration to this fact and consult again with the fishermen. There must be some way of establishing a revolving membership as far as west coast and east coast fishermen are concerned, so that they can see the process scientists must go through when making terribly important decisions.
One does not have to know very much about any industry to realize that a basic principle of management is administration. A basic principle in the management of the fishing industry, of course, is scientific administration. The input of biologists and others is terribly important in order for us to realize the potential of certain areas, and to ensure the conservation practices of the department are carried out based upon the best available scientific evidence. It is not sufficient to have intermediaries or to send out pamphlets to fishermen and their
Government Organization
organizations. They should be part and parcel of the research advisory council, even though they are a minority and do not have any scientific expertise. Certainly they are the best people to become involved, rather than just the officials of the department.
The Minister of State for the Environment (Mr. Marchand) referred heatedly to the division which is taking place. He feels that he will have a new mandate. Perhaps I am an amateur, but I recognize how terribly important this division is. The minister alluded to the fact that there must be close co-operation between him and the proposed minister of fisheries and oceans. As I understand it, from a pollution point of view, inland waters and fisheries will remain under the control of the Minister of State for the Environment. The minister should use his power directly, in so far as he can, and indirectly on the international joint commission between Canada and the United States, in order to clean up the inland waters of Canada as quickly as possible, particularly the Great Lakes.
We must remember how the pollution of the Great Lakes affects fishermen on the east coast. Recently these fishermen have told me that pollution from the Great Lakes is flowing into the Northumberland Strait. This is a very serious handicap to the quantity and quality of fish they are able to catch. I do not know if this is true respecting the Gulf of St. Lawrence, but I imagine that its waters would be affected by pollution in the St. Lawrence. Certainly our inland waters should be watched very closely. Not only should these waters be monitored, but they should receive the attention of the Minister of State for the Environment so that the fisheries industry can develop to its fullest potential.
As far as the proposed department of fisheries and oceans is concerned, I mention in passing that my party was in favour of its creation. I do not know if the Tories were in favour of it in 1974, but 1 presume they were. It has been a little over two years since the 200-mile limit was set up. The establishment of this department is better late than never. The minister is being given a mandate to zero in more radically on the existent potential of the east and west coasts.
I have had difficulty with the minister concerning some matters, and I still have qualms about vessel insurance for fishermen and so on. He has assured me that in the final analysis I will be satisfied. 1 hope he is correct. The fishermen in my area are concerned about the change in the vessel insurance scheme, that perhaps its effectiveness will be somewhat diminished by putting it into private hands. I realize the minister has other options available to him. I hope he deals with this subject when he participates in this debate.
There are other areas which will be disputed concerning the management of fish stock and the licensing procedure. These matters were referred to by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse). The fishermen in Cape Breton realize that perhaps one cause of the depletion of the lobster fishery in Richmond is the existence of the causeway on the Canso Strait. Those who are more active on a regular lifetime basis in the lobster industry are being approached in an attempt to protect the depletion of their resource. The government is

January 23, 1979
Government Organization
tightening up or freezing licences in order to restrict the occasional or casual fisherman. Many fishermen feel the department has a moral obligation to buy back these licences at a fair price, since they were purchased in the past by independent fishermen, with the consent of the department. One must remember the money these independent fishermen invested.
I realize the questions I have raised this evening are not easy ones. I sympathize with those people who have become involved in the fishing industry on a part-time basis along with holding down other jobs. Now they find themselves faced with a change in circumstance. I am not saying that the policy is a bad one. Perhaps it will be a good one in the long run and will protect the lobster industry. But I feel everything possible should be done to buy back these licences and to make an arrangement to reimburse to some degree the fishermen who have invested in equipment and licences.
I am not saying that the minister and the department have not attempted to do somehing. I am just saying I have the feeling, from talking to the fishermen, that they have not gone far enough in this regard. I realize the minister has to operate within a budget, like the minister of every other department, but it is only in recent years that his budget has been growing fast enough, especially with the establishment of the 200-mile limit and with everyone beginning to see the great potential.
Having made that kind of constructive criticism, I want to pay the minister a compliment. It is not usual for members of the opposition to pay compliments to the people in power or to those in the official opposition when they do good things. By and large I think we are pretty fiery about some things, particularly about the way the Atlantic region has been treated by successive governments of this country. I have in mind particularly my own area, Cape Breton.
Let me say to the minister that, generally, I do not hesitate to say that I think he has begun to take on the large corporations in the Atlantic region, although I disagree with him in certain aspects.
Some of my fishermen at times get really bitchy about the whole licensing procedure. I hope that word is parliamentary, and I assume it is as it is in the dictionary. They also get upset about other policies, and I will be talking about the snow-crab licensing policy in a little while. Having talked to the offshore fisherman it is my opinion that this minister has attempted to take on the large corporations. Even a minister of fisheries in Nova Scotia, a very likeable and personable man, wrote a pretty strong and severe letter to me intimating that 1 was too much on the side of the federal government in this issue. This is a social and philosophical issue and I compliment the minister for his efforts, even though I disagree with him as to detail of policy.

speechtext: Hear, hear!
