speechtext:
As a member of a socialist party who believes, like every other member of any socialist party in the western world, that we must have a strong private sector, I realize we

are living in a mechanized economy in which large corporations concentrate control in an effort to maximize profits. Let us take for example National Sea Products and the Nickerson Company. Their operations are carried on by very fine human beings, but the policies they advocate in the long run do not benefit 80 per cent of the fisherman in the inshore fisheries in the Atlantic region. I think the minister has grasped this situation. The policies they advocate benefit the large corporation. What is involved is not just private enterprise but, in addition, government controls. These fellows want to grow big and fast, and I refer to National Sea Products and Nickerson. They want a heck of a lot, and I almost used an unclerical word. They want government money before we are even sure that the fish stocks are being conserved and built up. Probably this is the nature of human beings. Certainly it seems to be the nature of private enterprise, which is concerned primarily with maximum profits.
These people do not take into consideration the social consequences which are so crucial in the Atlantic region, as pointed out by the hon. member for Humber-St George's-St. Barbe. There are about 2,000 part-time, full-time and occasional fishermen in Cape Breton. Most of them are part-time fisherman, just as the hon. member from Newfoundland suggested in respect of Newfoundlanders this afternoon.
The federal government has a primary responsibility in fisheries under the BNA Act, but there is room for diversity of views and for greater consultation with the provinces. I suggest there is perhaps room for a greater provincial share of responsibility in some aspects of fisheries. Nevertheless, it seems to me that in the long run, if not in the short run, the best economic policy would be for the federal government to pursue basic principles of management of fisheries in the Atlantic region.
The basic social principle is one of protecting inshore fisheries. This is particularly true when you remember that it is the inshore fisheries in the maritime provinces that support 80 per cent of our fisheries, helping to keep these communities together. I am not suggesting all these communities can be kept together.
There is a very strong economic argument or point of view that we should centralize in order to facilitate the large factory ships. To some extent they are taking species not ordinarily caught by our Canadian fleet. You can get too much of what appears to be a good thing from the point of view of the large corporations in that they are increasing production and making the industry more capital intensive, yet in the long run this creates all kinds of severe economic and social problems.
I have been observing the situation and have written to the Combines Investigation Branch to determine whether the Nickerson takeover of National Sea Products was within the law. I know the minister could not do much about this, but it is disheartening to know how long it takes before getting an answer from that branch. They keep telling me this is of high priority, and something about which they are concerned. They use a lot of technical language which does not give me any idea how the matter is progressing. It seems to me that the dominant policy and concern has to be in respect of inshore
January 23, 1979

fisheries, without suggesting that the offshore fisheries are not important to the Atlantic region and to the nation. There is a question of emphasis and a question of philosophy and social principle involved. In the long run I would say the matter of economics is important. I commend the minister for keeping these fellows at bay. I have in mind those "too big, too fast" people, as I am wont to call them.
Recently we held a seminar of fishermen on Cape Breton Island. About 120 fishermen attended. As I said earlier, we have about 2,000 fishermen on Cape Breton Island, in about 110 communities. I thought I should mention that during this debate because the fishing industry has been very vital in the past and I expect will continue to play a vital role in the future, even though coal is the most important resource in Cape Breton, with the steel industry also being a vital entity.
I have pleaded the case of the inshore fisheries rather successfully with Devco, and they are beginning to see the great potential for fishing in that area. Last year, for example, they had landing figures of 56,000 metric tons which had a total value of $18 million. That may not seem like a lot to some, but when one looks at the figures for the province of Quebec, which had a total landed value last year of $29 million, it is quite significant for a small island like Cape Breton. It reinforces the idea that there might be potential development which could be tapped in a very serious way, with the co-operation of the federal and provincial governments, Devco and, of course, the fishermen.
One of the comments at our seminar made by the maritime director for the federal fisheries department, Mr. Doug Johnston, was to tell the fishermen that they will not get participation in the industry unless they come together. It has become fashionable, for many reasons, to be anti-union, mostly because people are leaning more to the right and because some unions have abused their powers.
There were two priests in Nova Scotia some 50 years ago who had a philosophy, which I inherited, because I was brought up in the tradition of the St. Francis Xavier Antigon-ish movement, respecting co-operatives. They were considered to be communists, just as we in the New Democratic Party are considered by the extreme right-wingers as being proponents of the communist line. These men went about organizing the fishermen and, as a result, many co-operatives were formed.
I personally lean strongly toward that philosophy, but after 50 years there are still many fishermen who are not organized into co-operatives and who do not want to be. I think that this is primarily the jurisdiction of the provincial government, the whole question of unions and the civil aspects of the BNA Act, and the minister should use every occasion in this regard. I know that he has said this publicly, and that he does not want to come out for unions because a province such as Nova Scotia may set up such an association and pour $40,000 or $50,000 into it. To my mind this is the old situation of company unionism. It is very difficult to unionize independent fishermen, but if they are not going to form co-operatives, I believe this is their best alternative. It will give them a united voice in dealing with the ministry of fisheries at the federal level and
Government Organization
having some control over the future management and development of the fishing industry.
Having made that point, I am not saying there should be compulsory unionism, but that there is something wrong with the philosophy of the provincial governments of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. It does not mean that they have to join a union, but at least give them the right. After all, this is a democratic society, and if the fishermen decide to follow this course of action, then surely the provincial governments have the moral responsibility at least to say, "Look, we can no longer bar these people from the right to organize." Perhaps I am overdoing the point, but I believe it is important because there is no other way whereby we will get development in the fishing industry in the Atlantic region, both inshore and offshore, unless there is some kind of organization.
The snowcrab landing industry on the gulf side of Cape Breton has the potential of becoming the third fishery delicacy category in Nova Scotia after the scallop industry, which I believe has a value of approximately $58 million, and the lobster industry which has a value of $26 million. In Cape Breton last year there were 66 so-called exploratory licences given out for the snowcrab fishery. The figure for landing which was given to me at the seminar was $1.7 million.
This year there are 200 fishermen looking for a licence. We cannot have everybody rushing in, and there must be some form of restricted entry. It seems to me that the most equitable way of giving out these licences would be either through individual quotas or changing seasons. There could even be a modification of the size limit. There is here a potential source of discord between the fishermen and the federal Department of Fisheries if this is not handled well.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that I think all elements of the industry should co-operate. It is not a contradiction to say that I want unionization or that I do not want the big corporations to take over. One cannot talk out of both sides of his mouth and say that he wants monopoly or semimonopoly conditions, and at the same time argue for free enterprise, but that is what some are doing when they say that they want these large corporations to concentrate to such a degree that they will be able to control the pricing, marketing, and production of the fisheries in the Atlantic regions. Mr. Speaker, I call it ten o'clock.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-SALARY PAID TO NEWSREADER KNOWLTON NASH
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-SALARY PAID TO NEWSREADER KNOWLTON NASH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 8, 1978, during question period in the House I put a question to the Secretary of State (Mr. Roberts) on the reported salary of Knowlton Nash, the reader of the 11 p.m. National News on the CBC. First of all I asked how much the salary paid to Mr. Nash was, and I did not get an answer. I hope to get an answer tonight, Mr. Speaker.
I asked how the salary, rumoured to be $85,000 to $90,000 per year, could be justified. Even if we were not in a time of austerity-even if we were not trying to fight inflation at this time when workers everywhere are being asked to hold back on salary demands-such a salary for reading a 15 or 20-minute newscast five times a week, would be incredible. The Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) does not make $85,000 or $90,000 per year. That is more than just about anybody in Canada makes. That the management, the hierarchy of the CBC, should be so far removed from reality, is cause for great concern.
This is only the latest incident in the long history of the CBC's overspending and mismanagement that has strained the patience of the Canadian public, and of members of this parliament. I am calling for a complete public inquiry, financial and otherwise, into the operations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I am very curious about what they do with the half billion dollars they are gifted with each year by the Canadian taxpayer.
The CBC have made much of the fact that they are going to get $71 million less than they asked for, as a result of the latest budgetary cutbacks. The CBC asked for $593 million and are only going to get $522 million. Why, when they get so much of the taxpayers' money, are they virtually indistinguishable from the other Canadian network, that is, CTV?
I believe that when corporations, or people, get money from the public purse they should be accountable for that money. To me, what appears to be government policy of handing out taxpayers' money to any person or corporation, without accountability, is preposterous. It leads to bad management, inefficient operation, and a waste of money that is intolerable.
I think it would be worthwhile, Mr. Speaker, to read into the record portions of the Broadcasting Act of 1968, which was agreed to by all parties in the House of Commons.
Section 3(b) reads as follows:
the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians so as to safeguard, enrich and strengthen the cultural, political, social and economic fabric of Canada;
That broadcasting policy continues, as set out in section 3(d) as follows:
the programming provided by the Canadian broadcasting system should be varied and comprehensive and should provide reasonable, balanced opportunity for the expression of differing views on matters of public concern, and the programming provided by each broadcaster should be of high standard, using predominantly Canadian creative and other resources;
The act goes on to say in section 3(g):
the national broadcasting service should

(i) be a balanced service of information, enlightenment and entertainment for
people of different ages, interests and tastes covering the whole range of
programming in fair proportion,
I am sure that every Canadian would agree with the aims of the act, Mr. Speaker, but I also know that the CBC has been found wanting. As the member of parliament for the constituency of Burnaby-Seymour, I want the very best in broadcasting, Canadian and foreign. 1 believe that Canadians want their own national broadcasting service-as the CBC was set up to be-but Canadians are no longer willing to support a nationwide system of self-styled executives in broadloomed offices, safe in their lifetime jobs.
What we need in Canada is a quantum leap in communications. Quebec had its "quiet revolution." We need a quiet revolution in Canadian broadcasting. I am not talking about some timorous half-hour cooking show or some boring situation series. I mean a renaissance of information, of participation, of bringing out the best of the many cultures that make up Canada-a climate for interest in things other than the purely commercial.
I have had much communication, as we all have, with Canadians on this subject. They want programs that the entire family can watch at any hour of the day or night, without obscenity, and without the kind of senseless violence that has come to permeate the television screen.
So important is broadcasting, I believe, that we could change for the better the future of Canada, through better communication. I do not exaggerate when I say the future of Canada may depend on this.
Besides an inquiry and a complete reorganization of the CBC, I believe there should be a major inquiry into the entire broadcasting system in Canada. How far have broadcasting stations been allowed to stray from the promises they made when they were granted their licences? Why has broadcasting, which could be such a powerful medium for service, for understanding, for entertainment, deteriorated to the point where a broadcasting licence is now regarded simply as a licence to make money, in many cases?
The technology of the satellite age will have a widening impact in the next ten years, in television and in education. Broadcasting in Canada needs a whole new long look. In spite of the Canadian content regulations, broadcasters have not succeeded in giving talented Canadians an outlet. The attitude seems to be to throw on any old thing that is remotely Canadian, just to fulfill the requirement.
I must say in a number of instances the quality and integrity of the budgets of Crown corporations are insufficient to provide to the government and parliament information by which Crown corporations may be controlled and their performance assessed. As a member of the broadcasting committee since 1974, I can say that I and other members have received insufficient information on the budget of the CBC.
May I ask again tonight the question and now be told the exact salary of Knowlton Nash? I trust we will also learn of
January 23, 1979

the fringe benefits as well. Will the Department of the Secretary of State now take steps to ensure that the CBC uses its money more judiciously? Will that department use moral suasion and ensure that funds granted to the CBC, to wit, more than $500 million a year, will be used for furthering the broadcasting policy agreed to by all members of the House in 1967 and 1968?

As hon. members know, Mr. Speaker, parliament established the mandate of the CBC and annually votes the amount of money within which the corporation must operate in seeking to fulfil this mandate. It is the responsibility of the corporation and its board of directors to manage its operations in such a way as to maximize the carrying out of this parliamentary mandate. In its day to day operations the CBC must compete in the industry in which it operates, and therefore must pay competitive rates in order to get the people it requires.
In the specific case of those matters relating to the appointment of Knowlton Nash to his new position, they are the subject of arbitration arising out of a grievance filed by the Canadian Union of Public Employees, and it would be improper for the CBC to comment on any aspect of Mr. Nash's appointment. This position is reinforced by the fact that the parties agreed that the arbitration proceedings would be held in camera, and the CBC has not received a copy of the arbitration report to this date.

Mr. Speaker, I rise in the hope of obtaining a more satisfactory answer to a question I posed to the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Abbott) on December 11 regarding the use of social insurance numbers as identification devices in the processing of Canada Savings Bonds.
The question was based on a letter written by the previous minister of national revenue to a constituent in St. Boniface in which he stated that persons who did not wish to disclose their SIN when purchasing bonds could "invent a number themselves, or a number would be assigned to them by the bank. The then minister of national revenue cited a press report of an interview with a Bank of Canada information officer named Ralph Hager, now retired, as the source of this policy statement. I am tabling this press report along with the letter in which the former minister makes reference to it. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) has already acknowledged the confusion of the above suggestion regarding SIN.
I believe this haphazard from bottom to top type of decision making, particularly when it is concerned with a?. area as sensitive as the use and possible misuse of social insurance numbers, to be scandalous in the extreme. It reflects this government's total lack of interest, and ambivalence toward the question of social insurance numbers, and the government's lack of concern for the privacy of our citizens.
Adjournment Debate
The government and its agencies have claimed in defence of the use of the SIN that it has not been requested for any reason other than to promote administrative efficiency. This is a dangerous misunderstanding of the situation, in my view, because it begs the question of just how far the use of SIN as identification devices can be justified by the need for bureaucratic efficiency.
The Bank of Canada needs an identification device to identify holders of Canada Savings Bonds. Many other government departments and agencies, as well as countless private organizations, are making use of numbers or identification devices in order to carry out their responsibilities. Efficiency demands that some form of numerical device be used in many areas, but while recognizing the importance of efficiency we must not forget the basic right of every citizen to personal privacy. I am not at all convinced that the social insurance number is the only method of identification available, but I am convinced that it must not become so.
My alarm about the future use of social insurance numbers is well founded. Already we have seen the use of these numbers extend far beyond the social security application specified in the 1964 legislation. Five government departments are using the SIN as the prime identifier or registration number in their information banks. The Public Service Commission uses the social insurance number for all its files. Confidential information on every employee is theoretically at the fingertips of everyone knowing the relevant social insurance number. Moreover, this knowledge is progressively easier to obtain, given the widespread use of the number.
Use of the SIN by numerous government agencies and Crown corporations has also been documented. The Canadian Transport Commission uses it to identify domestic charter passengers; the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation uses these numbers for employee identification; they are required for access to all files of the Canadian Penitentiary Service and the National Parole Service. Provincial governments are also using the social insurance number with apparent impunity. School children are being registered under the SIN in Ontario and Saskatchewan-even newborn babies in Prince Edward Island. If this were not enough, the private use of social insurance numbers by corporations and other organizations has been expanding at an alarming rate.
All of this is being done in the name of efficiency, and in a very arbitrary fashion, I suspect. I suggest that the SIN is not the only identification device available to the governments and private organizations presently using it. In my view it is irresponsible to resort to using the number when no other method of identification has been tried.
The SIN was not intended to become a multi-purpose ID number, and it should not become one. Widespread use of it threatens the individual privacy of Canadians. Yet, judging from the evidence I have submitted, as well as that put forward by several of my hon. friends on this side, the question of personal privacy in the face of the pervasive use of social

insurance numbers has not even been considered by this government. Efficiency seems to be its only concern. This attitude is alarming because it can be applied to any of the various departments. We have reason to speculate that whenever objections to the disclosure of one's social insurance number are raised, the government will dredge up the efficiency argument. Individual privacy will thus be reduced, chip by chip, in favour of efficiency, so-called.
Recently, on November 2 of last year, the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) said the government was drawing up guidelines to prevent misuse of SIN as universal identification cards. However, he stated that there is no deadline for doing this, and he gave no undertaking that the government would stop the use of the numbers outside the social service and taxation areas for which they were originally designed.
Most federal cabinet ministers foresee greater use of social insurance numbers. The Minister of Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) has stated on several occasions that there will be more and more use of the SIN. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Buchanan) has encouraged the use of the SIN. Going back to October 25, 1972, the Toronto Globe and Mail reported that our Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) indicated his personal belief that at some point in the future, compulsory-I repeat, compulsory-identity cards will be required of all Canadians.
Thus, the policy of the present government is more numerical control over the private citizen. This is absolutely contrary to the policy of a Progressive Conservative government-

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Hare) does not seem to understand certain aspects of this matter. I shall try to explain them to him.
First of all, he should realize that the sales of Canada Savings Bonds does not come under the jurisdiction of the Department of Revenue. These savings bonds are sold through the Bank of Canada. The bank has records containing the names of millions of purchasers of these bonds and is now in the process of computerizing these records. Since it is necessary to use an identification number to distinguish among the various bondholders and since this number will be needed for the computerized records, the officials of my department have been informed that the bank will use the social insurance number of the purchaser if the purchaser provides it. Otherwise, it will have to program the computer so that it will produce a unique number which will be used for this purpose.

The letter mentioned by the hon. member perhaps gave the impression that the purchaser would be able to provide the identification number of his choice. Of course, this procedure cannot be used since it would be quite possible for two or more purchasers to choose the same number, which would cause bookkeeping problems.
Recently, when the hon. member asked a question of the Acting Prime Minister in the House, he seemed to be confusing the cashing of the bonds with the charging of interest on these bonds. This may explain how he could confuse the matter of choosing a unique identification number for bookkeeping purposes by the Bank of Canada and the requirement to provide a valid social insurance number when cashing in the coupons.
The interest on Canada Savings Bonds is taxable under the Income Tax Act. This law also provides that social insurance numbers should be used to identify income tax forms and records. Moreover, it stipulates that when the interest coupons on the bonds are cashed in, a social insurance number must be recorded in the report on the interest paid by the cashing agent, generally a chartered bank in that case. This bank must prepare and send to the department some particular forms called T-3 or TP-3, depending on which level of government is involved, either federal or provincial.
If the taxpayer does not provide his social insurance number, the cashing agent must, under the law, withhold 25 per cent of the interest due. This sum is credited to the taxpayer's account, and if it is not used to pay an outstanding balance in taxes, he will get a refund when he fills his income tax return form for the current year.
I admit that all this may be somewhat technical and difficult to understand, but I can assure the hon. member that the whole operation does not violate in any way the citizens' rights.
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-FRANCOPHONE SUMMIT MEETING____________

Mr. Speaker, my question to the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) last December 18 arose as a result of reports that France refuses to attend any meeting of Francophone nations that excludes Quebec as a participating state. Apparently France, with its customary realism, does not accept or recognize Canada as a Francophone state.
All I can say is that it is too bad that our government and our major political leaders are not as realistic. We have had more than a decade of effort on the part of the Liberal government to turn Canada into a Francophone country. The results, to my mind, are frightening, in terms of national unity at least.

Apart from the Official Languages Act, we have seen the labelling legislation and the broadcasting policy designed to spread two languages across the land, whether or not they are wanted or needed. I would suggest the metric system is also being forced on this country at great cost and dislocation to many parts of the economy, for the same reason. We have even heard of French being used in answering consular telephones in Australia.
Of course the Liberal party is not the only party striving to give Canada a French accent. We have the efforts of the Progressive Conservative party to change our ways in this very chamber to correspond to the ways of France. I refer, of course, to the practice of clapping which was introduced by the Progressive Conservatives in this chamber last fall. It is interesting to note where this practice originated, and in this connection I should like to refer to the Montreal Gazette issue of Wednesday, December 15, 1976, in which appeared the story about the new national assembly which was elected there on November 15 of that year.
Apparently the new government in the province of Quebec introduced the idea that members should clap in the chamber of the national assembly, instead of thumping their desks as had been the custom previously. The article states:
The applause itself marked another change in style introduced by the Parti Quebecois, complementing a slow conversion from British to French parliamentary tradition.
Government MNAs clapped their hands to exhibit approval instead of thumping their desk tops, a practice adopted from France's national assembly whose name was appropriated by the Quebec legislature under the Union Nationale government of Daniel Johnson.
My concern is that the efforts of the Government of Canada to turn our nation into a country which would entitle it to attend a Francophone summit or Commonwealth conference would be akin to the old saw about the great surgeon who was asked about the results of one of his heroic procedures, to which he replied that of course the operation was a great success but unfortunately the patient died.
I therefore call upon the government to cease its efforts to change the ways of our country by trying to force feed its misconceived ideas about language and culture on an unwilling population.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of a Francophone summit meeting has indeed been shortly discussed during the conversations which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had in Paris with the President of the French Republic on December 8. As a matter of fact, this is an idea
Adjournment Debate
which was put forward over ten years ago by various African heads of states, including President Senghor of Senegal, an idea in which Canada and our Prime Minister have shown a great deal of interest. We feel that periodical meetings of heads of states or of leaders of fully or partly Francophone countries could foster better understanding among nations and make a real contribution in the search for solutions to international problems.
For that matter, Mr. Speaker, such an organization could in a way establish itself on the model of what was formerly known as the British Commonwealth and which has become simply the Commonwealth, which has served for many years as an international forum for the exchange of ideas among representatives of nations from the four corners of the world.
As for participation in a future Francophone summit, most countries share the position of Canada that each individual country should decide its mode of participation. Since important international issues would be raised at these meetings, Canada feels that the head of the Canadian government should take part in them.
On the other hand, France has clearly indicated that it could hardly participate in a summit from which Quebec would be excluded. France's position is not to exclude Canada, but it concerns our form of participation. On that point, it is obvious that our stands are incompatible. As for the form and content of a possible Francophone summit, it would seem essential that there be a wide consensus among the countries which might be interested before this project gets off the ground.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, we believe that this idea should be well thought out until the conditions that would allow for a successful Francophone summit are met. It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that the hon. member for Palliser (Mr. Schumacher) took this opportunity to voice to the House his antipathy and his hostility towards the French fact, but he is at least honest enough to say clearly and out loud what unfortunately several, not all but several, of his former colleagues think to themselves.

January 23, 1979

Your Excellency,
It is a great pleasure to extend to you, as you assume the office of Governor General, an assurance of the warmest good will of the Government, Parliament and people of Canada, In their name, may I ask that your first official act be to convey to Her Majesty, the Queen of Canada, a message expressing our loyalty and affection.

You are taking on the responsibilities of your high office at a challenging time for Canada, and a no less challenging time for its Governor General.
The scope of that challenge is the true measure of both the trust which the citizens of this country place in your hands, and of their lively confidence that you will be a wise and helpful steward of that trust.
At first glance, the prerogatives of the Sovereign and of Her representative in our parliamentary democracy seem startlingly simple: the right to be consulted, to encourage and to warn.
But on closer examination, what a wealth of potential for furthering the common good lies hidden in those simple words. What great opportunities for helping to create and define the evolving spirit of a dynamic nation can be discovered in that simple description of your office.
Canadians look to their Governor General as a person of stature, broad experience, and commitment to Canada, a person whose insight and breadth of vision can lead us all to a deeper appreciation of the values we share, the greatness of character we have inherited, and the destiny which can be ours if together we will it into reality.
Above all, we look to you to help lead us toward a keener awareness of the strength and value of our country, its people, its system of government, and its rich history of achievement. Upon that awareness can be built an even stronger Canada, with a renewed commitment to individual liberty, and shared opportunity.
{English}
You and your office are therefore a potent symbol of our unity and united purpose, and a symbol as well of the many streams of humanity which flow together into a uniquely Canadian experience.
Your commitment to public service, demonstrated as a Member of Parliament and as Premier of Manitoba, together with your thoughtful perspective on this country's problems and opportunities, eminently suit you for the role you are about to play.
Canadians have two special reasons to look to your term of office with more than the usual sense of anticipation. For the first time, the meaning of Canada will be expressed in a vice-regal voice tinged with a truly western accent.
We will hear about ourselves and our potential from the vantage point of one who identifies strongly with the open spaces and open people of the west-with their history of pioneering struggle to set down new roots in a new land. We will be hearing from a man who shares the pride of the Canadian west in its achievements, and the enthusiasm of western Canadians to tackle the problems of further development.
The second reason why we look upon your appointment as an event of historic importance is that, again for the first time, our first family will represent those millions of Canadians who trace their ancestry to countries other than Great Britain or France.
I share with countless others the well-founded hope that you will help lead all Canadians toward a deeper understanding of the richness and variety of our cultural heritage.
Personally, I look forward to my weekly meetings with you, because I know that a man who has known the joys and anguish of elective office will offer unusually well-informed advice.
On behalf of Canadians everywhere, I thank you for accepting the responsibilities which are now yours.
I wish to acknowledge as well the great debt of gratitude which we owe to Her Excellency, Mrs. Schreyer. We are all mindful of the fact that, in supporting your decision, she has herself willingly assumed an equal share of your official responsibilities, and an equal share of the resulting personal sacrifices.
To both of you, and to your children, we extend our best wishes for many happy years in Ottawa.
May all your days in your new home be filled with joy and peace. May duty be a pleasure. May God grant you satisfaction and fulfilment in the service of Canada.

subtopic: REPLY OF HIS EXCELLENCY THE GOVERNOR GENERAL TO THE ADDRESS OF THE PRIME MINISTER

speechtext:
Prime Minister,
I shall be honoured to carry to our Gracious Sovereign Queen Elizabeth II the tidings of loyalty and affection which you have entrusted to me on behalf of the Canadian people. In accepting this task, I convey to you my determination to carry out those responsibilities which she has entrusted to me on Her behalf.
My wife, Lily, and I are grateful for the welcome and for the kind words you have expressed to us. We shall always cherish them.

I realize I am accepting a responsibility and honour that has been accorded to only four other Canadians. I am following in distinguished steps, and not only theirs. My lifetime has spanned the decades from Lord Tweedsmuir to the Right Honourable Jules Leger. Those who served Her Majesty as Governor General in those years brought great and varied distinction to the office. I pray I am equal to this task, to this office and to this time.
All previous Governors General of Canada have symbolized for Canadians that stability and continuity of national life and institutions so necessary to any cohesive civilization. This need is all the greater in a society whose very essence is the diversity of its culture and the vastness of its geography, in the society that is our Canada. The task is clear: the task is real.

As I undertake it, I have already received thousands of messages of good will and support. My wife and I are encouraged by them. In the coming days and weeks we shall seek continued support from all who care about Canada-and they are legion, whether Canada for them is the land of their ancestors or the land of their choice. All these Canadians, this blessedly overwhelming majority in every province of Canada, will provide, with the help of providence, a yearning for the preservation of one Canada that will not be frustrated, a wisdom that will not be denied. Canada remains our transcending objective. The reasons, both in our spiritual and in our material well-being, are self-evident.
[ Translation]
It is with profound sadness that I note a minority view that does not acknowledge that in an enlightened federal Canada there is scope for the fullest expression of cultural and linguistic heritage. The preservation of our country's economic capacities and its weight in the councils of the world surely need not be sacrificed in order to achieve a greater measure of freedom. The freedoms we now share and cherish are equal to the best of countries on this planet. They are surpassed by none. They can be greater still. It is not necessary to break the bonds of our common history to do so.
For, whatever our origins, wherever we live in Canada, we have all contributed to the building of this country. Each Canadian, though unable truly to realize the greatness of the collective achievement that is unfolding, is playing his part. I would recall the eloquence of my predecessor, the Right Honourable Jules Leger, in this regard:
This might be said of generations of honest and unassuming people of Quebec, who have always been faithful to their homeland, having no other and seeking no other. Men of the land, men of the sea, of the church and of business, I pay them warm tribute for without their courage and tenacity the Canada we know today would not exist. They lived their lives along the shores of the mighty river that bore their ancestors and shaped their destiny.
The faith of our history is borne in these, the words of a man of wisdom and patriotism and exemplary courage, who well understands the importance of French-speaking Canadians to our broadening mosaic. I can only concur with these words. They capture the pride we share in our diverse origins and the recognition we share that in those origins lies the source of our striving toward the larger horizons of spiritual tolerance and material progress that come with a larger unity.

To this, I must add the bringing to this new land, first to the Atlantic and then the central provinces, much more than a century ago, of British parliamentary institutions and English common law and jurisprudence. The stability and magnanimity of the English-speaking peoples who came to these shores is another great stream of our history.
But in the confluence of these two great streams that have shaped our Canadian character must surely be seen the force of two additional tributaries adding to the majestic flow of our culture and civilization. One is, of course, our brothers and sisters, Inuit and Indian. They constitute a group of Canadians who are caught between their traditional ways and contemporary opportunities. Whichever course they choose will bring grave difficulties for those involved, for those working with them.
The other stream is that multiplicity of groups that chose Canada or whose ancestors chose Canada. I know their contribution to Canada. The ethnic mosaic has made for a more colourful and interesting Canadian way of life. Those who make up this mosaic share the goal of retaining the clarity of that mosaic, for in the clarity of their cultural distinctiveness lies its beauty.
There is also shared experience-the shared experience of adversity. Whether we think of the earliest habitants, or the coureurs des bois; of the United Empire Loyalists of Upper Canada or the Maritimes; whether we think of the Scottish fur traders of the northwest, or that incredibly small pocket of English and French-speaking settlers known as the Red River Colony at the Fort Garry and the St. Boniface Missions; whether it be the Icelandic-speaking settlers after 1870 or German-speaking Mennonites and Hutterites at the same
time-one the victim of nature, the other of human persecution; whether it be central European immigrants pulling their belongings across the untilled Prairies by sheer physical exertion or the frustration of the Indian and Metis fearing the loss of hunting grounds, and the coming of malnutrition, pestilence and disease, in all this history one word stands out-adversity. Our problems of today are as nothing. To succumb to pessimism, to allow fragmentation, to accept the shattering of the Canadian mosaic is to break faith with all who endured so much to build so well what we have today.
What we have today can be secured if we remind ourselves of some self-evident truths spoken by a Canadian of venerable years but still active among us. He said, the truth is that Confederation was conceived of by men of two different but equally rich communities. Bilingualism and multiculturalism are facts of Canadian life, they cannot be avoided nor should they, for they are assets, not liabilities; positive factors, not negative ones.
But there is also a need to speak for all of Canada. It is what we share that allows us the richness of our diversity and we need to remind ourselves of this whenever we become preoccupied with our differences. As we shape present policies we preserve the necessary options for future generations of all Canadians.
What I believe many people earnestly hope for is not merely the toleration of our differences, but the realization that to be a good Canadian each of us must be true to his or her heritage. This noble sentiment was eloquently expressed by Sir Wilfrid Laurier when he said:
Three years ago when in England, I visited one of those models of Gothic architecture, which the hand of genius, guided by an unerring faith, had moulded into an harmonious whole. This cathedral was made of granite, oak and marble. It is the image of the nation I wish to see Canada become. For here, I want the granite to remain the granite, the oak to remain the oak, the marble to remain the marble. Out of these elements I would build a nation great among the nations of the world.

What Sir Wilfrid Laurier clearly believed, what he shared with others, with Sir John A. Macdonald, with Brown, with Blake, with Sir George-fitienne Cartier, what they share with my predecessors and with me, is that a diverse society in a vast land can experience a broadening of the mind and spirit-a magnanimity of the soul. Their idealistic dream has become almost the full reality. We need but work together to avoid slipping backward toward the fragmentation of intolerance.

Today I say with the deepest conviction that we can do this. Within 50 years, a moment in the sweep of history, our Canada has gone from aloofness to tolerance, and beyond tolerance to respect for, indeed a deep desire for, the retention of the differentiations of our heritage and culture.
But the need for this vigilance, for this effort, is incumbent upon us all and particularly on whoever holds this office.

It is said that Sir Wilfrid Laurier testified to Lord Grey's work as Governor General, that he gave his whole heart and his whole soul to Canada. If those words could ever in truth be applied to me, as a third generation Canadian from the wheatfields of the west, by my contemporary Prime Minister-only then could I feel that I have kept faith with all who love our country. One Canada, whole, undivided, the benefits of our pluralism intact.
